categories.title: Build the Network
categories.description: Build the complete air-gapped network, one system at a time: the domain controllers, DNS, domain time, STIG measurement and Group Policy hardening, the two-tier PKI, DHCP, tiered administration, the Linux repository, the logging pipeline (collector, protected archive, and analysis), the workstation fleet, Windows updates, the living inventory, business services, and proven recovery. Follow the courses in order, from 1.1 to 1.19.

lessons.title: Design the forest, domain and OUs
lessons.summary: Before promoting anything, decide the structure every later part inherits. The forest is the security boundary, the domain is a replication and administrative boundary, OUs exist for delegation and Group Policy, and the directory's control plane is Tier 0. This lesson records those decisions from the Active Directory design reference, so the build that follows has a reason for each choice.
objectives: Explain why the forest, not the domain, is the security boundary.
Plan OUs for delegation and Group Policy rather than replication.
Identify the systems and accounts that make up Tier 0.
recap: One forest is the security boundary; one domain keeps replication simple.
OUs serve delegation and Group Policy; part 5 builds them.
Tier 0 is the directory's control plane, administered only from the seats part 8 builds.
lessons.next: Lesson 2 gives every system a purpose and places both controllers on VLAN 10.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Use an isolated Windows Server practice environment. The network's routing and default-deny segmentation are in place, with the access control list (ACL) register that records every permitted path.

Provision each part's systems when the part begins: two Windows Server virtual machines for SBD-DC01 (10.0.10.10) and SBD-DC02 (10.0.10.11) on different hosts, then the PKI systems (part 6), the DHCP server (part 7) and the administration seats (part 8).

Work at each server's VM console with an authorized administrator account until part 8 builds AdminJumpBox01; after that, administration happens from the Tier 0 seats.

Have an approved connected system and the removable-media procedure for bringing downloaded DISA content and other software into the lab.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The addresses and names below continue the training example. Match every change to your own address plan. This network has no internet DNS dependency: names resolve on the domain controllers, and nothing is forwarded outside.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Active Directory Domain Services keeps one directory of users, computers and groups that every domain member trusts, and the domain controllers hold and replicate it. Everything later in this course, from DNS to tiered administration, depends on the decisions made here.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Microsoft calls the forest the security and administrative boundary for everything in it: whoever controls one domain controller can reach every domain in the forest. Prefer a single forest unless a hard isolation or autonomy requirement forces another. This network uses one forest, sbd.test.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: A domain is a replication and administrative boundary, not a security boundary. Add domains only for replication, administration or policy reasons, never for isolation. The domain name is also a DNS name, so part 2 settles the namespace with this decision.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Design OUs for two purposes only, delegating administration and applying Group Policy, not replication. Sketch the top level now (Tier 0, Admin, Servers, Workstations and Users) and plan to redirect the default containers; part 5 builds the structure and links the DISA baselines to it.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: List what controls the directory: both domain controllers, the PKI built in part 6, and the accounts, groups and workstations that manage them. That is Tier 0. Administer it only from devices of equal or higher trust; part 8 builds those seats. Write each decision and the authority behind it in the design record.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
Get-ComputerInfo | Select-Object CsName, WindowsProductName, OsBuildNumber
Get-NetIPConfiguration | Select-Object InterfaceAlias, IPv4Address, IPv4DefaultGateway
# Nothing is promoted yet: save this starting state beside the design record.

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: Both planned controllers are standalone Windows Server systems with static addresses on VLAN 10, and no directory exists yet. The design record names one forest, one domain, the OU plan and the Tier 0 inventory, each with its reason and source.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Save the design record: the forest and domain decision, the OU plan, the Tier 0 inventory, and the authority behind each choice.

lessons.title: Give every system a purpose
lessons.summary: Record the starting configuration, place both controllers on their own segment, and explain what they will do. Start by understanding the services you are about to build and where they will live. Then record the names, addresses, and dependencies for two controllers in the same domain.
objectives: Place both domain controllers on VLAN 10 with their final names and static addresses.
Point SBD-DC02 at SBD-DC01 for DNS so it can find the domain at promotion.
Record the starting configuration and the intended time source before anything is promoted.
recap: Record the starting configuration, place both controllers on their own segment, and explain what they will do.
The two names and static addresses match your plan, the default gateway is 10.0.10.1, and SBD-DC02 lists 10.0.10.10 as its DNS server.
Renaming a domain controller later is a separate procedure with its own steps and checks.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Use new, patched Windows Server installations (Desktop Experience) with console access and the required administrative credentials. Connect both to VLAN 10, the segment reserved for domain controllers; nothing else joins it. Obtain approved media and updates through your established offline process.

sections.heading: Step 2

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Use an isolated Windows Server practice environment. The network's routing and default-deny segmentation are in place, with the access control list (ACL) register that records every permitted path.

Provision each part's systems when the part begins: two Windows Server virtual machines for SBD-DC01 (10.0.10.10) and SBD-DC02 (10.0.10.11) on different hosts, then the PKI systems (part 6), the DHCP server (part 7) and the administration seats (part 8).

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The addresses and names below continue the training example. Match every change to your own address plan. This network has no internet DNS dependency: names resolve on the domain controllers, and nothing is forwarded outside.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: In an elevated PowerShell window on either controller, run DCDiag against SBD-DC01 and then SBD-DC02. Its default tests cover connectivity, advertising, replication, SYSVOL, services, and role holders. Read each test's result, not just the last line.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Run the replication summary, then list each controller's inbound partners. Expect recent successful attempts from DC01 to DC02 and from DC02 to DC01, with no failures. If an error appears right after promotion, wait a few minutes and run the checks again; record any error that persists.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: List both controllers with their global catalog status, then the operations master (FSMO) role holders; in this build SBD-DC01 holds all five. Confirm SYSVOL and NETLOGON are shared on SBD-DC02 as well. If they are not, its first SYSVOL replication has not finished.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: On each controller, confirm the network profile is DomainAuthenticated and that the effective firewall policy is on for the Domain, Private, and Public profiles and blocks unsolicited inbound connections. A controller that reports the Public or Private profile is applying a different rule set than the domain expects; find out why before you rely on it.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
dcdiag /s:SBD-DC01
dcdiag /s:SBD-DC02
repadmin /replsummary
repadmin /showrepl *
Get-ADDomainController -Filter * | Select-Object HostName, IsGlobalCatalog
netdom query fsmo
Get-SmbShare -Name SYSVOL,NETLOGON -CimSession SBD-DC02
Get-NetConnectionProfile | Select-Object InterfaceAlias, NetworkCategory
Get-NetFirewallProfile -PolicyStore ActiveStore |
  Select-Object Name, Enabled, DefaultInboundAction

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: Each controller passes its DCDiag tests, or every failure has a recorded cause. Replication shows recent successful attempts in both directions and no failures. Both controllers are global catalogs, SBD-DC01 holds the five operations master roles, SYSVOL and NETLOGON are shared on both, and each controller reports the DomainAuthenticated profile with every firewall profile on and inbound blocked by default. Save output with host, time, and interpretation; a command that ran is not a pass.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: For each controller, record the DCDiag results, replication status in both directions, the roles it holds, its network profile and firewall state, the test time, and what the results establish.

lessons.title: Map names to the network
lessons.summary: Domain Name System (DNS) turns names into addresses, and for Active Directory it does one more job: it tells every domain member where its domain controllers are. Start from the working directory build, learn what DNS answers and what it doesn't, set each controller's DNS client order, and record which server owns each name and how a client finds it.
objectives: Explain how DNS lets a domain member find a domain controller, and what a DNS answer does not prove.
Set each domain controller's DNS client order and point domain members only at internal DNS.
Inventory the existing sbd.test and _msdcs zones without creating duplicates.
Document the forwarding and recursion decision for an air-gapped network.
recap: DNS finds domain controllers through SRV records; it never checks a password.
Each controller lists its partner, then itself; members list both controllers only.
The AD zones are inventoried, not recreated, and the delegation warning is expected.
The forwarding and recursion decision is written down first.
The DNS design follows the government and vendor guidelines; record each deviation, such as the test-only sbd.test name.
lessons.next: Lesson 8 turns this plan into AD-integrated forward and reverse zones.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Use an isolated Windows Server practice environment. The network's routing and default-deny segmentation are in place, with the access control list (ACL) register that records every permitted path.

Provision each part's systems when the part begins: two Windows Server virtual machines for SBD-DC01 (10.0.10.10) and SBD-DC02 (10.0.10.11) on different hosts, then the PKI systems (part 6), the DHCP server (part 7) and the administration seats (part 8).

Work at each server's VM console with an authorized administrator account until part 8 builds AdminJumpBox01; after that, administration happens from the Tier 0 seats.

Have an approved connected system and the removable-media procedure for bringing downloaded DISA content and other software into the lab.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The addresses and names below continue the training example. Match every change to your own address plan. This network has no internet DNS dependency: names resolve on the domain controllers, and nothing is forwarded outside.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Start with what DNS answers. An A record maps a host name to an IPv4 address (AAAA maps to IPv6), so SBD-DC01.sbd.test resolves to 10.0.10.10. Service (SRV) records advertise which servers offer a service: a domain member asks for _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.sbd.test, resolves a listed controller's name, contacts it, and only then authenticates. DNS never checks a password, and it works on an isolated network with no internet access.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Record the domain, each subnet, both DNS addresses, and the owner of each service name. Keep host records and service aliases distinguishable.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: On each domain controller, confirm the DNS Server service is installed and running; an address typed into a network adapter installs nothing. Then open DNS Manager and review the sbd.test and _msdcs.sbd.test zones that promotion created, without creating duplicates. The DNS delegation warning from part 1's promotion is expected: no parent zone exists above the isolated .test namespace, so no action is needed.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Set each controller's DNS client order. Promotion pointed SBD-DC01 at itself (the loopback address, 127.0.0.1) while it was the only controller, and SBD-DC02 pointed at SBD-DC01 so it could find the domain. Run the replication summary first; once replication succeeds in both directions, list the partner controller first and the loopback address second on each, and never an outside resolver. Domain members list both controllers; a public resolver is not an alternate for this environment.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: Confirm the network's service-path register permits DNS: every networked system to both domain controllers on TCP and UDP 53 (rule F01 in the System Hub). A member has to find a controller before any Kerberos, LDAP, or Group Policy traffic can start.

sections.heading: Step 6
sections.body: Decide whether any separate internal namespace needs a conditional forwarder. With no recursive dependencies, document a no-recursion design; do not add internet forwarders or delete every root hint as a shortcut.

sections.heading: Step 7
sections.body: The DNS design reference sets the baseline this part follows. Name the forest as a subdomain of a domain you have registered, or use ICANN's reserved .internal; never use .local or a single-label name. sbd.test uses a name reserved for testing, which suits a practice network only. Store the zones in Active Directory with secure-only updates, run at least two DNS servers on different hosts, and forward only to an approved upstream; this air-gapped network forwards nothing. The authorities differ in places: NIST SP 800-81r3 prefers dedicated DNS servers and advises against signing internal zones unless a policy requires it, while Microsoft runs DNS on domain controllers and the DISA DNS STIG requires DNSSEC, with NSEC3 on internal zones. Record which rule your build follows, and why.

sections.body:

repadmin /replsummary
Get-DnsClientServerAddress -AddressFamily IPv4 -CimSession SBD-DC01,SBD-DC02
# After replication succeeds both ways (adapter name varies):
Set-DnsClientServerAddress -CimSession SBD-DC01 -InterfaceAlias Ethernet `
  -ServerAddresses 10.0.10.11,127.0.0.1
Set-DnsClientServerAddress -CimSession SBD-DC02 -InterfaceAlias Ethernet `
  -ServerAddresses 10.0.10.10,127.0.0.1
Get-DnsClientServerAddress -AddressFamily IPv4 -CimSession SBD-DC01,SBD-DC02
Get-DnsServerZone -ComputerName SBD-DC01

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: Both controllers run the DNS Server service and, once replication succeeds both ways, list their partner first and the loopback address second. Members list both controllers only; the AD zones, the recursion decision, and the register rows that permit DNS are recorded.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Save the address/name worksheet, each controller's DNS client order and the reason for it, and the initial zone inventory before changing anything else.

lessons.title: Configure forward and reverse zones
lessons.summary: A zone holds the records for one part of the namespace. Forward lookup answers where a name lives. Reverse lookup answers which name is assigned to an address. AD integration lets the directory replicate zone data between the selected DNS servers.
objectives: Confirm sbd.test is AD-integrated with the intended replication scope.
Create a secure, AD-integrated reverse zone for 10.0.10.0/24.
Explain how zone data moves between the two DNS hosts.
recap: Forward and reverse zones are AD-integrated with a deliberate replication scope.
Dynamic updates are secure-only.
Zone transfers stay restricted; directory replication moves the data.
lessons.next: Lesson 9 builds the record set your services will actually use.

lessons.title: Create and maintain service records
lessons.summary: Build a small, intentional record set. A host record identifies a machine; an alias provides a stable service name without making that alias a separate server.
objectives: Distinguish host records (A and PTR) from service aliases (CNAME).

recap: Host records identify machines; aliases provide stable service names.
pki.sbd.test is reserved for the internal publication host, never the offline root.

sections.heading: Step 1

sections.heading: Step 2

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: For a service alias, use New Alias (CNAME) and enter the intended fully qualified host. sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Set the record lifetime to the operational plan, record static ownership, and remove only records confirmed obsolete. An alias cannot coexist with other record types at the same name.

lessons.title: Prove resolution and directory discovery
lessons.summary: Test each server explicitly before testing client fallback. A successful cached answer does not prove that both DNS servers hold the right records, and a correct DNS answer proves neither a successful sign-in nor access to a protected resource.
objectives: Query each DNS server explicitly instead of trusting cached answers.
Verify the locator (SRV) records that let clients discover domain controllers.
Run a controlled failover test and record the result.
Optionally capture a locator query and compare it with the model's packet card.
recap: Both resolvers answer the host and SRV queries correctly.
dcdiag and repadmin confirm DNS and replication health, with isolated-design findings explained.
The failover test is documented with times, not just a passing screenshot.
lessons.next: Lesson 11 practices finding and recording a DNS fault, one layer at a time.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Use an isolated Windows Server practice environment. The network's routing and default-deny segmentation are in place, with the access control list (ACL) register that records every permitted path.

Provision each part's systems when the part begins: two Windows Server virtual machines for SBD-DC01 (10.0.10.10) and SBD-DC02 (10.0.10.11) on different hosts, then the PKI systems (part 6), the DHCP server (part 7) and the administration seats (part 8).

Work at each server's VM console with an authorized administrator account until part 8 builds AdminJumpBox01; after that, administration happens from the Tier 0 seats.

Have an approved connected system and the removable-media procedure for bringing downloaded DISA content and other software into the lab.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The addresses and names below continue the training example. Match every change to your own address plan. This network has no internet DNS dependency: names resolve on the domain controllers, and nothing is forwarded outside.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: From a domain client or either controller, query each DNS server by address for both controllers' host records, so each result tells you which server answered. Expect SBD-DC01.sbd.test at 10.0.10.10 and SBD-DC02.sbd.test at 10.0.10.11 from both servers.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Query the domain controller locator service (SRV) records against both servers. These records let a client discover domain controllers; an ordinary host lookup does not prove discovery works, and a locator answer does not by itself prove that every listed controller is reachable.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Run the DNS diagnostics against every domain controller, then the replication summary. Classify root-hint, forwarder, and delegation findings against the documented isolated design instead of treating them as faults, and investigate everything else.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: During an approved lab test, make one DNS server unavailable to the test client and verify resolution through the other. Restore connectivity and repeat for the opposite server. Do not interrupt shared production services for this exercise.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: Optional: see the locator query on the wire. On SBD-DC02, in an elevated PowerShell window, capture port 53 with Packet Monitor (pktmon), which is built into Windows Server, while you query SBD-DC01, so the request crosses the network. Expect a query from 10.0.10.11 to 10.0.10.10 on UDP port 53 and an answer naming both controllers on port 389. Read the text file, or open the .pcapng file in a packet analyzer such as Wireshark, and keep the capture with your evidence; it holds only the traffic the filter allowed.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
foreach ($server in '10.0.10.10','10.0.10.11') {
  Write-Output "DNS server: $server"
  Resolve-DnsName 'SBD-DC01.sbd.test' -Type A -Server $server
  Resolve-DnsName 'SBD-DC02.sbd.test' -Type A -Server $server
  Resolve-DnsName '_ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.sbd.test' -Type SRV -Server $server
}
dcdiag /test:DNS /e /v
repadmin /replsummary
# Optional, on SBD-DC02: capture the locator query
New-Item -ItemType Directory C:\Evidence -Force
pktmon filter remove
pktmon filter add DNS -p 53
pktmon start --capture --comp nics --pkt-size 0 --file-name C:\Evidence\dc-locator.etl
Resolve-DnsName '_ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.sbd.test' -Type SRV -Server 10.0.10.10
pktmon stop
pktmon etl2txt C:\Evidence\dc-locator.etl --out C:\Evidence\dc-locator.txt
pktmon etl2pcap C:\Evidence\dc-locator.etl --out C:\Evidence\dc-locator.pcapng
pktmon filter remove

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: Both DNS servers return both controllers' host records and the domain controller locator records, the DCDiag DNS findings are explained, replication is healthy, and the client still resolves internal names when either resolver is unavailable. If you ran the capture, it shows the query from 10.0.10.11 and the answer from 10.0.10.10.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep paired lookup results with the server queried, the DCDiag and replication output, the failover test record with start, restore, and final verification times, any capture file, and a short statement of what the results do and don't establish: DNS helps users find the identity service, but a correct answer proves nothing about authentication.

lessons.title: Plan the domain's time
lessons.summary: Every sign-in, log entry and certificate in this network depends on clocks that agree, and an air-gapped network has no internet time to lean on. Learn why time matters here and how the Windows Time hierarchy carries one clock from SBD-DC01 to every system, then write down the reference, the fallback and the service path you will hold the domain to.
objectives: Explain why Kerberos, log correlation, certificates and replication need clocks that agree.
Trace the Windows Time hierarchy from the forest root's PDC emulator to every member.
Record the reference, the fallback and the service path the domain's time is held to, and what verification must show.
recap: Kerberos fails past five minutes; small, stable offsets on every link show drift long before that.
One hierarchy: SBD-DC01, then SBD-DC02, then every member, with Linux servers pointed at both controllers.
The reference, its checks, the fallback and rule F09 are written down before anything changes.
The PDC emulator leads the hierarchy, and the air-gapped network records its missing upstream as a gap.
lessons.next: Lesson 13 makes SBD-DC01 the reliable source and takes the hypervisor out of both controllers' time.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Use an isolated Windows Server practice environment. The network's routing and default-deny segmentation are in place, with the access control list (ACL) register that records every permitted path.

Provision each part's systems when the part begins: two Windows Server virtual machines for SBD-DC01 (10.0.10.10) and SBD-DC02 (10.0.10.11) on different hosts, then the PKI systems (part 6), the DHCP server (part 7) and the administration seats (part 8).

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The addresses and names below continue the training example. Match every change to your own address plan. This network has no internet DNS dependency: names resolve on the domain controllers, and nothing is forwarded outside.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Start with why the clocks must agree. Kerberos refuses a request whose timestamp differs from the domain controller's clock by more than the domain's tolerance — five minutes by default — so drift turns into failed sign-ins and failed replication. The logging courses (1.3–1.5) line events up across systems by their timestamps, certificates from the part 6 PKI are valid only between two fixed times, and domain controllers need agreeing clocks to replicate accurately.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Learn the hierarchy that carries one clock everywhere. The PDC emulator of the forest root domain is at the top; every other domain controller takes its time from the PDC emulator, and every member server and workstation from the domain controller that authenticated it — the NT5DS client type every domain member uses by default. sbd.test is the forest's only domain, so SBD-DC01 is the top and SBD-DC02 follows it, and each Windows member's time arrives signed with its computer's Net Logon session key.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Face the air gap. With no internet or outside NTP server, SBD-DC01 serves time from its own clock and is the reference by declaration, so name an approved reference that never connects to this network, such as a GPS receiver's display, and write down who compares SBD-DC01 with it, when — after any restart, restore or revert of SBD-DC01 included — and how a correction is made and recorded. Record the fallback too: if SBD-DC01 is lost for long, SBD-DC02 eventually stops advertising as a time source, so the PDC emulator role moves to it and it becomes the source (lesson 16).

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Decide what verification will show. Every system should name the source the hierarchy gives it, and its measured offset from that source should be small and stay stable from one reading to the next. Five minutes is where Kerberos fails, not a target: an offset that grows or jumps is the warning to act on long before that.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: Confirm the service path. Rule F09 in the System Hub permits every domain member to both controllers on UDP 123, and each controller's inbound firewall rule for the Windows Time service accepts it; SBD-DC02's own requests to SBD-DC01 stay inside VLAN 10, where only the host firewalls see them. SBD-REPO01 (course 1.2) is not a domain member, so F09 does not list it yet; course 1.2 adds it.

sections.heading: Step 6
sections.body: The time design reference keeps the default Active Directory hierarchy: the forest-root PDC emulator, SBD-DC01, is the reliable source, and every other member follows the domain. Upstream counts differ by authority: CIS, NSA and CISA say at least two sources, Microsoft three or more, and RFC 8633 four or more; DoD systems must use USNO or another approved DoD source. This network is air-gapped and has no upstream, so record that as an accepted gap. Keep the Kerberos clock tolerance at 5 minutes, the default and the DISA requirement, and never let a virtualized domain controller take time from its host.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
Get-ADForest | Select-Object RootDomain, Domains       # sbd.test: the forest root and its only domain
Get-ADDomain | Select-Object PDCEmulator               # expected: SBD-DC01.sbd.test
# The domain's Kerberos tolerance, from the Default Domain Policy (expected: MaxClockSkew = 5, in minutes)
Select-String -Pattern MaxClockSkew -Path "\\sbd.test\SYSVOL\sbd.test\Policies\{31B2F340-016D-11D2-945F-00C04FB984F9}\MACHINE\Microsoft\Windows NT\SecEdit\GptTmpl.inf"
# Each controller's inbound UDP 123 rule, and where each takes its time today
Invoke-Command SBD-DC01,SBD-DC02 {
  Get-NetFirewallPortFilter -PolicyStore ActiveStore | Where-Object { $_.Protocol -eq 'UDP' -and $_.LocalPort -contains '123' } |
    Get-NetFirewallRule | Select-Object DisplayName, Direction, Enabled, Action
  w32tm /query /source }

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Use an isolated Windows Server practice environment. The network's routing and default-deny segmentation are in place, with the access control list (ACL) register that records every permitted path.

Provision each part's systems when the part begins: two Windows Server virtual machines for SBD-DC01 (10.0.10.10) and SBD-DC02 (10.0.10.11) on different hosts, then the PKI systems (part 6), the DHCP server (part 7) and the administration seats (part 8).

Work at each server's VM console with an authorized administrator account until part 8 builds AdminJumpBox01; after that, administration happens from the Tier 0 seats.

Have an approved connected system and the removable-media procedure for bringing downloaded DISA content and other software into the lab.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The addresses and names below continue the training example. Match every change to your own address plan. This network has no internet DNS dependency: names resolve on the domain controllers, and nothing is forwarded outside.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Confirm which domain controller holds the PDC emulator role — SBD-DC01 in this sample. The PDC emulator of the forest root domain sits at the top of the Windows Time hierarchy, so it is the one system you configure; everything else follows it.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Turn off the hypervisor's time synchronization for both controller VMs — SBD-DC01 on SBD-HV01 and SBD-DC02 on SBD-HV02 — so no host clock can silently override the PDC emulator. On Hyper-V that is the Time synchronization integration service; other hypervisors have an equivalent guest-tools setting, and some also set the guest clock after a resume or restore, so check those settings too. Inside each guest, w32tm /query /source must no longer name a hypervisor provider such as VM IC Time Synchronization Provider.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: On SBD-DC01, mark Windows Time as a reliable time source and restart the service. w32tm /config /reliable:yes writes AnnounceFlags 5 — always a time server (0x1) and always a reliable one (0x4) — in place of the automatic default, 10 (0x2 and 0x8). Leave the client type at NT5DS and add no manual peer: the forest root's PDC emulator has nothing above it, so it serves its own clock, and clients accept time from a server that synchronizes with nothing only because it is marked reliable.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Read what SBD-DC01 now advertises: source Local CMOS Clock, stratum 1, reference ID LOCL, and a root dispersion of 10 seconds — the default LocalClockDispersion for a local clock, which you leave alone (lesson 14 sets the Linux servers to accept it). Expect Time-Service warning 12, which says the forest root's PDC emulator has nothing above it and will act as the authoritative source: that is the designed state, so record it rather than fix it. nltest /dsgetdc:sbd.test /gtimeserv should return SBD-DC01 with the GTIMESERV flag, the reliable time server Net Logon now advertises.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: Run the first reference check with lesson 12's procedure: read the approved reference and SBD-DC01's clock at the same moment and record both. If they differ, correct SBD-DC01 by the measured difference (Set-Date -Adjust), never by typing a time from memory; Security event 4616 records the change, and your log records who made it and why.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
Get-ADDomain | Select-Object PDCEmulator   # expected: SBD-DC01.sbd.test
# Hyper-V example (other hypervisors have an equivalent setting). On SBD-HV01, and the same for SBD-DC02 on SBD-HV02:
Disable-VMIntegrationService -VMName SBD-DC01 -Name 'Time Synchronization'
Get-VMIntegrationService -VMName SBD-DC01 -Name 'Time Synchronization'   # Enabled: False
# On SBD-DC01 (the PDC emulator): the reliable source, serving its own clock
w32tm /config /reliable:yes /update
Restart-Service w32time
w32tm /query /configuration   # AnnounceFlags: 5 (Local); NtpClient Type: NT5DS (Local)
w32tm /query /source          # Local CMOS Clock
w32tm /query /status          # Stratum: 1, ReferenceId: LOCL, Root Dispersion: 10s
nltest /dsgetdc:sbd.test /gtimeserv   # DC: \\SBD-DC01.sbd.test; Flags include GTIMESERV
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='System'; ProviderName='Microsoft-Windows-Time-Service'; Id=12} -MaxEvents 1 |
  Format-List TimeCreated, Message
# Reference check: run this as you read the approved reference, and log both readings
Get-Date -Format 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.fff K'
# A correction is made only by the measured difference (example: SBD-DC01 two seconds slow):
# Set-Date -Adjust ([TimeSpan]::FromSeconds(2))

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: Hypervisor time synchronization is off for both controller VMs; SBD-DC01 reports AnnounceFlags 5 and NT5DS, source Local CMOS Clock, stratum 1 and reference LOCL; nltest returns it with the GTIMESERV flag; event 12 is recorded as expected; and the first reference check is logged with both readings and any correction.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Record the hypervisor setting for both controller VMs; SBD-DC01's configuration, source and status output; the nltest result; the event 12 text; and the first reference check — both readings, the difference, any correction with its 4616 event, who and when.

Provision each part's systems when the part begins: two Windows Server virtual machines for SBD-DC01 (10.0.10.10) and SBD-DC02 (10.0.10.11) on different hosts, then the PKI systems (part 6), the DHCP server (part 7) and the administration seats (part 8).

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The addresses and names below continue the training example. Match every change to your own address plan. This network has no internet DNS dependency: names resolve on the domain controllers, and nothing is forwarded outside.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Leave SBD-DC02 and every Windows member on the defaults: client type NT5DS, no manual peer list, and on SBD-DC02 the automatic AnnounceFlags 10, so it serves time without claiming to be the reliable source. w32tm /query /configuration shows each value with where it came from, (Local) or (Policy), and a system someone once set by hand returns with w32tm /config /syncfromflags:domhier /update and a restart of the service.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Keep time out of Group Policy. The Windows Time Service policies (Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > System > Windows Time Service) overwrite the local W32Time settings, so one that names an NTP server or sets the type to NTP pulls its targets off the hierarchy, and one that reaches SBD-DC01 overrides what makes it the source. Leave them Not Configured in every GPO, the STIG GPOs of parts 4–5 included: the STIGs expect members on the domain hierarchy, and their rule that the PDC emulator take time from an authorized external source becomes a recorded deviation in part 5's exception record.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Keep hypervisors out of every virtual machine's time, as you did for the controllers. When a later course builds a virtual machine, server or client — SBD-ADMIN-PC01, the Tier 2 seat on SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, included — turn off its hypervisor time synchronization, so the domain stays the only time authority: a Windows guest whose source reads VM IC Time Synchronization Provider, or any other hypervisor provider, is not following the domain.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Write the chrony configuration every Linux server uses. In /etc/chrony.conf (Red Hat Enterprise Linux family), remove every pool, server and sourcedir line, add server SBD-DC01.sbd.test iburst, server SBD-DC02.sbd.test iburst and maxdistance 16, and add no allow line, because these servers serve time to no one; then enable and restart chronyd. Domain-joined Linux servers authenticate with Kerberos through SSSD, so the same five-minute limit applies to them.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: Record why maxdistance 16 is this path's choice. Serving its own clock, SBD-DC01 advertises 10 seconds of root dispersion and SBD-DC02 a little more, while chrony refuses any source whose root distance is above 3 seconds by default, so without the line chronyc sources marks both controllers ^? (unusable). Sixteen seconds is the largest dispersion NTP defines, so the setting admits both controllers without admitting an unsynchronized source; the time itself is unsigned, which is why F09 limits it to the two controllers.

sections.heading: Step 6
sections.body: Apply the same file to every Linux server before its first domain join or package update: SBD-REPO01 (course 1.2), which is not domain-joined, so F09's member list leaves it out until course 1.2 adds it; SBD-SPLUNK01 (course 1.5) and SBD-WEB01 (course 1.11) when they are built; and SBD-NESSUS01 when course 1.10, coming soon, arrives. The offline root CA (part 6) is the one clock no network reaches: set it against the approved reference before each signing ceremony.

w32tm /query /configuration | Select-String '\(Policy\)'           # expected: no output

# The Linux chrony file, filed now (/etc/chrony.conf on the Red Hat Enterprise Linux family):

lessons.title: Prove the time chain
lessons.summary: A source you configured is a claim until every link answers to it. Read each system's source and status, measure its offsets and confirm they are small and stable, and keep the events and readings that let an assessor see the time chain for themselves.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Use an isolated Windows Server practice environment. The network's routing and default-deny segmentation are in place, with the access control list (ACL) register that records every permitted path.

Provision each part's systems when the part begins: two Windows Server virtual machines for SBD-DC01 (10.0.10.10) and SBD-DC02 (10.0.10.11) on different hosts, then the PKI systems (part 6), the DHCP server (part 7) and the administration seats (part 8).

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The addresses and names below continue the training example. Match every change to your own address plan. This network has no internet DNS dependency: names resolve on the domain controllers, and nothing is forwarded outside.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Read each link's source and status, from the top down. SBD-DC01 reports Local CMOS Clock at stratum 1, SBD-DC02 reports SBD-DC01.sbd.test at stratum 2, and a member reports a controller at stratum 2 or 3; a member showing Local CMOS Clock, Free-running System Clock or a hypervisor provider is not following the domain (lesson 16).

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Measure the controllers against each other: w32tm /monitor queries each controller in the domain, marks the PDC emulator, and reports every other controller's NTP offset from it. SBD-DC02's offset should be small and stay small from one reading to the next; the ICMP line is only a ping, and the NTP offset is the measurement.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Measure a member from the member itself: w32tm /stripchart against SBD-DC01 takes timed samples of its offset, and five that are small and close to one another show a member following its source. On a Linux server later, chronyc tracking reports the same measure as System time, beside a root dispersion of about 10 seconds that is the controllers' advertised error, not an offset.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Keep the Time-Service events that tell the chain's story, from the System log: 12 on SBD-DC01 (it serves as the authoritative source), 35 and 37 on the followers (a source chosen, valid time arriving), and 36, 129 and 142 as warnings worth an alert (no synchronization for a long period, no domain source found, a controller no longer advertising as a time source). Security event 4616 records every change to a clock, your reference corrections included; list these for the event set course 1.3 collects.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: Write the dated evidence record: for each system, its source, stratum and measured offsets, plus its time zone, since audit time stamps must be in UTC or carry their offset; then the event extracts, the reference check log, and who ran each check. Repeat the offset checks after any change to a controller.

lessons.title: Find the time fault and record the fix
lessons.summary: Time faults rarely look like time: a refused sign-in, a replication error, a certificate that is suddenly not yet valid. Measure the offset first, find where the hierarchy broke — a member off its source, a moved PDC emulator role, a restored or reverted VM — then fix the cause, resync safely and record what happened.
objectives: Recognize clock skew behind Kerberos, replication and certificate errors, and measure it before changing anything.
Return a member to the hierarchy, and move the time source with the PDC emulator role.
Resync safely after a restore or revert, and record the fix with its rollback.
recap: Measure the offset first; a symptom only tells you which clock to look at.
A member off its source, a moved role and a restored VM each have their own fix.
Every fix is recorded with cause, evidence and rollback, and the time plan follows the role.
lessons.next: That completes Configure domain time. Part 4, Measure against the STIG, scans both controllers — and meets the one rule this design answers with a declared, checked clock.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Use an isolated Windows Server practice environment. The network's routing and default-deny segmentation are in place, with the access control list (ACL) register that records every permitted path.

Provision each part's systems when the part begins: two Windows Server virtual machines for SBD-DC01 (10.0.10.10) and SBD-DC02 (10.0.10.11) on different hosts, then the PKI systems (part 6), the DHCP server (part 7) and the administration seats (part 8).

Work at each server's VM console with an authorized administrator account until part 8 builds AdminJumpBox01; after that, administration happens from the Tier 0 seats.

Have an approved connected system and the removable-media procedure for bringing downloaded DISA content and other software into the lab.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The addresses and names below continue the training example. Match every change to your own address plan. This network has no internet DNS dependency: names resolve on the domain controllers, and nothing is forwarded outside.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Recognize skew by its symptoms. Kerberos errors that name time — KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW, or 'There is a time and/or date difference between the client and server' at sign-in — access-denied errors in replication between the controllers, and certificates reported as not yet valid all point at a clock; if the controllers audit Kerberos failures, Security event 4771 with failure code 0x25 names the client. Measure before you change anything: w32tm /stripchart from the failing system to SBD-DC01 shows the offset.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Find out why a member left its source. Local CMOS Clock or Free-running System Clock means no usable source, a hypervisor provider means its host's time sync is on, and a peer name means someone set it by hand; a (Policy) value in w32tm /query /configuration points at a GPO, and events 129 and 36 show how long it has been adrift. Practice on the test client or SBD-DC02: set a manual peer with w32tm /config /manualpeerlist:SBD-DC01.sbd.test,0x8 /syncfromflags:manual /update, note that its time is still right but unauthenticated and off the hierarchy, then put it back with /syncfromflags:domhier.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Move the source with the PDC emulator role. When the role moves — a planned transfer, or a seizure after SBD-DC01 is lost — run w32tm /config /reliable:yes /update on the new holder and w32tm /config /syncfromflags:domhier /reliable:no /update on the old one, restart Windows Time on both, move the reference check to the new holder, and confirm that nltest /gtimeserv names it. Otherwise the old holder still advertises itself as the reliable source and the domain's time can keep flowing from a controller that is no longer the PDC emulator; practice only if you can move the role back the same day, because later courses expect SBD-DC01 to hold it.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Treat a restored or reverted VM as a clock problem as well as a directory one. It can come back with the clock it had when it was saved: members correct themselves, a domain controller corrects at most 48 hours each way (MaxPosPhaseCorrection and MaxNegPhaseCorrection) and logs an event instead, and SBD-DC01 has nothing to correct it at all, so every member follows its old time. After any restore or revert of SBD-DC01, compare it with the reference before you trust it.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: Resync safely. On Windows, w32tm /resync /rediscover finds the source again and resynchronizes; on Linux, sudo chronyc makestep steps the clock once a controller is selectable. When an offset is beyond what the service will correct, set the clock close by hand first, correct SBD-DC01 only by the measured difference, and never point a system at an outside or manual source to make an error go away.

sections.heading: Step 6
sections.body: Record the fix like any other change: the symptom and when it started, the first offset measured, the cause, what you changed, the evidence that the chain is whole again — source, offset and events — and the rollback. A moved role also updates the time plan: who now runs the reference check, and the reverse procedure for when the role returns.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
# Measure before changing anything (on the failing system)
w32tm /stripchart /computer:SBD-DC01.sbd.test /samples:3 /dataonly
w32tm /query /source
w32tm /query /configuration | Select-String 'Type:|NtpServer:|\(Policy\)'
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='System'; ProviderName='Microsoft-Windows-Time-Service'; Id=36,129} -MaxEvents 10 |
  Format-Table TimeCreated, Id -AutoSize
# Practice fault, then the fix (test client or SBD-DC02)
w32tm /config /manualpeerlist:SBD-DC01.sbd.test,0x8 /syncfromflags:manual /update
w32tm /query /source            # SBD-DC01.sbd.test,0x8: a manual peer, off the hierarchy
w32tm /config /syncfromflags:domhier /update
Restart-Service w32time
w32tm /resync /rediscover
w32tm /query /source            # a controller again
# If the PDC emulator role moves to SBD-DC02:
#   SBD-DC02: w32tm /config /reliable:yes /update; Restart-Service w32time
#   SBD-DC01: w32tm /config /syncfromflags:domhier /reliable:no /update; Restart-Service w32time
nltest /dsgetdc:sbd.test /gtimeserv   # must name the current PDC emulator
# Linux: sudo chronyc makestep, then chronyc tracking

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: The practice fault was found from the system's configuration before anything changed, the system names a controller again with Type NT5DS and a small, stable offset, nltest names the PDC emulator as the reliable source, and the record explains the cause rather than only showing a passing result.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep the fault record: the symptom and start time, the first offset, the source and configuration output before and after, the events, the change and its rollback, and the final offsets; after a role move, the updated time plan.

lessons.title: Understand STIGs, SCAP and checklists
lessons.summary: A Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG) is DISA's configuration standard for one product, and every scan and checklist in this part measures against one. Learn how a rule is identified, rated and traced to NIST SP 800-53, which rules a scanner can read and which a person must answer, then record which STIGs apply to each controller.
objectives: Explain how SRGs, STIGs, SCAP benchmarks and CCIs relate.
Read a STIG rule's identifiers and severity category.
Record which STIGs apply to each controller, and what a scan can and cannot prove.
recap: SRGs set requirements for a technology class; STIGs implement them for one product.
Every rule has its identifiers, a CAT severity, and CCIs that reach a NIST control.
SCC measures the benchmark, STIG Viewer holds the human answers, and neither is an authorization.
STIG rules cite CCIs, and CCIs trace to SP 800-53 controls; decide the baseline set before scanning.
lessons.next: Lesson 18 carries the DISA content across the air gap: the tools, the benchmarks, the STIGs and the GPO package part 5 will import.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Use an isolated Windows Server practice environment. The network's routing and default-deny segmentation are in place, with the access control list (ACL) register that records every permitted path.

Provision each part's systems when the part begins: two Windows Server virtual machines for SBD-DC01 (10.0.10.10) and SBD-DC02 (10.0.10.11) on different hosts, then the PKI systems (part 6), the DHCP server (part 7) and the administration seats (part 8).

Work at each server's VM console with an authorized administrator account until part 8 builds AdminJumpBox01; after that, administration happens from the Tier 0 seats.

Have an approved connected system and the removable-media procedure for bringing downloaded DISA content and other software into the lab.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The addresses and names below continue the training example. Match every change to your own address plan. This network has no internet DNS dependency: names resolve on the domain controllers, and nothing is forwarded outside.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Start with the two layers the Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) publishes. A Security Requirements Guide (SRG) states requirements for a class of technology, such as general-purpose operating systems; a STIG turns them into checks and fixes for one product, so every STIG rule traces back to an SRG requirement.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Read a rule's identity and weight. Each rule has a Group ID (V-…), a Rule ID (SV-…r…_rule, where the r number is its revision), a STIG ID naming the product and check, and a severity category: CAT I (high) when exploiting the weakness directly and immediately causes loss of confidentiality, integrity or availability, CAT II (medium) when it has the potential to, and CAT III (low) when it degrades the protections against that loss.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Separate what a scanner can read from what a person must answer. A Security Content Automation Protocol (SCAP) benchmark is the automated part of a STIG — rules written in XCCDF with OVAL checks — which the SCAP Compliance Checker (SCC) evaluates on a host. Every other rule is a manual check, and STIG Viewer is where you build a checklist for each assessed asset, import SCC's results and record the human answers.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Trace rules to controls and keep a scan's limits honest. Each rule cites Control Correlation Identifiers (CCIs), DISA's single, actionable requirement statements, each mapped to a NIST SP 800-53 control, so a result can serve as control evidence. A scan shows settings on one host, at one moment, against one release: it can err or miss, it says nothing about procedures, and a pass is not an authorization.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: Record what applies. These controllers take the Windows Server STIG (its domain controller rules included) plus the Active Directory Domain and Active Directory Forest STIGs. They also run DNS and Windows Defender Firewall, which have STIGs of their own — list those with an owner and a review date instead of dropping them silently.

sections.heading: Step 6
sections.body: The DISA STIGs reference ties each rule to the Risk Management Framework: every STIG rule cites one or more CCIs, and each CCI breaks a NIST SP 800-53 control into one testable statement. NIST's National Checklist Program re-lists DISA's STIGs, with their SCAP content and the GPO package, beside CIS and vendor checklists. The unclassified STIGs, SCAP benchmarks, the GPO package, STIG Viewer and SCC are free downloads from the DoD Cyber Exchange (cyber.mil). Decide the baseline set for each system before you scan, so this part and the Group Policy part measure the same thing.

sections.heading: Step 1

sections.heading: Step 2

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration

New-Item -ItemType Directory C:\Evidence\baseline -Force | Out-Null
$session = Get-ChildItem "$env:USERPROFILE\SCC\Sessions" -Directory | Sort-Object Name | Select-Object -Last 1
Copy-Item $session.FullName -Destination "C:\Evidence\baseline\$env:COMPUTERNAME" -Recurse
Get-ChildItem "C:\Evidence\baseline\$env:COMPUTERNAME" -Recurse -Filter '*XCCDF-Results*.xml' | Select-Object Name, LastWriteTime
Get-ChildItem "C:\Evidence\baseline\$env:COMPUTERNAME" -Recurse -File | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 | Export-Csv "C:\Evidence\baseline\$env:COMPUTERNAME-hashes.csv" -NoTypeInformation
# On SBD-DC02: carry its set to SBD-DC01. Then, on SBD-DC01, no output means the copy is identical.
Copy-Item C:\Evidence\baseline\SBD-DC02, C:\Evidence\baseline\SBD-DC02-hashes.csv -Destination '\\SBD-DC01\C$\Evidence\baseline\' -Recurse
Compare-Object (Import-Csv C:\Evidence\baseline\SBD-DC02-hashes.csv).Hash (Get-ChildItem C:\Evidence\baseline\SBD-DC02 -Recurse -File | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256).Hash

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Use an isolated Windows Server practice environment. The network's routing and default-deny segmentation are in place, with the access control list (ACL) register that records every permitted path.

Provision each part's systems when the part begins: two Windows Server virtual machines for SBD-DC01 (10.0.10.10) and SBD-DC02 (10.0.10.11) on different hosts, then the PKI systems (part 6), the DHCP server (part 7) and the administration seats (part 8).

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The addresses and names below continue the training example. Match every change to your own address plan. This network has no internet DNS dependency: names resolve on the domain controllers, and nothing is forwarded outside.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Export the open rules from all three checklists into one findings record, C:\Evidence\baseline\findings\findings-record.csv, and count them per checklist by severity. Read the CAT I items first: their exploitation directly and immediately causes loss.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Classify every open item with one of three values. Fix by GPO: the DISA package sets it, so part 5's import should close it. Deviation candidate: the setting conflicts with a design decision — for example a rule expecting the PDC emulator to synchronize with an authorized external time source, where the part 3 design declares and checks its own clock — and part 5 decides and records it. POA&M candidate: the fix lies outside Group Policy, such as the PKI server certificate the STIG expects on every domain controller, which the part 6 PKI issues, so it needs an owner and a planned date — the start of a Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M) entry.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Trace each finding to its controls. A rule's CCIs map to NIST SP 800-53 controls in DISA's CCI list, and STIG Viewer shows them with each rule — CCI-000366, for example, is implementing the security configuration settings under CM-6 — so the record tells an assessor which control each open item weakens.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Write the handoff part 5 works from as C:\Evidence\baseline\findings\handoff.txt: SCC's version, the benchmark release and profile, the STIG releases, the GPO package release waiting hashed in C:\Staging\DISA, and where the checklists and this record live. Then hash the whole folder into C:\Evidence\baseline-manifest.csv. Part 5 checks that manifest, rescans with exactly those versions into C:\Evidence\hardened, updates copies of the checklists there, and closes or records every item.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
New-Item -ItemType Directory C:\Evidence\baseline\findings -Force | Out-Null
$rows = foreach ($t in 'SBD-DC01', 'SBD-DC02', 'sbd.test') {
  $ckl = Get-Content "C:\Evidence\baseline\checklists\$t.cklb" -Raw -Encoding UTF8 | ConvertFrom-Json
  $ckl.stigs.rules | Where-Object status -eq 'open' | Select-Object @{n='Target';e={$t}}, @{n='GroupId';e={$_.group_id}}, @{n='StigId';e={$_.rule_version}}, @{n='Severity';e={$_.severity}}, @{n='CCIs';e={$_.ccis -join ' '}}, @{n='Title';e={$_.rule_title}}, Classification, Owner, TargetDate
}
$rows | Group-Object Target, Severity | Select-Object Name, Count
$rows | Export-Csv C:\Evidence\baseline\findings\findings-record.csv -NoTypeInformation
# After you fill in Classification, Owner and TargetDate and write handoff.txt, close the baseline:
Get-ChildItem C:\Evidence\baseline -Recurse -File | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 | Export-Csv C:\Evidence\baseline-manifest.csv -NoTypeInformation
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 C:\Evidence\baseline-manifest.csv

sections.body: The findings record lists every open rule from the three checklists with target, severity and CCIs; each carries one of the three classifications and an owner, POA&M candidates also a planned date; the counts by severity are recorded; and handoff.txt and the manifest give part 5 every version, path and hash it reuses.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep findings-record.csv, the counts by severity per checklist, the CCI-to-control notes for the open items, handoff.txt, and C:\Evidence\baseline-manifest.csv with its own hash.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Use an isolated Windows Server practice environment. The network's routing and default-deny segmentation are in place, with the access control list (ACL) register that records every permitted path.

Provision each part's systems when the part begins: two Windows Server virtual machines for SBD-DC01 (10.0.10.10) and SBD-DC02 (10.0.10.11) on different hosts, then the PKI systems (part 6), the DHCP server (part 7) and the administration seats (part 8).

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The addresses and names below continue the training example. Match every change to your own address plan. This network has no internet DNS dependency: names resolve on the domain controllers, and nothing is forwarded outside.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Design the structure by administration: a top-level SBD OU containing Servers, Workstations, Users, Groups, and an Admin OU for privileged accounts. The built-in Domain Controllers OU stays where it is and keeps its name.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Create the planned OUs with accidental-deletion protection enabled. Record each OU's purpose and who will administer its contents; an OU with no delegation or policy purpose is clutter.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Redirect the default containers with redircmp and redirusr: new computer accounts to the Workstations OU and new user accounts to the Users OU. Group Policy cannot be linked to the default containers, so anything landing there would get only domain-level policy, never the OU-linked hardening. Join servers straight into the Servers OU with Add-Computer -OUPath, so they never pass through the workstation policies.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Keep privileged accounts and systems separate: the Admin OU holds the identities that administer the domain controllers. The domain-joined PKI servers from part 6 and SBD-DHCP01 from part 7 join the Servers OU, and part 8 adds a Tier 0 Servers OU and the admin seats' sub-OUs. Do not nest deeper than the delegation plan requires.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: The Active Directory design reference says OUs exist for exactly two purposes, delegating administration and applying Group Policy, not replication. Redirect the default Users and Computers containers so new objects land where policy reaches them. Keep GPOs few and well scoped, and deliver baselines such as the DISA GPO package through GPOs linked to the right OUs, tested first. Block Inheritance hides policy and is discouraged; use Enforced sparingly, for settings that must apply.

lessons.title: Learn how Group Policy applies
lessons.summary: Before the DISA settings arrive, learn how a computer decides which Group Policy objects (GPOs) apply and which setting wins. Map the order, build the central store the import will use, and record what both controllers apply today.
objectives: Predict which GPO wins from processing order, link order, inheritance, Enforced and Block Inheritance.
Explain how security filtering, WMI filters and loopback processing change a GPO's reach.
Build the central store and record each controller's starting policy with gpresult.
recap: The closest link applies last and wins; at one OU, link order 1 wins.
Enforced and Block Inheritance are exceptions to record, not tools to reach for.
gpresult shows what actually applied, and why the rest was filtered out.
lessons.next: Lesson 24 imports the DISA policies part 4 staged and links them where they belong.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Use an isolated Windows Server practice environment. The network's routing and default-deny segmentation are in place, with the access control list (ACL) register that records every permitted path.

Provision each part's systems when the part begins: two Windows Server virtual machines for SBD-DC01 (10.0.10.10) and SBD-DC02 (10.0.10.11) on different hosts, then the PKI systems (part 6), the DHCP server (part 7) and the administration seats (part 8).

Work at each server's VM console with an authorized administrator account until part 8 builds AdminJumpBox01; after that, administration happens from the Tier 0 seats.

Have an approved connected system and the removable-media procedure for bringing downloaded DISA content and other software into the lab.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The addresses and names below continue the training example. Match every change to your own address plan. This network has no internet DNS dependency: names resolve on the domain controllers, and nothing is forwarded outside.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Know where a GPO lives. Its settings sit in two halves — a container object in Active Directory and a template folder in SYSVOL — and they replicate separately, by directory replication and by DFS Replication. A change made on SBD-DC01 therefore reaches SBD-DC02 in two steps: before you judge a result there, check that the GPO's AD and SYSVOL version numbers agree.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Learn the order. Policy applies local first, then site, domain and OU, parent OU before child, so the GPO linked closest to the computer is applied last and wins a conflict; at one OU, link order 1 is processed last and wins. Different settings add up across GPOs, but a single setting's values generally don't merge: the highest-precedence GPO that configures it wins, so a user-rights list in one GPO replaces another's instead of adding to it.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Treat the two overrides as exceptions. Block Inheritance on an OU stops GPOs linked above it; Enforced on a link makes that GPO win over everything below it and pierces Block Inheritance. Enforced is not a shortcut — it hides a precedence problem instead of solving it — so this network uses neither unless the exception record says why.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Read what narrows a GPO's reach. Security filtering applies it only to accounts with both Read and Apply group policy (Authenticated Users by default), and computers still need Read on GPOs that apply only to users, because user policy is read in the computer's security context; a WMI filter applies it only where its query is true. Loopback processing gives anyone who signs in to a computer the user settings from that computer's GPOs — merge adds them after the user's own, replace uses only the computer's — so use it only where the computer should decide; lesson 24 meets the one place this part needs it.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: Know when policy arrives, and build the central store. Members refresh in the background every 90 minutes with a random offset of up to 30, controllers every five minutes, and gpupdate /force reapplies everything at once, though some extensions run only at startup or sign-in. On SBD-DC01, copy C:\Windows\PolicyDefinitions with its en-US folder to \\sbd.test\SYSVOL\sbd.test\Policies\PolicyDefinitions: from then on, every Group Policy editor in the domain uses these templates instead of its local ones.

sections.heading: Step 6
sections.body: Record the starting state before anything is imported. On both controllers, save a gpresult report of the Resultant Set of Policy (RSoP), what actually applied: the Default Domain Policy and the Default Domain Controllers Policy should be the only domain GPOs listed. Read the applied and filtered-out lists — the reasons gpresult gives, such as a security denial or a false WMI filter, are how you will troubleshoot the import.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
# Once, on SBD-DC01: create the central store from the controller's own templates
Copy-Item C:\Windows\PolicyDefinitions -Destination \\sbd.test\SYSVOL\sbd.test\Policies\PolicyDefinitions -Recurse
# On SBD-DC01: links in precedence order, and each GPO's AD and SYSVOL versions
Get-GPInheritance -Target 'DC=sbd,DC=test'
Get-GPInheritance -Target 'OU=Domain Controllers,DC=sbd,DC=test'
foreach ($dc in 'SBD-DC01', 'SBD-DC02') { Get-GPO -All -Server $dc | Select-Object @{n='DC';e={$dc}}, DisplayName, GpoStatus, @{n='AD';e={$_.Computer.DSVersion}}, @{n='SYSVOL';e={$_.Computer.SysvolVersion}} }
# On each controller's console; carry SBD-DC02's report to the same folder on SBD-DC01
New-Item -ItemType Directory C:\Evidence\hardened\policy-before -Force | Out-Null
gpresult /r /scope:computer
gpresult /h "C:\Evidence\hardened\policy-before\$env:COMPUTERNAME-gpresult.html" /f

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: You can list both controllers' GPOs in precedence order and say why each applies, nothing is Enforced or blocked, every GPO's AD and SYSVOL versions agree, the central store holds SBD-DC01's templates, and each controller's starting gpresult report is saved.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep both starting gpresult reports in C:\Evidence\hardened\policy-before, the inheritance output for the domain and the Domain Controllers OU, the GPO version listing, and a note of the central store's source and date.

lessons.title: Import and link the DISA GPOs
lessons.summary: Group Policy is how the STIG becomes configuration. Import the package part 4 staged, link each policy where its systems live so the findings marked fix by GPO can close, and keep the lab's deliberate deviations written down rather than silently skipped.
objectives: Verify the staged package and add its templates to the central store.
Import DISA's policies and link them by OU, with account policies at the domain root.
Handle lab-specific deviations with documentation instead of silent edits.
recap: The central store keeps policy definitions consistent across controllers.
Links follow the OU design; account policies live at the domain root.
Deviations are documented decisions, not deletions.
lessons.next: Lesson 25 rescans with part 4's versions to prove what the policies changed.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Use an isolated Windows Server practice environment. The network's routing and default-deny segmentation are in place, with the access control list (ACL) register that records every permitted path.

Provision each part's systems when the part begins: two Windows Server virtual machines for SBD-DC01 (10.0.10.10) and SBD-DC02 (10.0.10.11) on different hosts, then the PKI systems (part 6), the DHCP server (part 7) and the administration seats (part 8).

Work at each server's VM console with an authorized administrator account until part 8 builds AdminJumpBox01; after that, administration happens from the Tier 0 seats.

Have an approved connected system and the removable-media procedure for bringing downloaded DISA content and other software into the lab.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The addresses and names below continue the training example. Match every change to your own address plan. This network has no internet DNS dependency: names resolve on the domain controllers, and nothing is forwarded outside.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Start from part 4's handoff. Read the package release in C:\Evidence\baseline\findings\handoff.txt, confirm the package in C:\Staging\DISA still matches its connected-side hash, and only then extract it. Copy its ADMX files and their en-US ADML files into the central store from lesson 23, without replacing a newer Microsoft template with an older copy of the same file.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Import each policy this network uses into a new GPO with the GPMC Import Settings wizard or Import-GPO: the Windows Server domain controller, member server and user policies, and the Windows client policies for your fleet's release, which stay unlinked until courses 1.1 and 1.6 link them. Keep DISA's names behind an SBD prefix so the source release stays identifiable. An import replaces every setting in the target GPO and brings no links, security filtering or WMI filter. Where the package's user-rights settings name placeholder groups such as ADD YOUR DOMAIN ADMINS, map them to sbd.test's real groups with a migration table — check the package's support files for one before building your own in GPMC's Migration Table Editor.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Link by OU. Link the domain controller policy to the Domain Controllers OU at link order 1, above the Default Domain Controllers Policy, and the member-server policy to the Servers OU, so the systems later courses build there are hardened from first boot. Domain controllers read password, lockout and Kerberos policy only from GPOs linked at the domain root: if the package carries account policies, set those values in a GPO linked there above the Default Domain Policy, because at an OU they do nothing for domain accounts. Use neither Enforced nor Block Inheritance.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Apply the user policy where people sign in. Its settings belong to every session on a hardened server, whoever signs in — an administrator from the Admin OU, or the built-in Administrator in the default Users container, where no GPO can link. So link the DISA user policy to the Domain Controllers and Servers OUs and, in a small GPO linked to both, enable Configure user Group Policy loopback processing mode set to Merge. Record that decision — it is the only loopback this part uses — and compare it with the package's own instructions for its user policy.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: Walk the settings that need a decision in this network — anything that assumes infrastructure the lab does not have or conflicts with an earlier design — and record each deviation with its rationale instead of deleting the setting. Check each fix-by-GPO item in part 4's findings record against the imported settings, so you know which ones the rescan should show closed. Then, once SBD-DC02 shows the same GPO versions, refresh policy on both controllers and confirm with gpresult that the SBD DISA GPOs apply and that replication still succeeds both ways. Finally, confirm the part 3 time design is intact with no time setting from Group Policy: w32tm /query /configuration must show no (Policy) value, and any Windows Time Service setting an imported GPO carries goes back to Not Configured, with the change recorded.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
# On SBD-DC01. True means the package matches the hash recorded on the connected side.
$package = Get-ChildItem C:\Staging\DISA -Filter '*GPO*.zip' | Select-Object -First 1
(Get-FileHash $package.FullName -Algorithm SHA256).Hash -in (Import-Csv C:\Evidence\baseline\transfer\connected-side-hashes.csv).Hash
Expand-Archive $package.FullName -DestinationPath C:\Staging\GPO
# Per policy; take the exact names and folders from the package:
Import-GPO -BackupGpoName '<DISA GPO name>' -TargetName 'SBD <DISA GPO name>' -Path '<package GPOs folder>' -MigrationTable '<migration table>' -CreateIfNeeded
New-GPLink -Name 'SBD <DISA domain controller GPO name>' -Target 'OU=Domain Controllers,DC=sbd,DC=test' -Order 1
Get-GPInheritance -Target 'OU=Domain Controllers,DC=sbd,DC=test'
# On each controller's console; carry SBD-DC02's report to SBD-DC01:
gpupdate /force
gpresult /r /scope:computer
New-Item -ItemType Directory C:\Evidence\hardened\import -Force | Out-Null
gpresult /h "C:\Evidence\hardened\import\$env:COMPUTERNAME-gpresult.html" /f
w32tm /query /source   # SBD-DC01: Local CMOS Clock; SBD-DC02: a domain controller
w32tm /query /configuration | Select-String '\(Policy\)'   # expected: no output, so no time setting comes from Group Policy
repadmin /replsummary

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: The package matched its connected-side hash, the central store serves its templates, placeholder groups map to real ones, the links follow the OU design with the domain controller policy at link order 1 and nothing Enforced or blocked, gpresult on both controllers lists the SBD DISA GPOs as applied, time and replication are unchanged with no time setting from Group Policy, and every deviation has a written reason and owner.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep the import record — package release and hash check, each GPO's name and source, the migration table, the links with their order, the loopback decision, and both gpresult reports in C:\Evidence\hardened\import — and the deviation list with rationale and owner.

lessons.title: Design the two-tier trust hierarchy
lessons.summary: The root establishes trust. The subordinate, also called the issuing CA in this design, handles approved end-entity certificates. Keeping these roles separate protects the root from daily network exposure.
objectives: Explain why the root stays offline while the issuing CA handles enrollment.

recap: Trust, issuance, publication, and administration are separated in writing.
Cryptography, names, lifetimes, and CRL periods are approved before installation, starting from this lab's example values.

lessons.next: Lesson 28 performs the controlled offline root installation.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Use an isolated Windows Server practice environment. The network's routing and default-deny segmentation are in place, with the access control list (ACL) register that records every permitted path.

Provision each part's systems when the part begins: two Windows Server virtual machines for SBD-DC01 (10.0.10.10) and SBD-DC02 (10.0.10.11) on different hosts, then the PKI systems (part 6), the DHCP server (part 7) and the administration seats (part 8).
