sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The addresses and names below continue the training example. Match every change to your own address plan. This network has no internet DNS dependency: names resolve on the domain controllers, and nothing is forwarded outside.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Draw the hierarchy: offline standalone root → enterprise issuing CA → approved server/client certificates. There is no network connection to the root.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Record final host and CA names, key provider, algorithm, key sizes, hashes, validity periods, renewal owners, and recovery arrangements. Start from this lab's example values in the next step and change any that your own policy requires: they are examples, not universal requirements.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Example values for this lab: the root CA uses an RSA 4096 key with SHA-256 and a 20-year certificate, and publishes a base CRL every 26 weeks with an overlap period and no delta CRL, refreshed at each offline ceremony. The issuing CA uses RSA 4096 (3072 at minimum) with SHA-256 and a 10-year certificate, a weekly base CRL, and a daily delta CRL. End-entity certificates last one to two years. NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 rates RSA 2048 at 112 bits of security, which it accepts for new signatures only through 2030, so a CA that will still be signing after 2030 uses at least 3072 bits (128 bits of security); the newest Windows Server release requires at least 2,048-bit RSA for TLS server authentication.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Know where each value is set. You choose the key, the hash, and the root's 20-year validity in the AD CS Configuration wizard. Each CA's CAPolicy.inf sets its CRL periods (CRLPeriod, CRLPeriodUnits, CRLDeltaPeriod, CRLDeltaPeriodUnits), which certutil -setreg can change later. The issuing CA's 10-year lifetime is set on the root (CA\ValidityPeriod and CA\ValidityPeriodUnits) before the signing ceremony, because a subordinate CA's lifetime comes from the CA that signs it.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: Plan a stable internal publication name such as pki.sbd.test. The Authority Information Access (AIA) location supplies issuer certificates; the CRL Distribution Point (CDP) supplies certificate revocation lists.

sections.heading: Step 6
sections.body: Choose the publication host, paths, access rules, and refresh schedule before issuing certificates. Clients inside this air-gapped network must reach those locations without relying on the public internet.

sections.heading: Step 7
sections.body: The PKI design reference agrees with this design: an offline standalone root and an online enterprise issuing CA. Add a policy tier only for a concrete policy, legal or delegation need. Set the CDP and AIA locations, HTTP first, before the first certificate is issued, renew CA certificates at half-life, and avoid delta CRLs on an offline root. Microsoft, CISA, NSA and DISA agree that AD CS is Tier 0: manage it only from Tier 0 seats with dedicated CA administrator accounts, and encrypt CA backups. CISA and NSA list a hardware security module for CA keys; record whether your lab uses one.

Resolve-DnsName SBD-DC01.sbd.test

sections.body: The written plan separates trust, issuance, publication, and administration. It identifies who renews CRLs before they expire, and every key size, hash, lifetime, and CRL period has a recorded value and the setting that applies it.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep the approved hierarchy, the cryptography and lifetime table with the setting that applies each value, and a worksheet mapping every certificate/CRL URL to its actual publisher and file.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The addresses and names below continue the training example. Match every change to your own address plan. This network has no internet DNS dependency: names resolve on the domain controllers, and nothing is forwarded outside.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Turn on autoenrollment: create SBD Certificate Autoenrollment, a GPO that enables Certificate Services Client - Auto-Enrollment with renewal and template updates, and link it at the domain root, so each member enrolls only for the templates whose permissions name it. The controllers' requests reach SBD-SUBCA01 over RPC across the core from VLAN 10, so confirm the register's enrollment row first. Refresh policy: both controllers receive SBD Domain Controller Authentication certificates and the pilot, SBD-PKI-MGMT01, an SBD Computer Authentication certificate, without a human touching a request.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: On SBD-DC01, outside VLAN 30, export its new certificate and the pilot's, clear the URL cache, and run the full verification on each: the chain must reach the approved root and every AIA and CDP URL must answer from pki.sbd.test with current CRL dates — cached success is not evidence of publication.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Enroll a disposable test certificate, revoke only that one, publish an updated issuing CRL, and verify on SBD-DC01, with the cache cleared again, that a fresh evaluation detects the revocation. Diagnose retrieval or stale-publication problems rather than turning off revocation checks.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Record owners and reminders for root and issuing CRL publication and certificate renewal. Schedule offline root ceremonies early enough to transfer and publish replacement CRLs before expiry, and start each one by setting the root's clock against the approved reference. Backups are not set up here: course 1.12 defines and schedules the issuing CA's backup — database, key and configuration — with the rest of the network's, accounts for the root's ceremony backup from lesson 28, and rehearses recovery, so list those items for it in the record.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: Take the first SCAP baselines of SBD-SUBCA01 and SBD-PKI-MGMT01 the part 4 way: SCC and the Windows Server benchmark from the part 4 media set, checked against its hashes, at the same versions and profile, run locally, with each session hashed and carried to C:\Evidence\pki\<host name> on SBD-DC01, where its hashes must match again, as SBD-DC02's did in part 4. List the IIS STIGs the publication site now falls under with an owner and a review date, then rescan both controllers the same way, because their certificates, root trust and autoenrollment policy are this part's change.

sections.heading: Step 6
sections.body: Close what this part fixed: in copies of the part 5 checklists in C:\Evidence\pki\checklists on SBD-DC01, answer the rule that every domain controller has a PKI server certificate Not A Finding, with each controller's certificate as the observation, and record part 4's POA&M candidate as closed. The companion rule, that those certificates come from the DoD PKI or an approved External Certificate Authority, stays open: record it in C:\Evidence\exception-record.csv if it is not there yet, because this lab's own hierarchy stands in for DoD's. Export the new GPOs' reports and links for the change record (course 1.12 backs the GPOs up), file the enrollment, urlfetch, revocation, template and owner records with the scans, and seal C:\Evidence\pki.

sections.body:

gpupdate /force
certutil -pulse
Get-ChildItem Cert:\LocalMachine\My | Select-Object @{n='Template';e={ $x = $_.Extensions | Where-Object { $_.Oid.Value -eq '1.3.6.1.4.1.311.21.7' }; if ($x) { $x.Format($false) } }}, DnsNameList, NotAfter, Thumbprint
# On SBD-DC01 (outside VLAN 30): export its certificate, then verify it and the pilot's with nothing cached
New-Item -ItemType Directory C:\Evidence\pki -Force | Out-Null
$dc = Get-ChildItem Cert:\LocalMachine\My | Where-Object { $_.EnhancedKeyUsageList.ObjectId -contains '1.3.6.1.5.2.3.5' } | Select-Object -First 1   # KDC Authentication
Export-Certificate -Cert $dc -FilePath C:\Evidence\pki\SBD-DC01-dc.cer
certutil -urlcache * delete
certutil -verify -urlfetch C:\Evidence\pki\SBD-DC01-dc.cer
certutil -verify -urlfetch C:\Evidence\pki\pilot.cer   # the pilot's certificate, exported on SBD-PKI-MGMT01 with Export-Certificate
# On SBD-SUBCA01: revoke only the disposable test certificate, then publish a new CRL

certutil -crl
# Back on SBD-DC01: the test certificate must now fail as revoked
certutil -urlcache * delete
certutil -verify -urlfetch C:\Evidence\pki\test.cer
# After the scans (each carried to C:\Evidence\pki\<host name> on SBD-DC01) and the checklist updates: record the new GPOs (course 1.12 backs them up), then seal the evidence

(Get-GPInheritance -Target 'DC=sbd,DC=test').GpoLinks | Select-Object Target, Order, DisplayName, Enabled, Enforced | Export-Csv C:\Evidence\pki\gpo-links.csv -NoTypeInformation
Get-ChildItem C:\Evidence\pki -Recurse -File | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 | Export-Csv C:\Evidence\pki-manifest.csv -NoTypeInformation
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 C:\Evidence\pki-manifest.csv

lessons.title: Design the addressing service
lessons.summary: DHCP decides the first things every workstation believes: its address, its gateway, and which servers answer its names. Design that service before building it — one scope for VLAN 80, the options clients will trust, and the identities that authorize, run, and register for it — and confirm the core already relays VLAN 80's requests.
objectives: Decide which segment gets leases and design its scope: range, exclusions, reservations, and lease length.
Choose the options clients will trust and the identities that authorize, run, and register for the server.
Confirm the register rows and the core's relay for VLAN 80 without changing the router.
recap: One leased segment, VLAN 80, with a full-subnet scope, two exclusions, and no reservations.
The lease length is the outage budget, and three options are all clients get.
Authorization, administration, and registration each have their own identity; the relay is confirmed, not built.
DHCP runs on a dedicated member server; rogue-server protection belongs to the switch and hypervisor.
lessons.next: Lesson 38 builds SBD-DHCP01, authorizes it, and creates the scope.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Use an isolated Windows Server practice environment. The network's routing and default-deny segmentation are in place, with the access control list (ACL) register that records every permitted path.

Provision each part's systems when the part begins: two Windows Server virtual machines for SBD-DC01 (10.0.10.10) and SBD-DC02 (10.0.10.11) on different hosts, then the PKI systems (part 6), the DHCP server (part 7) and the administration seats (part 8).

Work at each server's VM console with an authorized administrator account until part 8 builds AdminJumpBox01; after that, administration happens from the Tier 0 seats.

Have an approved connected system and the removable-media procedure for bringing downloaded DISA content and other software into the lab.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The addresses and names below continue the training example. Match every change to your own address plan. This network has no internet DNS dependency: names resolve on the domain controllers, and nothing is forwarded outside.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Decide where DHCP runs and for whom. Only VLAN 80 gets leases — the 50 PCs, and in this part a temporary test client; every server, every admin seat, and the core keep static addresses, because the register names them by address. SBD-DHCP01 is a member server at 10.0.20.10 on VLAN 20, never a domain controller: a DHCP server on a controller inherits the controller's right to change any record in a secure DNS zone.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Design the scope the way Microsoft recommends: the whole subnet, 10.0.80.1–254 with mask 255.255.255.0, then exclusion ranges for what must never be leased — 10.0.80.1–99, which holds the core's gateway at .1, and 10.0.80.200–254 — leaving the pool at 10.0.80.100–199, as the System Hub records it. One hundred addresses cover the fifty PCs, test clients, and replacement machines whose old leases haven't expired. Plan no reservations: a reservation is keyed to a MAC address that any device can claim, so it is an addressing convenience, never an identity check; if a device ever needs one, record it with an owner and a reason.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Set the lease length as the outage budget: with one DHCP server, a lease is how long clients keep working while SBD-DHCP01 is down. Keep the Windows default of 8 days as the sample value — clients try to renew halfway through (day 4) and rebind at seven-eighths (day 7) — and record your own value with that reason. Then choose the options, because every option is something every client trusts: router (option 3) 10.0.80.1, DNS servers (option 6) 10.0.10.10 and 10.0.10.11, both domain controllers and never an outside resolver, and DNS domain name (option 15) sbd.test. Add nothing else: no WINS, no boot server, no proxy auto-discovery.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Assign three identities. Authorizing a DHCP server writes to the forest's configuration partition, so an Enterprise Admins member does it — Tier 0 work, done at SBD-DC01's console until part 8 builds AdminJumpBox01. The server is built and run by named server-administration accounts in a new group, SBD Tier 1 Admins in this sample, because part 8 makes member-server administration Tier 1; and client names are registered by a third, unprivileged account in lesson 3.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: Confirm the paths. Rule F04 in the System Hub lets VLAN 80 reach SBD-DHCP01 on UDP 67/68 through the core's DHCP relay, owned by the network owner; the relay is part of the network's build, so verify it from the network's record with the network owner — it must forward to 10.0.20.10 and nowhere else, which lesson 38's first lease then proves — and take any gap to the network owner rather than changing the router. As a domain member, SBD-DHCP01 also uses F01 (DNS), F02 (Kerberos), F03 (directory), and F09 (time); its registrations ride F01, and A02 already lists it for part 8's Tier 1 seat.

sections.heading: Step 6
sections.body: The DHCP design reference places the service on dedicated domain-member servers authorized in Active Directory, never on a domain controller, because a DHCP service on a controller inherits its rights over AD-integrated DNS records. If DHCP registers names for clients, use one dedicated, non-privileged DNS credential on every DHCP server, enable Name Protection, keep the zones secure-only and keep DnsUpdateProxy empty. Message-level DHCP authentication is effectively unused, so protection against rogue servers belongs to the switch and the hypervisor (DHCP snooping and DHCP guard). Log the hostname, MAC address, IP address and time of every lease.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
# At SBD-DC01's console (Tier 0): the values and identities the design names
Resolve-DnsName SBD-DC01.sbd.test -Server 10.0.10.11; Resolve-DnsName SBD-DC02.sbd.test -Server 10.0.10.10
Get-ADOrganizationalUnit -Identity 'OU=Servers,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test' | Select-Object Name, DistinguishedName
Get-ADGroupMember 'Enterprise Admins' | Select-Object Name   # who can authorize a DHCP server
Get-ADGroupMember DnsUpdateProxy   # expected: no members
Get-DnsServerZone -ComputerName SBD-DC01 | Select-Object ZoneName, IsDsIntegrated, DynamicUpdate, ReplicationScope

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: The design records VLAN 80 as the only leased segment, the full-subnet scope with its two exclusion ranges and no reservations, the lease length with its reason, the three options, who holds each of the three identities, and the network's confirmation that the core relays VLAN 80 to 10.0.20.10 under F04.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep the DHCP design (scope, exclusions, lease length, options, identities), the relay confirmation with where it came from, and the register rows that name SBD-DHCP01.

quizzes.question: Why does SBD-DHCP01 run on a member server instead of a domain controller?
answers: DHCP can't be installed on a domain controller
A DHCP server on a controller inherits the controller's right to change any record in a secure DNS zone
Member servers hand out leases faster
quizzes.explanation: Microsoft's guidance is direct: on a domain controller, the DHCP service carries the controller's permissions in DNS. A member server that registers through a dedicated, unprivileged account keeps that power out of the address service.

quizzes.question: The scope covers 10.0.80.1–254, but only .100–.199 are ever leased. What keeps the rest out of the pool?
answers: Exclusion ranges inside the scope
A reservation for every unused address
The core drops requests for those addresses
quizzes.explanation: Microsoft recommends defining the whole subnet as the scope and excluding what must never be leased. The exclusions keep the core's gateway and the held-back ranges out of every offer.

quizzes.question: Why does this part verify the core's DHCP relay instead of configuring it?
answers: The relay is optional for VLAN 80
SBD-DHCP01 configures the relay automatically
The router belongs to the network's own build: later courses read and test it but never change it
quizzes.explanation: Routing, segmentation, and the relay already exist. This part confirms that F04 does what the register says and takes any gap to the network owner.

quizzes.question: Why does DHCP not run on a domain controller in this design?
answers: It would inherit the controller's rights over AD-integrated DNS records
It needs more memory than a controller has
Domain controllers cannot lease addresses
quizzes.explanation: A DHCP service on a domain controller registers DNS records with the controller's rights; a dedicated member server with a non-privileged credential avoids that.

sections.body: The addresses and names below continue the training example. Match every change to your own address plan. This network has no internet DNS dependency: names resolve on the domain controllers, and nothing is forwarded outside.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: At SBD-DC01's console, create SBD Tier 1 Admins and a named server-administration account for each person who will run SBD-DHCP01, all in the Admin OU, and let the group create computer objects in the Servers OU. The delegation covers that OU and computer objects only, so the group can add servers but gains no rights over the ones already there, including SBD-SUBCA01 and SBD-PKI-MGMT01, which part 8 moves to their own OU.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Install Windows Server on SBD-DHCP01 with its static address (10.0.20.10/24, the core's 10.0.20.1 as gateway, both domain controllers as DNS servers) and its hypervisor time synchronization off, then, at its console, join it straight into the Servers OU with Add-Computer -OUPath and a server-administration account, so part 5's member-server policies apply from first boot. After the restart, still as the local Administrator (the STIG policy may have renamed it), make SBD Tier 1 Admins the only domain group in its local Administrators group, in place of Domain Admins, per the current member-server STIG; from then on, work as your server-administration account.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Install the DHCP role with its tools, create the DHCP Administrators and DHCP Users groups, and restart the service. An Enterprise Admins member then authorizes the server at SBD-DC01's console, after adding the DHCP management tools there (part 8 moves this work to AdminJumpBox01). Restart the DHCP Server service on SBD-DHCP01 so it checks its authorization now, and find event 1044: authorized, and servicing clients.

sections.heading: Step 4

Turn dynamic DNS updates off for now (DynamicUpdates Never): a record registered under the server's own computer account stays owned by that account, so lesson 39's dedicated account could never update it. Then activate the scope.

sections.heading: Step 5

The relay wrote its own VLAN 80 address, 10.0.80.1, into each request's gateway address field; that is how SBD-DHCP01 picked the 10.0.80.0 scope. On SBD-DHCP01, find the lease in the scope — and no DNS record yet, by design.

lessons.title: Register client names securely
lessons.summary: Part 2's zone accepts only secure updates, so the real question is who writes VLAN 80's records. Give that job to one dedicated, unprivileged account, turn on name protection so no device can take over another's name, and keep the DnsUpdateProxy group empty — it strips the protection off every record its members create.
objectives: Create the reverse zone and the dedicated update account, and give SBD-DHCP01 its credential.
Register A and PTR records for every client, with name protection and cleanup when leases end.
Explain why DnsUpdateProxy is a trap, and prove the records belong to the update account.
recap: VLAN 80's names are written by one dedicated, unprivileged account, not a computer account.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Use an isolated Windows Server practice environment. The network's routing and default-deny segmentation are in place, with the access control list (ACL) register that records every permitted path.

Provision each part's systems when the part begins: two Windows Server virtual machines for SBD-DC01 (10.0.10.10) and SBD-DC02 (10.0.10.11) on different hosts, then the PKI systems (part 6), the DHCP server (part 7) and the administration seats (part 8).

Work at each server's VM console with an authorized administrator account until part 8 builds AdminJumpBox01; after that, administration happens from the Tier 0 seats.

Have an approved connected system and the removable-media procedure for bringing downloaded DISA content and other software into the lab.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The addresses and names below continue the training example. Match every change to your own address plan. This network has no internet DNS dependency: names resolve on the domain controllers, and nothing is forwarded outside.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: At SBD-DC01's console, create the reverse lookup zone for 10.0.80.0/24 — Active Directory-integrated, with the replication scope you chose in part 2, and secure updates only — so client PTR records have somewhere to go; part 2 created only 10.0.10's.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Create the update account there too: a standard user (svc-dhcp-dns in this sample) in the Admin OU and in Domain Users only, with a long random password — at least the length the current STIG sets for manually managed application accounts — set not to expire, which the current STIG allows for an application account whose owner changes the password on the schedule the STIG sets and whenever someone who knew it leaves. It needs no DNS permission of its own: any authenticated account may create a record in a secure zone and becomes the owner of what it creates. Keep DnsUpdateProxy empty: records its members create are left unsecured, so the next device to update the name takes it over.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: On SBD-DHCP01, store the credential with Set-DhcpServerDnsCredential, then set the server to register both A and PTR records for every client (DynamicUpdates Always), including clients that don't ask (UpdateDnsRRForOlderClients), to remove them when a lease expires or is deleted (DeleteDnsRROnLeaseExpiry), and to protect names (NameProtection). Name protection adds a DHCID record that ties each name to the client that registered it, and an update for that name from a different client fails instead of overwriting it.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: On SBD-TEST80, renew the lease and watch registration happen: SBD-DHCP01's audit log shows the update requested (30) and done (32), both controllers answer for the name and the address, and a DHCID record sits beside the A record. At SBD-DC01's console, read the record's owner: it must be SBD\svc-dhcp-dns, not SBD-DHCP01's computer account.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: Record the decision: one update identity for VLAN 80, its owner, where the sealed password lives, and that after any password change you set the credential again on SBD-DHCP01, because registrations fail until you do. With every VLAN 80 record owned by that one account, the server cleans up names when leases end, so VLAN 80 doesn't depend on scavenging, which part 2 left as a separate decision. Course 1.6 finishes the picture for the fleet: it turns off the workstations' own DNS self-registration by GPO on the Workstations OU, with the reason recorded, so SBD-DHCP01, as svc-dhcp-dns, stays the only writer of their records.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
# At SBD-DC01's console (Tier 0): the reverse zone (part 2's replication scope), the update account, an empty proxy group
Add-DnsServerPrimaryZone -NetworkId '10.0.80.0/24' -ReplicationScope Domain -DynamicUpdate Secure
New-ADUser svc-dhcp-dns -Path 'OU=Admin,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test' -AccountPassword (Read-Host -AsSecureString) -PasswordNeverExpires $true -Enabled $true
Get-ADGroupMember DnsUpdateProxy   # expected: no members
# On SBD-DHCP01: the credential, then registration for every client, with name protection
Set-DhcpServerDnsCredential -Credential (Get-Credential 'SBD\svc-dhcp-dns')
Set-DhcpServerv4DnsSetting -DynamicUpdates Always -UpdateDnsRRForOlderClients $true -DeleteDnsRROnLeaseExpiry $true -NameProtection $true
Get-DhcpServerDnsCredential; Get-DhcpServerv4DnsSetting
# On SBD-TEST80: renew, then ask both controllers for the name, the address, and the DHCID record
ipconfig /renew
Resolve-DnsName SBD-TEST80.sbd.test -Server 10.0.10.11
Resolve-DnsName (Resolve-DnsName SBD-TEST80.sbd.test -Type A -Server 10.0.10.10).IPAddress -Type PTR -Server 10.0.10.10
Resolve-DnsName SBD-TEST80.sbd.test -Type DHCID -Server 10.0.10.10
# At SBD-DC01's console: the record's owner (sbd.test lives in DomainDnsZones in this sample)
Import-Module ActiveDirectory
(Get-Acl 'AD:DC=SBD-TEST80,DC=sbd.test,CN=MicrosoftDNS,DC=DomainDnsZones,DC=sbd,DC=test').Owner   # SBD\svc-dhcp-dns

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: The 10.0.80 reverse zone exists with secure updates; svc-dhcp-dns is in Domain Users only and DnsUpdateProxy is empty; Get-DhcpServerDnsCredential names svc-dhcp-dns; the server registers A and PTR records for every client with name protection and cleanup on; and the test client's A, PTR, and DHCID records answer from both controllers, owned by SBD\svc-dhcp-dns.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep the zone and account settings, the empty DnsUpdateProxy result, the server's DNS settings and the credential's account name (never the password), the audit-log lines for the update, both controllers' answers, and the record's owner.

lessons.title: Audit leases and write the restore note
lessons.summary: A router's deny log names addresses, not machines; the DHCP audit log is how you turn an address at a moment in time into a workstation. Keep that log longer than the week Windows keeps it, review who holds leases, know what an unauthorized DHCP server can and can't do here, and write the restore note that course 1.12's backup of the server relies on.
objectives: Read the DHCP audit log and keep each day's file beyond its weekly reuse.
Review leases and the authorized-server list, and explain what an unauthorized DHCP server does in a domain.
Explain why the automatic database copy isn't a backup, and write the restore note course 1.12's DHCP backup relies on.
recap: Each day's lease history is archived with a hash before Windows reuses the file.
Leases and the authorized-server list are reviewed; authorization stops only Windows servers.
The automatic database copy isn't a backup: course 1.12 backs the server up, and the credential step is written for its restore.
lessons.next: Lesson 41 proves the whole service with the test client and takes SBD-DHCP01's first baseline.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Use an isolated Windows Server practice environment. The network's routing and default-deny segmentation are in place, with the access control list (ACL) register that records every permitted path.

Provision each part's systems when the part begins: two Windows Server virtual machines for SBD-DC01 (10.0.10.10) and SBD-DC02 (10.0.10.11) on different hosts, then the PKI systems (part 6), the DHCP server (part 7) and the administration seats (part 8).

Work at each server's VM console with an authorized administrator account until part 8 builds AdminJumpBox01; after that, administration happens from the Tier 0 seats.

Have an approved connected system and the removable-media procedure for bringing downloaded DISA content and other software into the lab.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The addresses and names below continue the training example. Match every change to your own address plan. This network has no internet DNS dependency: names resolve on the domain controllers, and nothing is forwarded outside.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Read the audit log. Windows writes one file per weekday (DhcpSrvLog-Mon.log, and so on) in %windir%\System32\dhcp, each line carrying an event code, the time, the address, the host name, and the MAC address: 10 for a new lease, 11 a renewal, 12 a release, 30 and 32 a DNS update requested and done, 31 a failed one. Each file is reused a week later, and logging pauses when free disk space drops below the configured minimum, so check Get-DhcpServerAuditLog and keep that volume's free space well above it.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Keep every day: a daily task, running as SYSTEM shortly after midnight, copies the previous day's file to D:\DHCP\AuditArchive under its date and appends its SHA-256 hash to a catalog. Keep the copies as long as your records requirement says — the period depends on your environment and policy, so record the value you chose and why — because lease history is what ties an address in any log to a machine.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Review the leases each week: scope statistics show how full the pool is, and the lease list should hold only machines you know — today, just the test client. An unknown host name or MAC address is a finding to trace, not something to delete. The server's own event logs record every scope, option, exclusion, and reservation change with the account that made it, and warn when the scope is nearly full.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Know what an unauthorized DHCP server can do here. A Windows DHCP server in the domain that isn't authorized refuses to lease and logs event 1046, and a workgroup Windows server stops when it meets an authorized one on its network; a server of any other kind ignores authorization entirely and can hand clients its own gateway and DNS servers, a ready-made interception point. So check that Get-DhcpServerInDC lists SBD-DHCP01 alone and that clients' DHCP server is 10.0.20.10, and record that network controls, such as 802.1X admission in course 1.6, carry the rest.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: Write the restore note. Windows backs the DHCP database up every 60 minutes, but to %windir%\System32\dhcp\backup on the same disk, so that copy fails with the server and isn't a backup of it. Course 1.12 defines and schedules SBD-DHCP01's backup — the database and an export of the configuration and leases — with every other system's, so this part sets up no backup job. What belongs here is what a restore will need: the DNS update credential isn't in a DHCP backup, so after any restore it is set again with Set-DhcpServerDnsCredential from the sealed record, before names register.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
Get-DhcpServerAuditLog   # Enable: True; Path: C:\Windows\system32\dhcp
$dir = Join-Path $env:windir 'System32\dhcp'
Get-Content (Join-Path $dir ('DhcpSrvLog-{0}.log' -f (Get-Date).ToString('ddd', [cultureinfo]'en-US'))) -Tail 5
# The daily task's work (SYSTEM, 00:15): yesterday's file kept under its date, with its hash
New-Item -ItemType Directory D:\DHCP\AuditArchive -Force | Out-Null
$y = (Get-Date).AddDays(-1); $copy = 'D:\DHCP\AuditArchive\DhcpSrvLog-{0:yyyy-MM-dd}.log' -f $y
Copy-Item (Join-Path $dir ('DhcpSrvLog-{0}.log' -f $y.ToString('ddd', [cultureinfo]'en-US'))) $copy
Get-FileHash $copy -Algorithm SHA256 | Export-Csv D:\DHCP\AuditArchive\catalog.csv -Append -NoTypeInformation
# Weekly review: pool use, who holds leases, who may serve
Get-DhcpServerv4ScopeStatistics -ScopeId 10.0.80.0 | Select-Object ScopeId, InUse, Free, PercentageInUse
Get-DhcpServerv4Lease -ScopeId 10.0.80.0 | Select-Object IPAddress, HostName, ClientId, AddressState, LeaseExpiryTime
Get-DhcpServerInDC   # SBD-DHCP01 alone
# For the restore note: the automatic copy sits on the same disk (BackupPath), so course 1.12 schedules the real backup
Get-DhcpServerDatabase
Get-DhcpServerDnsCredential   # the account the note says to set again after any restore (never the password)

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: Audit logging is on with free space to spare; yesterday's file sits in the archive under its date, with its hash in the catalog; the lease list holds only known machines; Get-DhcpServerInDC lists SBD-DHCP01 alone; and the restore note names the credential step for course 1.12's backup.

quizzes.question: Why copy the DHCP audit log every day?
answers: Windows reuses each weekday's file a week later, so without copies the lease history is gone after seven days
The audit log is encrypted until it's copied

quizzes.explanation: The audit log is the bridge between an address in a router or firewall log and a machine. A week of history is rarely enough for an investigation, so the dated, hashed copies are the record.

quizzes.question: A server that isn't running Windows starts answering DHCP requests on VLAN 80. What does directory authorization do about it?
answers: It shuts the rogue server down
Nothing: authorization is a check Windows DHCP servers run on themselves, so other servers ignore it

quizzes.explanation: Authorization stops unauthorized Windows servers in the domain. Anything else is caught by network controls such as 802.1X admission, and by checking that clients got their lease from 10.0.20.10.

quizzes.question: SBD-DHCP01 is restored from a backup. What must happen before names register again?
answers: Nothing: everything is in the backup
The domain controllers must be authorized again
The DNS update credential must be set again, because the backup doesn't include it
quizzes.explanation: Microsoft notes that DHCP's DNS credentials aren't backed up. Keeping that step in the restore note that course 1.12 files with the backup means the rebuilt server registers names as the dedicated account again.

Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 C:\Evidence\dhcp-manifest.csv

lessons.title: Design the tiers and the admin seats
lessons.summary: Tiering is one sentence with teeth: credentials that control a tier never touch a less-trusted one. Write that policy against the OU structure and give each tier its seat and its group — all before any host is built.
objectives: Define the tiers and map each to systems, OUs, and admin accounts.
Assign each tier its admin seat under the Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) privileged access workstation (PAW) rules.
Write the credential rule each tier enforces.
recap: Three tiers, each with its systems, OU, admin seat, accounts, and group.
The credential rule is written before any host enforces it.
Each tier's management path and the VLAN 80 → VLAN 60 deny are register rows.
Tier 0 is the control plane; administer it only from seats of equal or higher trust.
lessons.next: Lesson 43 builds the seats the administrators will work from: two physical systems and one virtual machine.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Use an isolated Windows Server practice environment. The network's routing and default-deny segmentation are in place, with the access control list (ACL) register that records every permitted path.

Provision each part's systems when the part begins: two Windows Server virtual machines for SBD-DC01 (10.0.10.10) and SBD-DC02 (10.0.10.11) on different hosts, then the PKI systems (part 6), the DHCP server (part 7) and the administration seats (part 8).

Work at each server's VM console with an authorized administrator account until part 8 builds AdminJumpBox01; after that, administration happens from the Tier 0 seats.

Have an approved connected system and the removable-media procedure for bringing downloaded DISA content and other software into the lab.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The addresses and names below continue the training example. Match every change to your own address plan. This network has no internet DNS dependency: names resolve on the domain controllers, and nothing is forwarded outside.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Define three tiers against what exists, using Microsoft's rule: anything that can control a Tier 0 system is Tier 0. Tier 0 is the identity and trust fabric (DCs, both CAs, PKI-MGMT01) plus what controls it — the hypervisor hosts and their console, the core router's management, and the DC-facing parts of the tools that patch, protect, scan, monitor, and back up the DCs. Tier 1 is the member servers; Tier 2 the user endpoints. Map each tier to its OUs: Tier 0 to the Domain Controllers OU plus a new Tier 0 Servers OU for SBD-SUBCA01 and SBD-PKI-MGMT01 (lesson 44 moves them out of the Servers OU), Tier 1 to the Servers OU, where part 7's SBD-DHCP01 already sits, and Tier 2 to the Workstations OU.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Assign the admin seats under DISA's Windows PAW Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG): each privileged access workstation serves one tier (V-243445), and the one that manages the domain controllers is reserved for that work (V-243454, high severity). Where workstations are scarce, V-243445 allows one exception: lower-tier admin accounts in a virtual machine on a higher-tier seat, with the higher-tier accounts on the host. This network uses it to run three seats on two machines: AdminJumpBox01 for Tier 0, running no virtual machines, and SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 for Tier 1, which also runs SBD-ADMIN-PC01, the Tier 2 seat, as a virtual machine with its own name and address. Record the STIG differences in the exception record (AdminJumpBox01 manages all of Tier 0, not only the domain controllers; both physical seats run Windows Server where the STIG expects a Windows client, V-243447), and the PAW rules left open, such as smart-card sign-in (V-243457) and application allowlisting (V-243450, V-243451).

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Write the credential rule per tier: a Tier 0 account signs in only on Tier 0 systems and AdminJumpBox01; Tier 1 admins work on the SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 host; Tier 2 admins only inside the SBD-ADMIN-PC01 virtual machine, never on its host. The audit custodian uses separate accounts and sessions on SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 that ordinary server operators cannot use, and is refused on Tier 2 machines like the higher tiers. Each administrator gets separate per-tier accounts — the daily account holds no admin rights anywhere — gathered in one group per role in the Admin OU: SBD Tier 0 Admins, SBD Tier 1 Admins (part 7 created it for SBD-DHCP01), SBD Tier 2 Admins, and SBD Audit Custodians in this sample.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Add the register rows this part needs: VLAN 60 to each tier's management ports (rules A01–A04 in the System Hub), and explicit denies from VLAN 80 into VLAN 60 — user space never initiates toward the admin plane. A02 already names SBD-DHCP01, whose administration moves to SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 in lesson 2.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: The Active Directory design reference treats the directory's control plane as Tier 0: the domain controllers, AD CS, and the accounts, groups and workstations that manage them. Administer each tier only from a device of equal or higher trust, the clean-source principle; put privileged accounts in Protected Users; and keep Tier 0 credentials off lower-tier systems. This part builds the administration seats that put those rules into practice.

sections.body: The tier map names systems, OUs, admin seats, accounts, and groups per tier, with SBD-ADMIN-PC01 a virtual machine on SBD-ADMIN-SRV01; the exception record holds the seat plan's STIG differences and open PAW items; the role groups exist in the Admin OU; and the register has the new permit and deny rows with owners.

quizzes.question: What is the one-sentence tiering rule?
answers: Admins should use strong passwords
Credentials that control a tier never sign in to a less-trusted tier
Every admin needs Domain Admin rights
quizzes.explanation: Everything else in the model — hosts, OUs, logon policies — exists to enforce that single sentence.

quizzes.question: Why does each administrator get separate per-tier accounts?
answers: So a credential captured on a lower tier cannot open a higher one
Licensing counts accounts per tier
Password policies require it
quizzes.explanation: Credential theft travels with sign-ins. Separate accounts bound what any one capture is worth.

quizzes.question: Which direction does the register explicitly deny?
answers: Admin VLAN to the tiers it manages
DCs to anything
User VLAN 80 initiating into the admin VLAN 60
quizzes.explanation: The admin plane reaches down to manage; user space never reaches up. The deny row makes that a logged fact, not an intention.

quizzes.question: SBD-WSUS01 approves the updates the domain controllers install. Which tier administers the domain controllers' update ring?
answers: Tier 1, because WSUS is a member server
Tier 0, because anything that can push code to a DC can control it
Tier 2, because updates start on workstations
quizzes.explanation: Microsoft's tier model treats systems that patch, scan, monitor, protect, back up, or host Tier 0 as Tier 0. The DC-facing scope of a tool belongs to Tier 0 even when the server itself sits in a member-server VLAN.

quizzes.question: To save a machine, one admin seat will run another as a virtual machine. Which arrangement does DISA's Windows PAW STIG accept?
answers: The Tier 2 seat as a virtual machine on AdminJumpBox01
Tier 1 and Tier 2 accounts both signed in on the SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 host
The Tier 2 seat as a virtual machine on SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, with Tier 1 accounts on the host and Tier 2 accounts only inside it
quizzes.explanation: The exception puts lower-tier admin accounts in a virtual machine on a higher-tier seat, with the higher-tier accounts on the host. The seat that manages the domain controllers is reserved for that work, so it never hosts a lower tier.

quizzes.question: What does the clean-source principle require?
answers: Administer a tier only from a device of equal or higher trust
Use one administrator account everywhere
Keep administration workstations off the domain
quizzes.explanation: A device that manages Tier 0 must be at least as trusted as Tier 0, so administration happens only from the Tier 0 seats.

lessons.title: Build the administration systems
lessons.summary: Privileged work gets dedicated, hardened seats: a Tier 0 jump host that runs no virtual machines, and a server-administration seat that also runs the endpoint seat as a virtual machine. Each seat sits in the Admin OU, does nothing but administer, and is maintained by its own group.
objectives: Link the hardening policies to the Admin OU's computer sub-OUs, then build the two seats and the seat virtual machine into them, each with its own Group Policy object (GPO) and maintenance group.
Run SBD-ADMIN-PC01 as a virtual machine on SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 with its own name and address, and close the channels that share data between host and guest.
Keep the seats single-purpose, with each tier's tools on its own seat, and move earlier courses' console work onto them.
Register and restrict their management paths.
recap: Two seats and a seat virtual machine, hardened from first boot; AdminJumpBox01 runs no virtual machines.
Each seat has its own maintenance group; host and guest share no clipboard, drives, or folders.
Management flows outward only; VLAN 60 accepts nothing inbound.
Every management path is a register row.
lessons.next: Lesson 44 makes the credential rule something the directory enforces.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Use an isolated Windows Server practice environment. The network's routing and default-deny segmentation are in place, with the access control list (ACL) register that records every permitted path.

Provision each part's systems when the part begins: two Windows Server virtual machines for SBD-DC01 (10.0.10.10) and SBD-DC02 (10.0.10.11) on different hosts, then the PKI systems (part 6), the DHCP server (part 7) and the administration seats (part 8).

Work at each server's VM console with an authorized administrator account until part 8 builds AdminJumpBox01; after that, administration happens from the Tier 0 seats.

Have an approved connected system and the removable-media procedure for bringing downloaded DISA content and other software into the lab.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The addresses and names below continue the training example. Match every change to your own address plan. This network has no internet DNS dependency: names resolve on the domain controllers, and nothing is forwarded outside.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Create two computer sub-OUs under the Admin OU — Admin Servers for AdminJumpBox01 and SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, Admin Workstations for the SBD-ADMIN-PC01 virtual machine — and link part 5's STIG GPOs to them before any seat joins: the member-server computer policy, the user policy, and the loopback (Merge) GPO to Admin Servers, and the Windows client computer and user policies, which part 5 imported but left unlinked, with the same loopback GPO to Admin Workstations. Part 5 linked them only to the Domain Controllers and Servers OUs, so without this step the seats would boot unhardened.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Build AdminJumpBox01 and SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 as clean Windows Server installs and join both into Admin Servers, so the hardening applies from first boot; AdminJumpBox01 never gets the Hyper-V role or a virtual machine, because the seat that manages the domain controllers never hosts a lower tier. Give every seat its own seat GPO, linked above the STIG GPO — one on Admin Workstations, and two on Admin Servers, each filtered to its seat (deny Apply group policy to the other) — that makes the seat's own maintenance group (SBD PAW Maintenance T0, T1, or T2 in this sample), used for nothing else, the only domain group in its local Administrators: the PAW STIG gives tier accounts user rights only on their seat (V-243456, V-243462), and no group spans tiers. SBD-ADMIN-SRV01's GPO also adds NT VIRTUAL MACHINE\Virtual Machines (*S-1-5-83-0) to Create symbolic links beside Administrators: Group Policy replaces the right's local value, and without that entry, which the STIG accepts on Hyper-V hosts, the virtual machine won't start. Lesson 44 adds each seat's sign-in rights.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Add the Hyper-V role to SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 and create SBD-ADMIN-PC01 as a generation 2 virtual machine with Secure Boot and a virtual Trusted Platform Module (TPM), set to start whenever the host starts. The Windows client needs the TPM, and Credential Guard, which the Windows client STIG requires, runs in a virtual machine only on generation 2 and on a host with an input–output memory management unit (IOMMU). Connect it through an external virtual switch on the seat's VLAN 60 adapter with its own address, 10.0.60.30, install the Enterprise or Education edition of the Windows client, and join it into Admin Workstations. Because it keeps its own name and address, the register's rule for SBD-ADMIN-PC01 (A03) still names it alone, never its host.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Close the channels that share data between host and guest, because the virtual machine separates the tiers only while they share nothing they don't need: turn off enhanced session mode on the host, so the console carries only screen, keyboard, and mouse, with no shared clipboard, drives, or devices; keep the Guest Service Interface off, so the host can't copy files in; turn off Key-Value Pair Exchange, which passes data both ways; turn off Time Synchronization, because the guest takes its time from the domain like every virtual machine (part 3); and add no shared folders. What remains, the basic integration services and PowerShell Direct (which can run commands and copy files either way), needs Hyper-V administrator rights on the host, and PowerShell Direct also needs an account in the guest. Administrators who hold both a Tier 1 and a Tier 2 account open the console from the host with the Tier 1 account, which SBD-ADMIN-SRV01's seat GPO puts in the local Hyper-V Administrators group — the one privileged local group the PAW STIG lets a Hyper-V seat fill (V-243463), so they need no host administrator rights — and sign in inside with the Tier 2 one. One person uses the console at a time and signs out of the virtual machine before closing it, because without enhanced session mode the next person to connect takes over an open desktop; a Tier 2-only administrator needs a seat of their own.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: Strip them to purpose: no browsing to anything but internal admin interfaces, no mail, no file shares hosted, and the management tools for exactly their tier — Remote Server Administration Tools (RSAT) on the two server seats, endpoint tooling inside the SBD-ADMIN-PC01 virtual machine — with SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 running that one virtual machine and no other. Then move the console work earlier courses did onto the seats: Tier 0 directory, DNS, and DHCP authorization work moves from SBD-DC01's console to AdminJumpBox01, so remove the DHCP management tools part 7 added to SBD-DC01; and SBD-DHCP01 is administered from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 with Tier 1 accounts, over the remote desktop and remote management paths rule A02 registers, no longer at its console.

sections.heading: Step 6
sections.body: Register the management paths: VLAN 60 to Tier 0 and Tier 1 ports (remote desktop 3389, remote management 5985–5986, AD Web Services 9389 to the domain controllers, SSH 22 for the domain-joined Linux servers) from the specific admin host each tier allows, and the router's management on VLAN 100 from AdminJumpBox01 only; keep the VLAN 80 → VLAN 60 deny from lesson 42 in force. Require the admin seats' own local firewalls, the virtual machine's included, to accept management inbound from nowhere — sessions originate here, they never terminate here, so neither the host nor its guest can manage the other over the network. On both domain controllers, scope the existing Remote Desktop, Windows Remote Management, and Active Directory Web Services firewall rules to AdminJumpBox01 and VLAN 10: allow rules add up, so a new, narrower rule would not restrict the broad ones already enabled.

(Get-VMFirmware SBD-ADMIN-PC01).SecureBoot; (Get-VMSecurity SBD-ADMIN-PC01).TpmEnabled
Get-VMHost | Select-Object EnableEnhancedSessionMode   # False
Get-VMIntegrationService SBD-ADMIN-PC01 | Select-Object Name, Enabled   # Guest Service Interface, Key-Value Pair Exchange, Time Synchronization: False

Test-NetConnection SBD-DC01.sbd.test -Port 5985
gpresult /r /scope:computer

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: AdminJumpBox01 and SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 sit in Admin Servers and the SBD-ADMIN-PC01 virtual machine in Admin Workstations, with the STIG and seat GPOs applied; each seat's local Administrators holds its maintenance group, no tier group; SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 runs only SBD-ADMIN-PC01 (10.0.60.30, generation 2, Secure Boot on, TPM, Credential Guard, starts with the host) with enhanced session mode, the Guest Service Interface, Key-Value Pair Exchange, and Time Synchronization off, and the guest takes its time from a domain controller; AdminJumpBox01 has no Hyper-V role; SBD-DHCP01 is managed from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 and the DHCP tools are gone from SBD-DC01; management ports answer from the correct seat per tier; and user space can open no session toward VLAN 60.

quizzes.question: Why do the admin hosts run nothing but administration?
answers: Extra software costs licenses
Every extra capability — mail, browsing, documents — is a way to phish or poison the most valuable sessions on the network
Admin tools conflict with browsers
quizzes.explanation: These hosts carry privileged credentials. Minimizing what runs on them minimizes what can steal from them.

quizzes.question: Which way do management sessions flow?
answers: From the admin hosts outward to their tier — never inbound to the admin hosts
In both directions equally
From workstations to the jump box
quizzes.explanation: The admin plane originates; it never serves. Inbound-nothing is what keeps a compromised endpoint from riding into VLAN 60.

quizzes.question: Why link the STIG GPOs to the Admin sub-OUs before the seats join?
answers: The seats cannot join the domain otherwise
The OU name requires it
Part 5 linked them only to the Domain Controllers and Servers OUs, so the seats would otherwise boot unhardened
quizzes.explanation: Policy follows links, not names. Linking first means each seat is STIG-configured from its first boot, before it ever does privileged work.

quizzes.question: Why does SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 run with enhanced session mode off?
answers: It makes the virtual machine start faster
Enhanced session mode carries the clipboard, drives, and devices between host and guest — exactly what the tier boundary must stop
The Windows client cannot run in enhanced session mode
quizzes.explanation: The virtual machine separates the tiers only while host and guest share nothing they don't need. Enhanced session mode shares local resources such as the clipboard, drives, and devices with the guest; without it, the console carries only the screen, keyboard, and mouse.

quizzes.question: Why does SBD-ADMIN-PC01 keep its own name and address as a virtual machine?
answers: So the register and the host firewalls still tell the Tier 2 seat apart from its host
Hyper-V cannot start a virtual machine without its own address
It lets the virtual machine skip the Admin Workstations policies
quizzes.explanation: Rule A03 names SBD-ADMIN-PC01 alone, and later courses let the workstations accept management only from 10.0.60.30. With its own address, the Tier 2 seat stays a separate source on the network, and its host gets nothing those rules allow.

quizzes.question: Who holds administrator rights on the admin seats?
answers: The tier accounts that work on each seat
Each seat's own maintenance group, used for nothing else
Domain Admins, added when each seat joins the domain
quizzes.explanation: The PAW STIG keeps the accounts that manage high-value systems to user rights on their seat, so they can't weaken it. A maintenance group per seat builds and patches it, so no group spans tiers, and the seat GPO makes it the only domain group in that seat's local Administrators.

checklist: I linked the STIG GPOs to Admin Servers and Admin Workstations before joining the seats, and gpresult shows them applied.
I confirmed each tier’s management ports answer from that tier’s admin seat and that nothing in user space can open a session toward VLAN 60.
I scoped the existing Remote Desktop, Windows Remote Management, and AD Web Services rules on both domain controllers to AdminJumpBox01 and VLAN 10.

lessons.title: Restrict where privilege can sign in
lessons.summary: The tier rule becomes real when the directory refuses the wrong sign-in. Give Tier 0 servers their own OU first, deny privileged logons on lower tiers by policy, protect the highest accounts, and make the refusal something you can show in a log.
objectives: Move the Tier 0 member servers into their own OU before any deny policy lands.

Enforce per-tier sign-in restrictions and administrators with Group Policy — on the tier OUs, every admin seat, and both sides of the seat virtual machine — and record the one network-logon exception.
Protect Tier 0 accounts and prove a cross-tier sign-in is denied and logged.
recap: Tier 0 servers have their own OU, so the deny policies never lock Tier 0 out.

sections.body:
Use an isolated Windows Server practice environment. The network's routing and default-deny segmentation are in place, with the access control list (ACL) register that records every permitted path.

Provision each part's systems when the part begins: two Windows Server virtual machines for SBD-DC01 (10.0.10.10) and SBD-DC02 (10.0.10.11) on different hosts, then the PKI systems (part 6), the DHCP server (part 7) and the administration seats (part 8).

Have an approved connected system and the removable-media procedure for bringing downloaded DISA content and other software into the lab.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The addresses and names below continue the training example. Match every change to your own address plan. This network has no internet DNS dependency: names resolve on the domain controllers, and nothing is forwarded outside.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Create the Tier 0 Servers OU (OU=Tier 0 Servers,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test) with deletion protection, link part 5's member-server STIG GPOs to it — the computer policy, the user policy, and the loopback GPO — so nothing loses its hardening, and move SBD-SUBCA01 and SBD-PKI-MGMT01 there. Both are Tier 0, and the Servers OU is about to deny Tier 0 sign-ins — left there, they would lock Tier 0 out of its own systems.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Create one tier logon GPO for the Servers OU — now Tier 1 only — and one for the Workstations OU, and never link either to the Domain Controllers or Tier 0 Servers OUs. User rights don't merge across GPOs: for each right, the highest-precedence GPO that sets it wins, so each list repeats the entries part 5's STIG GPO sets for that right (such as Domain Admins and Enterprise Admins), and the tier GPO links above the STIG GPO. On the Servers OU, give SBD Tier 0 Admins Deny log on locally, Deny log on through Remote Desktop Services, Deny log on as a batch job, and Deny log on as a service. On the Workstations OU, give SBD Tier 0 Admins, SBD Tier 1 Admins, and SBD Audit Custodians those four denies plus Deny access to this computer from the network: the custodian's accounts administer the audit record, so they never sign in where Tier 2 risks apply.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Give the tier OUs their administrators. Now that the Tier 0 servers are out, a GPO linked only to the Servers OU adds SBD Tier 1 Admins to each server's local Administrators group and removes Domain Admins (Group Policy Preferences, Local Users and Groups), as the member-server STIG expects, so every server joined there, starting with SBD-DHCP01, is run by Tier 1 from first boot; kept apart from the tier logon GPO, it lets an OU with its own administrators, such as course 1.4's Audit Servers OU, take the denies without this grant. Then join part 7's VLAN 80 test client to the domain with a Tier 2 account, delegated Create Computer objects on the Workstations OU as part 7 did for Tier 1 on the Servers OU; the part 5 redirect lands it in Workstations. Add SBD Tier 2 Admins to its local Administrators and turn on remote management there, accepted only from SBD-ADMIN-PC01 (10.0.60.30), so it can serve as this part's Tier 2 test machine.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: On the Servers OU, set Deny access to this computer from the network — SBD Tier 0 Admins plus the STIG's entries — in a separate GPO that excludes the SBD Tier 0 Console Hosts group through security filtering (deny Apply group policy). Course 1.7 adds SBD-WSUS01 to that group, so Tier 0 can manage the domain controllers' update ring there from AdminJumpBox01 with Tier 0 task accounts outside Domain Admins and Enterprise Admins (which the STIG denies network logon on member servers), and SBD-EPO01's console will join it when course 1.9, coming soon, arrives; a Kerberos network logon leaves no reusable credentials on the server. Record the exception — the group, the servers as they join it, the accounts, the reason, and its owner — in the part 5 exception record. Link both deny GPOs, this one and the tier logon GPO, to any OU created later for member servers, such as course 1.4's Audit Servers OU, before a server joins it; step 3's administrators GPO never goes there.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: Finish the seat GPOs from lesson 43 so each seat admits only its own tier, on both sides of the seat virtual machine. Allow log on locally replaces the STIG's list with Administrators and the seat's own groups: SBD Tier 0 Admins on AdminJumpBox01 (every Tier 0 account, Domain Admins and Enterprise Admins members included), SBD Tier 1 Admins and SBD Audit Custodians on SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, and SBD Tier 2 Admins inside SBD-ADMIN-PC01 (V-243452; V-243455 for the seat that manages Active Directory). The four denies plus Deny access to this computer from the network go to the other tiers: Tier 0, Tier 1, and SBD Audit Custodians inside the virtual machine, Tier 0 and Tier 2 on SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, Tier 1 and Tier 2 on AdminJumpBox01. The PAW STIG requires the higher-tier denies (V-243453, high severity if a Tier 0 account can sign in). Each deny list repeats the STIG GPO's entries for that right, except that AdminJumpBox01 leaves Domain Admins and Enterprise Admins out of Deny log on locally, because V-243455 admits them there. Record every STIG value these settings change in the exception record.

sections.heading: Step 6
sections.body: Add Tier 0 administrators to the Protected Users group so the domain refuses their weaker authentication paths, and note the behavior of the newest Windows Server release that supports this design: RC4 ticket-granting tickets are gone and legacy remote password changes are blocked for protected accounts. Protected Users accounts also cannot be delegated, which keeps the console exception free of reusable credentials. Keep the built-in safety valve: one documented break-glass account, excluded from the deny policies and used at a domain controller's console (the admin seats admit only their own tiers), with its password sealed and its every use alarmed once course 1.5 builds the alerts. Record the multifactor decision the model calls for on VLAN 60 — smart card or certificate-based sign-in for privileged accounts is the natural follow-on to part 6's templates — with its target date, even if implementation waits.

sections.body:
Get-ADComputer -SearchBase 'OU=Tier 0 Servers,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test' -Filter * | Select-Object Name
Get-ADGroupMember 'Protected Users' | Select-Object Name
Invoke-Command SBD-DHCP01.sbd.test { Get-LocalGroupMember Administrators }   # from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01: SBD Tier 1 Admins, no Domain Admins
dsacls 'OU=Workstations,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test' /G 'SBD\SBD Tier 2 Admins:CC;computer'   # from AdminJumpBox01 (Tier 0)
# On the test client, as its local administrator: join with a Tier 2 account, then, after the restart, its managers
Add-Computer -DomainName sbd.test -Credential (Get-Credential) -Restart
Add-LocalGroupMember Administrators -Member 'SBD\SBD Tier 2 Admins'; Enable-PSRemoting -Force
Set-NetFirewallRule -DisplayGroup 'Windows Remote Management' -RemoteAddress 10.0.60.30
# On the Tier 2 test machine: export the effective logon rights and read the deny lines.
secedit /export /mergedpolicy /cfg C:\Evidence\tiered-admin\user-rights.inf /areas user_rights
Select-String -Path C:\Evidence\tiered-admin\user-rights.inf -Pattern 'SeDeny'
'SBD Tier 0 Admins', 'SBD Tier 1 Admins', 'SBD Audit Custodians' | ForEach-Object { (Get-ADGroup $_).SID.Value }   # from an admin seat: these SIDs must appear on those lines
# Repeat on each seat as its maintenance account, and read who may sign in there.
Select-String -Path C:\Evidence\tiered-admin\user-rights.inf -Pattern 'SeInteractive'
# After the refused Tier 0 sign-in: event 4625 with status 0xC000015B (logon type not granted).
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4625; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddHours(-1)} | Where-Object Message -match '0xC000015B' | Select-Object TimeCreated, Id

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: SBD-SUBCA01 and SBD-PKI-MGMT01 sit in the Tier 0 Servers OU and still accept Tier 0 sign-ins; the Servers OU's administrators GPO puts SBD Tier 1 Admins, not Domain Admins, in SBD-DHCP01's local Administrators; on the Tier 2 test machine, part 7's test client now in the Workstations OU, the deny rights list the SIDs of the Tier 0, Tier 1, and audit custodian groups, and a Tier 0 sign-in there is refused with Security event 4625 (status 0xC000015B); each admin seat lets only its own groups sign in and denies the other tiers — Tier 0, Tier 1, and the audit custodians inside SBD-ADMIN-PC01, Tier 0 and Tier 2 on SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, Tier 1 and Tier 2 on AdminJumpBox01; the exception record holds the console network-logon exception and the seat GPOs' STIG differences; Protected Users contains the Tier 0 admins; and the break-glass and MFA decisions are written.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep the Tier 0 Servers OU move, the logon-rights and administrators GPO reports with their links and security filtering, the user-rights exports from the test machine and each seat, the refused sign-in's 4625 event, the exception record entries, the Protected Users membership, and the break-glass and MFA decision records.

quizzes.question: What turns the tier rule from policy into enforcement?
answers: An email to administrators
Deny-logon rights applied by GPO at each lower tier's OU
Renaming the admin accounts
quizzes.explanation: The OU-linked deny rights are the mechanism: the directory itself refuses the out-of-tier sign-in.

quizzes.question: What does Protected Users membership buy a Tier 0 account?
answers: Faster sign-ins
Exemption from password changes
The domain refuses its weaker authentication paths, shrinking what a credential thief can replay
quizzes.explanation: Protected Users trades convenience for resistance — appropriate exactly for the accounts whose theft ends the network.

quizzes.question: Why does a break-glass account exist outside the deny policies?
answers: So a policy mistake cannot lock every administrator out — and its sealed, alarmed use keeps the exception honest
Because every admin wants one
Deny policies cannot apply to more than ten accounts
quizzes.explanation: Strict tiering needs one documented escape hatch. Sealing and alarming it is what keeps the hatch from becoming a habit.

quizzes.question: Why do SBD-SUBCA01 and SBD-PKI-MGMT01 move out of the Servers OU before the deny policy is linked?
answers: The Servers OU has reached its size limit
They are Tier 0: the Servers OU now denies Tier 0 sign-ins, so they would lock Tier 0 out of its own systems
Certificate Services cannot run in an OU with linked policies
quizzes.explanation: Tier follows control, not hostname. Systems that control Tier 0 need an OU where Tier 0 can sign in and the lower-tier denies never apply.

quizzes.question: Why may Tier 0 still use a network logon on SBD-WSUS01 once course 1.7 builds it?
answers: Tier 0 manages the domain controllers' update ring there, and a Kerberos network logon leaves no reusable credentials on the server
Network logons are never logged
SBD-WSUS01 sits in the Tier 0 Servers OU
quizzes.explanation: Interactive, Remote Desktop, batch, and service logons leave reusable credentials behind; a Kerberos network logon does not, and Protected Users accounts cannot be delegated. The exception is narrow, named, and recorded.

quizzes.question: Why deny Tier 1 accounts inside the SBD-ADMIN-PC01 virtual machine when its host is the Tier 1 seat?
answers: Tier 1 accounts cannot use Hyper-V
Virtual machines refuse every domain account by default
The virtual machine is a Tier 2 system: a Tier 1 credential used inside it could be stolen there
quizzes.explanation: The host's tier doesn't travel into the guest. Inside the virtual machine, Tier 2 accounts work and Tier 2 risks apply, so a higher-tier sign-in there — or an audit custodian's — is exactly the exposure the tier rule forbids.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Complete course 1.1: the domain with DNS and part 3's time design with its chrony file, the part 4 media procedure and DISA tooling, part 6's root certificate and the hash it recorded, and the tiered administration plane, with SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 as the Tier 1 seat.

Provision a virtual machine for SBD-REPO01 on VLAN 70 (10.0.70.20) with a separate data disk for /srv (it holds /srv/repo, /srv/incoming and /srv/repo-records), and install media for the one Red Hat Enterprise Linux–family release your Linux servers will use, with the vendor's published checksum.

Have an approved connected system that can reach the distribution's repositories (for Red Hat Enterprise Linux, a registered system of the same release and architecture) and the removable-media procedure for carrying the mirror across.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: SBD-REPO01 is the Linux side's one road for operating-system packages, built before any Linux server exists so that SBD-SPLUNK01 (course 1.5) patches from it from its first day. It also stages the Linux assessment set, SCC for Linux and the distribution's STIG benchmark, that every Linux server is scanned with. Every Linux server in the lab runs a Red Hat Enterprise Linux–family distribution, so the commands use dnf, rpm, firewalld and update-ca-trust; choose one release for every Linux server and follow it throughout.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Write the repository's job: the only source of operating-system packages for the domain-joined Linux servers (SBD-SPLUNK01 in course 1.5, SBD-WEB01 in course 1.11, and SBD-NESSUS01 when course 1.10, coming soon, arrives) and for SBD-REPO01 itself. Application software, such as Splunk in course 1.5 and SCC for Linux in lesson 5, still arrives as hashed vendor media; anything else is a documented exception, never a second source.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Choose one Red Hat Enterprise Linux–family distribution and major release for every Linux server, one with a published DISA STIG and a SCAP benchmark that SCC for Linux supports, so there is one mirror to feed and one benchmark to scan against. Mirror only its operating-system repositories for one architecture: BaseOS and AppStream. Third-party repositories stay out.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Decide the trust anchor: the vendor's signing keys. Get each key file, read its fingerprint, and compare it with the vendor's published value through a second channel before anything is published; the fingerprints go into the snapshot catalog. Each published mirror is a dated snapshot, and that date is the repository's version.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Place it as the System Hub does: SBD-REPO01 at 10.0.70.20 on VLAN 70, not domain-joined, administered over SSH 22 from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 only (rule A02, Tier 1). Confirm the register rows: the Linux servers to REPO01 on HTTP 80 (F19), REPO01 to both domain controllers for DNS (F01), and REPO01's syslog over TLS to the collector (F07, enabled when course 1.3 builds it). Rule F09 lists only domain members for time, so add SBD-REPO01's own time row, to both controllers on UDP 123, with an owner and a reason, as course 1.1, part 3 planned.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
# On SBD-ADMIN-SRV01: start the evidence folder and confirm no record exists yet
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force C:\Evidence\linux-repository | Out-Null
Resolve-DnsName SBD-REPO01.sbd.test -Server 10.0.10.10 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue   # expected: no answer yet
# On the approved connected system: read each upstream signing key's fingerprint
gpg --show-keys --with-fingerprint /etc/pki/rpm-gpg/RPM-GPG-KEY-redhat-release   # or the distribution's own key file

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: The design names the consumers, the one distribution and the repositories mirrored; each upstream key's fingerprint matches the vendor's published value; and the register carries F19, F01, F07 and SBD-REPO01's added time row, each with an owner.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep the repository design (job, consumers, distribution, repositories, snapshot naming), the verified key fingerprints with where you checked them, and the register rows that name SBD-REPO01.
