lessons.title: Prepare the fleet rollout
lessons.summary: Fifty of anything needs a factory, not fifty craft projects. Settle the image, the names, the join account, and the policy links so every endpoint is born identical — then prove it on paper before proving it on metal.
objectives: Finalize the reference image and naming plan for fifty endpoints.
Create a least-privilege join account scoped to the Workstations OU.
Link the Windows client STIG policies and the local Administrators, firewall and DNS registration policies to the Workstations OU before any join, below course 1.1's tier logon GPO.
recap: One hashed image, one naming plan, waves instead of a big bang.
The join credential can create computer objects and nothing else.
The Workstations OU is armed with policy, and its managers named, before it holds a machine — with course 1.1's tier denies still first.
Peer SMB and Remote Desktop are blocked by each PC's own firewall, set by policy before the first join.
lessons.next: Lesson 2 joins the pilot and inspects everything a first boot should bring.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Complete courses 1.1–1.5: the part 6 PKI with its SBD Computer Authentication template and the SBD Certificate Autoenrollment GPO at the domain root, SBD-DHCP01 (part 7), whose relay part 7 verified, the three administration seats (part 8), with SBD-ADMIN-PC01's own SCC copy and first baseline, and the logging pipeline (courses 1.3–1.5), on the network's routed, segmented VLANs.

Prepare a patched Windows client reference image (or template) for the fifty endpoints, obtained through the approved offline media process.

Confirm the Workstations OU and the computer redirect from course 1.1, part 5, and the Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG) Group Policy objects (GPOs) for your Windows client release, imported in part 5 from the package part 4 staged and still unlinked there. Lesson 7 reuses SBD-ADMIN-PC01's own SCC copy, which part 8 installed with the Windows client benchmark part 4 staged, and the checked installer and connected-side-hashes.csv part 8 kept in C:\Staging\DISA there.

Confirm the VLAN 80 access switch supports 802.1X port authentication, including a monitor (audit) mode that logs each result without blocking traffic. No new server is needed: the Network Policy Server (NPS) role goes on SBD-DHCP01.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: Fifty endpoints join a network that is finally ready for them: addressed by DHCP, landed by OU redirect, hardened by policy at first boot, certified by autoenrollment, and watched by the pipeline from their first sign-in. Tier 0 steps run from AdminJumpBox01, Tier 1 steps on SBD-DHCP01 from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, and Tier 2 steps inside SBD-ADMIN-PC01; each seat keeps its part of the record under C:\Evidence\workstation-fleet. The sample names run SBD-PC01 through SBD-PC50; match them to your own plan.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Finalize the Windows client reference image: current patches via the approved media process, no preinstalled extras, one local administrator account for Windows LAPS to manage (the Windows client STIG disables the built-in Administrator), and a generalized state so each clone takes its own identity. Record the image version and hash — it is the fleet's common ancestor and belongs in evidence.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Write the naming and rollout plan: SBD-PC01–SBD-PC50, addressed by the course 1.1 DHCP scope, joined in waves (pilot of three, then batches) rather than all fifty at once.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: From AdminJumpBox01, create a dedicated domain-join account delegated only Create Computer objects on the Workstations OU — no broader privilege rides along with fifty join operations — and record it beside the same delegation course 1.1, part 8 gave SBD Tier 2 Admins for its test client. The part 5 redirect already guarantees machines land in that OU. Add a GPO, linked only to the Workstations OU, that makes SBD Tier 2 Admins the managing group in each PC's local Administrators (Group Policy Preferences, Local Users and Groups), as part 8 did by hand on its test client; part 8's tier logon GPO already denies sign-ins there to SBD Tier 0 Admins, SBD Tier 1 Admins and SBD Audit Custodians.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Link the DISA Windows client policies that course 1.1, part 5 imported and left unlinked to the Workstations OU now — the computer policy, the user policy, and part 5's loopback (Merge) GPO, as part 8 did for Admin Workstations — so the very first pilot boots into the hardened state, and note that the Windows client's own secure defaults will already satisfy some checks, just as Windows Server's did. Link each of them below part 8's tier logon GPO, which keeps link order 1 on the Workstations OU: user rights don't merge across GPOs, so a STIG GPO linked above it would win and drop the denies for Tier 0, Tier 1 and SBD Audit Custodians. Every GPO this course links to the OU goes below it.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: Create the workstation firewall GPO (SBD Workstation Firewall in this sample) on the Workstations OU: Windows Defender Firewall on for every profile with inbound traffic blocked by default, and inbound rules that allow Remote Desktop (TCP 3389) and remote management (TCP 5985–5986) only from SBD-ADMIN-PC01 at 10.0.60.30 — the ports its register row, A03, carries. No rule allows SMB or Remote Desktop between workstations: traffic inside VLAN 80 never reaches the router, so this policy, not the core router's rules, enforces the register's peer denies. Then turn off the PCs' own DNS registration in a separate GPO on the same OU (SBD Workstation DNS in this sample): Computer Configuration > Policies > Administrative Templates > Network > DNS Client > Dynamic update, Disabled. Record the reason with the GPO: SBD-DHCP01 already registers each PC's A and PTR records under svc-dhcp-dns (course 1.1, part 7), and a client that registers its own record can take it over, so the DHCP server's account can no longer update it — one owner per record.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 C:\Staging\Windows-client-reference.vhdx
# On AdminJumpBox01 (Tier 0): the join account's delegation (svc-fleet-join in this sample) and the OU's links
(Get-Acl 'AD:\OU=Workstations,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test').Access | Where-Object IdentityReference -match 'svc-fleet-join|SBD Tier 2 Admins' | Select-Object IdentityReference, ActiveDirectoryRights, ObjectType
(Get-GPInheritance -Target 'OU=Workstations,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test').GpoLinks | Select-Object Order, DisplayName   # course 1.1's tier logon GPO stays at order 1
Get-GPOReport -Name 'SBD Workstation Firewall' -ReportType Html -Path C:\Evidence\workstation-fleet\workstation-firewall.html
Get-GPOReport -Name 'SBD Workstation DNS' -ReportType Html -Path C:\Evidence\workstation-fleet\workstation-dns.html

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: The image is hashed and recorded, the join account holds only Create Computer objects on the Workstations OU, and the client STIG, loopback, local Administrators, firewall and DNS registration GPO links show on that OU below course 1.1's tier logon GPO, still at link order 1, before any machine exists in it.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep the image record with its hash, the naming and wave plan, the delegation output for the join account and SBD Tier 2 Admins, the OU's GPO links in order, and the firewall and DNS registration GPO reports with the recorded reason.

quizzes.question: Why does the join account get only create-computer rights on one OU?
answers: Join operations fail with more rights
Fifty joins should carry the least privilege possible — a stolen join credential then creates computer objects, nothing more
Delegation is faster than Domain Admin
quizzes.explanation: Scale multiplies exposure. Scoping the account bounds what the rollout's most-used credential is worth to an attacker.

quizzes.question: Why link the STIG policies before the first machine joins?
answers: So every endpoint's first boot is already the hardened state — no window where an unmanaged machine exists
GPO links expire if unused
The OU cannot be created otherwise
quizzes.explanation: The redirect lands them in the OU, and the pre-linked policy means compliance from minute one — the course 1.1 design, now paying off at scale.

quizzes.question: What makes the reference image part of the evidence?
answers: Images are always evidence
It contains the domain password
Its recorded version and hash are what make fifty 'identical' endpoints a claim you can verify
quizzes.explanation: A configuration record for the fleet starts with the common ancestor. The hash is how an assessor — or future you — confirms descent.

quizzes.question: What stops one workstation from opening SMB or Remote Desktop to another?
answers: The router's access control lists
Each PC's own firewall, set by the workstation firewall GPO — traffic inside VLAN 80 never reaches the router
SBD-DHCP01, which refuses leases to a PC that tries it
quizzes.explanation: Two PCs in VLAN 80 talk through the access switch, so the router never sees their traffic. Each PC's Windows Defender Firewall enforces the register's peer denies, which the System Hub shows as rules D01 and D02; DHCP only hands out addresses.

quizzes.question: Why does the Workstations OU turn off the PCs' own DNS registration?
answers: Workstations don't need DNS records
SBD-DHCP01 registers each PC's records under svc-dhcp-dns; a PC that registers its own can take a record over so the DHCP server can no longer update it
Dynamic registration is blocked by the router
quizzes.explanation: One owner per record. Course 1.1, part 7 made SBD-DHCP01 the registrar for every lease, so the PCs leave registration to it, and the reason is recorded with the GPO.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: Fifty endpoints join a network that is finally ready for them: addressed by DHCP, landed by OU redirect, hardened by policy at first boot, certified by autoenrollment, and watched by the pipeline from their first sign-in. Tier 0 steps run from AdminJumpBox01, Tier 1 steps on SBD-DHCP01 from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, and Tier 2 steps inside SBD-ADMIN-PC01; each seat keeps its part of the record under C:\Evidence\workstation-fleet. The sample names run SBD-PC01 through SBD-PC50; match them to your own plan.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: From AdminJumpBox01, extend the directory schema for Windows LAPS (Update-LapsADSchema, which needs Schema Admins) and grant the Workstations OU's computers the right to update their own password attributes (Set-LapsADComputerSelfPermission) — a one-time Tier 0 action, recorded like any schema change.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Grant read access on the managed passwords to SBD Tier 2 Admins (Set-LapsADReadPasswordPermission) — exactly the people SBD-ADMIN-PC01 exists for. Domain Admins can read them by default; no other group gets the right, and Tier 0 accounts don't sign in on workstations to use one. The tier model decides who may know an endpoint's local secret.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Create the LAPS GPO on the Workstations OU: back up to Active Directory, manage the local administrator account the image carries (named in the policy, because Windows LAPS manages the built-in Administrator unless told otherwise and doesn't create accounts), encrypt the password with SBD Tier 2 Admins as its authorized decryptor (otherwise only Domain Admins can decrypt it), the complexity, length and age the plan sets, and post-authentication actions that reset the password and sign the account out after a short grace period, so a used password does not live on.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: On a pilot, confirm the policy applied, retrieve the password from SBD-ADMIN-PC01, use it once, and watch rotation after the grace period — one cycle, fully observed, is the proof the other forty-nine inherit.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration

# Inside SBD-ADMIN-PC01 (Tier 2)

Get-LapsADPassword -Identity SBD-PC01 -AsPlainText | Select-Object ComputerName, Account, ExpirationTimestamp
# On the pilot
gpresult /r /scope:computer

lessons.title: Admit only enrolled devices with 802.1X
lessons.summary: Until now, anything plugged into a VLAN 80 port got an address. With 802.1X, the switch asks each machine to prove who it is with the certificate it enrolled. This lesson turns that check on in monitor mode — every result is logged, nothing is blocked yet — because 47 PCs have no certificate until they join the domain; lesson 6 enforces it once the whole fleet has enrolled. No new server: the NPS role joins DHCP on SBD-DHCP01.
objectives: Add the Network Policy Server (NPS) role to SBD-DHCP01 for port authentication.
Configure Extensible Authentication Protocol–Transport Layer Security (EAP-TLS) with machine certificates on the VLAN 80 access ports, in monitor mode.
Prove the pilots authenticate and that NPS logs every result.
recap: 802.1X runs on every VLAN 80 port in monitor mode: every result is logged, nothing is blocked yet.
The pilots authenticate with machine certificates; enforcement waits until the whole fleet has enrolled.
No new server: NPS runs on SBD-DHCP01, and its decisions are logged with everything else.
lessons.next: Lesson 6 scales from three machines to fifty, then switches the ports to enforcement.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Add the Network Policy Server role to SBD-DHCP01 in a Tier 1 session from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, and register it in Active Directory from AdminJumpBox01 (a Tier 0 action: it adds the server to RAS and IAS Servers). Give it an SBD Server Authentication certificate (course 1.1, part 6) for SBD-DHCP01.sbd.test, adding SBD-DHCP01 to the SBD TLS Servers group before it requests. It handles port admission only; router logins stay named local accounts, so the server stays in the member-server tier.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Add the VLAN 80 access switch as a RADIUS client with a long, unique shared secret, then create the network policy: wired 802.1X, EAP-TLS only, machine certificates that chain to the approved root and carry the Client Authentication purpose, from the Domain Computers group — any domain-joined computer, servers included where one sits on an 802.1X port. Don't narrow it to SBD Fleet Computers: that group decides who enrolls the fleet's certificate, not who may connect.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Create quarantine VLAN 90 on the access switch with no gateway and no routes (the core gets no VLAN 90 interface) and set it as the ports' failure and guest VLAN, but enable 802.1X on the VLAN 80 access ports in monitor (audit) mode: the switch runs every authentication and reports the result, yet keeps forwarding on VLAN 80 whatever the outcome (vendors name this mode differently). The other 47 PCs have no machine certificate until they join the domain in lesson 6, so enforcing now would strand them in VLAN 90, with no route to a domain controller. Push the wired 802.1X client settings to the Workstations OU by Group Policy (Wired AutoConfig, EAP-TLS, the approved root as the trusted CA).

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Turn on Audit Network Policy Server (success and failure) for SBD-DHCP01 in a separate GPO linked above the STIG GPO, recorded as course 1.3 records audit additions — the STIG's audit policy leaves it off. Then prove monitor mode with the pilots: each authenticates with EAP-TLS and NPS logs a grant (event 6272), while a failed attempt is logged — as event 6273 when the request reaches NPS — but still forwards on VLAN 80. Add register row F20 with its owner, as the System Hub records it, and confirm the NPS events reach the course 1.3 collector, adding 6272 and 6273 to SBD-ForwardedSecurity's query if it doesn't carry them yet.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
# On an enrolled pilot: the wired interface authenticated with EAP-TLS.
netsh lan show interfaces
# On SBD-DHCP01 (Tier 1): NPS auditing is on, then recent grants (6272) and denials (6273).
auditpol /get /subcategory:"Network Policy Server"
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=6272,6273} -MaxEvents 5 | Select-Object TimeCreated, Id

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: The network policy admits Domain Computers with EAP-TLS; NPS auditing records success and failure; every pilot authenticates with EAP-TLS and NPS logs the grant (6272); a failed authentication is logged but, in monitor mode, the port still forwards on VLAN 80; the ports name VLAN 90 as their failure VLAN; and the NPS events appear in the collector.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep the network policy export, the RADIUS client list (without the secret), the audit GPO report, the monitor-mode port configuration, the pilots' grant events and the failed test, and the F20 register row.

Its machine certificate, checked by NPS through EAP-TLS
Being plugged in before the switch boots

answers: Quarantine VLAN 90, which has no routes
VLAN 80, with a warning
The domain controller VLAN, so it can enroll
quizzes.explanation: The failure VLAN gives an unknown device a place to be that leads nowhere: VLAN 90 has no gateway, so nothing it sends is routed.

quizzes.question: Why does NPS on SBD-DHCP01 handle port admission only, not router logins?
answers: NPS cannot authenticate people
Router logins need a separate license
If it authenticated the router's administrators, it could control Tier 0 and would have to be managed as Tier 0
quizzes.explanation: Anything that can control a Tier 0 system is Tier 0. Keeping NPS to port admission keeps SBD-DHCP01 in the member-server tier.

quizzes.question: Why does this lesson start 802.1X in monitor mode instead of enforcing it?
answers: Monitor mode is faster
The other 47 PCs have no machine certificate until they join the domain; enforcing now would strand them in VLAN 90, where they could never reach a domain controller
NPS cannot enforce on wired ports
quizzes.explanation: A PC enrolls its certificate only after it joins, and it can join only if the port lets it reach a domain controller. Monitor mode proves the configuration with the pilots without locking the rest of the fleet out.

Confirm the Workstations OU and the computer redirect from course 1.1, part 5, and the Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG) Group Policy objects (GPOs) for your Windows client release, imported in part 5 from the package part 4 staged and still unlinked there. Lesson 7 reuses SBD-ADMIN-PC01's own SCC copy, which part 8 installed with the Windows client benchmark part 4 staged, and the checked installer and connected-side-hashes.csv part 8 kept in C:\Staging\DISA there.

Confirm the VLAN 80 access switch supports 802.1X port authentication, including a monitor (audit) mode that logs each result without blocking traffic. No new server is needed: the Network Policy Server (NPS) role goes on SBD-DHCP01.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: Fifty endpoints join a network that is finally ready for them: addressed by DHCP, landed by OU redirect, hardened by policy at first boot, certified by autoenrollment, and watched by the pipeline from their first sign-in. Tier 0 steps run from AdminJumpBox01, Tier 1 steps on SBD-DHCP01 from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, and Tier 2 steps inside SBD-ADMIN-PC01; each seat keeps its part of the record under C:\Evidence\workstation-fleet. The sample names run SBD-PC01 through SBD-PC50; match them to your own plan.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Baseline the lesson 6 sample with the Windows client benchmark from SBD-ADMIN-PC01, reusing the SCC copy course 1.1, part 8 installed there and baselined the seat with — this course scans only the fleet sample. First check the installer part 8 kept in C:\Staging\DISA against connected-side-hashes.csv. Rule A03 carries remote management, not the file-sharing and RPC ports a remote SCC scan uses, so copy SCC to each sampled PC over PowerShell remoting, check its hash there, scan locally in a Tier 2 session, bring the results back to C:\Evidence\workstation-fleet\baseline, and remove SCC from the PC. Note how much the pre-linked policies and the OS defaults already satisfy, and classify open items the part 4 way.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Rescan what changed and attribute each delta to its lesson: the DCs (schema and LAPS attributes) and SBD-SUBCA01 (fleet enrollment volume) from AdminJumpBox01, and SBD-DHCP01 (the NPS role, its audit GPO and a scope in daily use) locally in a Tier 1 session from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01. Send any new deviation to the exception record's owner on AdminJumpBox01.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Assemble the fleet inventory — names, image ancestry, certificate thumbprints, sample status — as the course's closing artifact; course 1.8 makes it a source of SBD-MGMT01's living inventory.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Write the handoff: the fleet exists, watched and hardened, but takes no updates yet — course 1.7 builds SBD-WSUS01, with SBD-PC01–SBD-PC03 as its pilot ring and the other 47 PCs as Ring 2, and course 1.8 keeps the inventory current.

# Inside SBD-ADMIN-PC01 (Tier 2): the installer course 1.1, part 8 kept still matches the record (expected: True)

# Per sampled PC: carry the installer over remote management (A03), install and scan there, bring the results back

sections.body: The installer course 1.1, part 8 kept on SBD-ADMIN-PC01 still matches its recorded hash, the sampled endpoints hold dated Windows client baselines with SCC removed afterwards, the infrastructure rescans carry attributed deltas, and the fleet inventory is complete and filed.

lessons.title: Design the rings and the Windows update rule
lessons.summary: Decide how Windows updates reach the network before any arrive: one road through SBD-WSUS01, four rings that try every update on what the network can lose before what it can't, and a monthly crossing on the media procedure. Then confirm the register already carries the road.
objectives: Write the Windows update rule and its documented exceptions.
Place every Windows system in one of four rings, in order.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Complete courses 1.1–1.6: the domain with its DNS and time design, the STIG baselines and hardening policies, the PKI, DHCP, the tiered administration seats, SBD-REPO01, the logging pipeline with SBD-AUDIT01, run by its audit custodian (course 1.4), and the fleet of SBD-PC01–SBD-PC50 with its three pilot machines.

Provision SBD-WSUS01 (10.0.20.30, VLAN 20) as a Windows Server virtual machine with a separate data volume (D: in this sample) sized for the update files.

Outside the boundary, have an approved connected system that can run a second WSUS server with access to Microsoft Update, and the course 1.1 removable-media procedure for carrying its output across.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: This course gives every Windows system one road for updates. SBD-WSUS01 never touches the internet: each month a WSUS server on the connected side synchronizes the same scope, and its metadata and update files cross on hashed media to be imported inside. Microsoft deprecated WSUS in September 2024 — it gets no new features — but it still ships in Windows Server and is supported for production use, with security and quality updates under the product lifecycle. Ring timings and dates are sample values for your patch owner to set. Linux packages already have their road, SBD-REPO01 (course 1.2); endpoint protection and credentialed scanning are coming soon, as courses 1.9 and 1.10, and nothing here depends on them.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Write the Windows update rule — the network's one-source-per-type rule, applied to Windows: every Windows system takes updates only from SBD-WSUS01, and anything else is a documented exception. SBD-ROOTCA01 is the standing one: it has no network, so any update it takes is carried by hand at its next ceremony and recorded. Linux packages already have their one source, SBD-REPO01 (course 1.2); protection and scanner content are outside this course.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Place every Windows system in one of four rings, in the order rule F06 names. Ring 1, the pilot: the three course 1.6 pilot PCs (SBD-PC01–SBD-PC03) and SBD-WSUS01 itself, the first server to take each server update and one whose loss stops only patching. Ring 2: the other 47 workstations. Ring 3: the member servers and the Tier 1 and Tier 2 seats — SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 and its SBD-ADMIN-PC01 virtual machine — so the seats that would fix a broken workstation update still run the proven one. SBD-AUDIT01 takes Ring 3's updates at Ring 3's time but in a computer group of its own, Ring 3 - Audit archive: they download only, and its audit custodian installs them, Ring 4-style, because the custodian alone administers that server (course 1.4) — never ordinary Tier 1 operators.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Ring 4 holds the domain controllers and the rest of Tier 0: SBD-SUBCA01, SBD-PKI-MGMT01 and AdminJumpBox01. It goes last and is Tier 0 work, approved and installed from AdminJumpBox01 with Tier 0 accounts, one system at a time. SBD-WSUS01 itself stays a Tier 1 member server run by the patch operators: Tier 0's hold on Ring 4 is a written procedure (lesson 2), and moving SBD-WSUS01 to Tier 0 is recorded as the target.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Write the timing as sample values your patch owner approves: a ring advances only after its machines have installed and reported cleanly for a set soak time — three days after Ring 1 and five after Rings 2 and 3 in this sample. A failed or harmful update stops promotion until it is understood, and nothing skips a ring.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: Set the crossing cadence: one crossing a month, after Microsoft's monthly security release on the second Tuesday, through the course 1.1 media procedure and on the same run as SBD-REPO01's monthly snapshot (course 1.2) — one custody record, one approval. An urgent out-of-band fix gets an expedited crossing on the same procedure, with shorter soak times the owner approves in writing.

sections.heading: Step 6
sections.body: Confirm the register: F06 already lets every Windows system reach SBD-WSUS01 — metadata over HTTPS 8531, signed content over HTTP 8530 — with the patch owner as its owner, and A01 and A02 carry the two consoles. Nothing leads out of the network and no row is added for one: the content arrives on media.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
# On SBD-ADMIN-SRV01: every Windows computer object and its OU, the input for the ring table
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force C:\Evidence\patch-protect | Out-Null
([adsisearcher]'(&(objectCategory=computer)(operatingSystem=Windows*))').FindAll() | ForEach-Object { $_.Properties.distinguishedname[0] } | Sort-Object | Set-Content C:\Evidence\patch-protect\windows-computers.txt
(Get-Content C:\Evidence\patch-protect\windows-computers.txt).Count
# On any member: no update policy yet, so no WSUS server is named (expected: no output)
Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WindowsUpdate' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: The rule names its one source and its exceptions, the ring table places every Windows computer object in exactly one ring with the reason for its place, SBD-AUDIT01 in its custodian-installed group, the timing and crossing calendar are written with an approver, and F06, A01 and A02 are confirmed with owners.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep the Windows update rule, the computer list and the ring table built from it, the timing and crossing calendar, and the confirmed register rows.

answers: They update fastest
A bad update should burn a pilot machine, not the identity fabric — criticality decides order

quizzes.explanation: Rings are a blast-radius design: change proves itself on what the network can lose before touching what it cannot.

quizzes.question: What does one-approved-source-per-type actually buy?
answers: Cheaper licensing
Faster downloads
'Unauthorized software' becomes checkable — anything not from the named source is a finding by definition
quizzes.explanation: A rule you can test is a control; a preference you cannot is a hope. One source per type draws the testable line.

answers: An expedited crossing on the same media procedure, through every ring, with soak times the owner shortens in writing

lessons.title: Build SBD-WSUS01 as a disconnected server
lessons.summary: Build the server the network will take its updates from: a hardened member server on VLAN 20 that never synchronizes, serves metadata over TLS and signed files over HTTP, and is administered only from the two seats the tier model allows. Its scope is decided here, because what crosses each month is whatever that scope holds.
objectives: Install WSUS on a hardened member server configured never to synchronize.
Decide and record the update scope the monthly crossing will carry.
Protect its metadata with TLS and its administration with the tier model.
recap: A hardened member server that never synchronizes.
Metadata over TLS on 8531; signed files over HTTP on 8530.
Two consoles, named administrators, and a written Ring 4 procedure for the limit WSUS can't enforce, with Tier 0 as the recorded target.
lessons.next: Lesson 3 carries the first month's updates across the air gap.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Complete courses 1.1–1.6: the domain with its DNS and time design, the STIG baselines and hardening policies, the PKI, DHCP, the tiered administration seats, SBD-REPO01, the logging pipeline with SBD-AUDIT01, run by its audit custodian (course 1.4), and the fleet of SBD-PC01–SBD-PC50 with its three pilot machines.

Provision SBD-WSUS01 (10.0.20.30, VLAN 20) as a Windows Server virtual machine with a separate data volume (D: in this sample) sized for the update files.

Outside the boundary, have an approved connected system that can run a second WSUS server with access to Microsoft Update, and the course 1.1 removable-media procedure for carrying its output across.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: This course gives every Windows system one road for updates. SBD-WSUS01 never touches the internet: each month a WSUS server on the connected side synchronizes the same scope, and its metadata and update files cross on hashed media to be imported inside. Microsoft deprecated WSUS in September 2024 — it gets no new features — but it still ships in Windows Server and is supported for production use, with security and quality updates under the product lifecycle. Ring timings and dates are sample values for your patch owner to set. Linux packages already have their road, SBD-REPO01 (course 1.2); endpoint protection and credentialed scanning are coming soon, as courses 1.9 and 1.10, and nothing here depends on them.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Build SBD-WSUS01 as a Windows Server virtual machine at 10.0.20.30 on VLAN 20, with a separate data volume for the update files (D: in this sample), both domain controllers for DNS, and the hypervisor's time synchronization turned off, so it takes time from the domain hierarchy (course 1.1, part 3). Join it straight into the Servers OU, so part 5's member-server STIG policies, part 8's tier logon policies and course 1.3's enrolling GPO, linked to the Servers OU when course 1.3 enrolled SBD-DHCP01, apply from its first boot; confirm with w32tm /query /source that it takes time from a domain controller.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Install the role with its default database, the Windows Internal Database (WID), and run the post-installation step with the content folder on D:. Microsoft announced in September 2024 that WSUS is deprecated: it gets no new features, but it still ships in Windows Server and is supported for production use, with security and quality updates under the product lifecycle. WID is deprecated too — Microsoft suggests SQL Server for the roles that use it — so record the database choice as a decision to revisit before either is removed.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Configure it as a disconnected server: cancel the configuration wizard, which needs Microsoft Update to list products, then in Options store update files locally, enable only the languages your systems use, leave express installation files off (the default), and keep synchronization manual — and never run it. SBD-WSUS01 has no route out; its updates arrive only by import (lesson 3).

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Decide the scope and record it: the Windows Server and Windows client products the network runs, security and critical updates and — if Microsoft Defender Antivirus protects the endpoints — its definition updates; no upgrades and no drivers, which are planned changes of their own. The connected-side server in lesson 3 synchronizes exactly this scope, because whatever it holds is what crosses.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: Protect the metadata: add SBD-WSUS01 to the SBD TLS Servers group, then request an SBD Server Authentication certificate (course 1.1, part 6) for SBD-WSUS01.sbd.test, bind it to the WSUS Administration site's HTTPS port 8531, require TLS on the five web services Microsoft lists (APIRemoting30, ClientWebService, DSSAuthWebService, ServerSyncWebService and SimpleAuthWebService), and run wsusutil configuressl. Update files stay on HTTP 8530, as F06 says: each one is signed, and its hash reaches the client inside the TLS-protected metadata, so a changed file is refused.

sections.heading: Step 6
sections.body: Hold the administration to the tier model: scope the 8530 and 8531 inbound rules to the VLANs that hold F06's Windows systems, install the WSUS console on SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 and AdminJumpBox01, and keep WSUS Administrators to the named patch operators and the Tier 0 task accounts that run Ring 4. From AdminJumpBox01, add SBD-WSUS01 to SBD Tier 0 Console Hosts (course 1.1's recorded network-logon exception for this console) and to SBD Event Sources (course 1.3), and restart it once the collector's WinRM scope includes 10.0.20.30 (F17). WSUS can't limit an administrator to some computer groups, so Ring 4's Tier 0 rule — like the audit custodian's separation for SBD-AUDIT01 — is a written procedure, not a technical boundary. Write the Ring 4 procedure — Ring 4 is approved and installed only by Tier 0 accounts from AdminJumpBox01, and every Ring 4 approval is checked by name before a controller installs (lesson 5) — and record in the exception record the residual risk that a Tier 1 operator could still approve for Ring 4, with the target that closes it: moving SBD-WSUS01 to Tier 0, administered only from AdminJumpBox01. Until then SBD-WSUS01 stays Tier 1.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
w32tm /query /source   # a domain controller, never the hypervisor's time provider
Install-WindowsFeature -Name UpdateServices -IncludeManagementTools
& "$env:ProgramFiles\Update Services\Tools\wsusutil.exe" postinstall CONTENT_DIR=D:\WSUS
$wsus = Get-WsusServer
$wsus.GetConfiguration() | Select-Object HostBinariesOnMicrosoftUpdate, DownloadExpressPackages, AllUpdateLanguagesEnabled   # expected after Options: False, False, False
$wsus.GetSubscription() | Select-Object SynchronizeAutomatically   # expected: False
# TLS for metadata: the certificate, the 8531 binding, the five services, then wsusutil
$cert = (Get-Certificate -Template SBDServerAuthentication -SubjectName 'CN=SBD-WSUS01.sbd.test' -DnsName SBD-WSUS01.sbd.test -CertStoreLocation Cert:\LocalMachine\My).Certificate
(Get-WebBinding -Name 'WSUS Administration' -Protocol https).AddSslCertificate($cert.Thumbprint, 'My')
'APIRemoting30', 'ClientWebService', 'DSSAuthWebService', 'ServerSyncWebService', 'SimpleAuthWebService' | ForEach-Object { Set-WebConfigurationProperty -PSPath 'IIS:\' -Location "WSUS Administration/$_" -Filter system.webServer/security/access -Name sslFlags -Value Ssl }
& "$env:ProgramFiles\Update Services\Tools\wsusutil.exe" configuressl SBD-WSUS01.sbd.test
Get-WebBinding -Name 'WSUS Administration' | Select-Object protocol, bindingInformation   # http *:8530, https *:8531
Get-LocalGroupMember 'WSUS Administrators'

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: SBD-WSUS01 sits in the Servers OU, takes time from a domain controller, and runs WSUS on WID, stores files locally, never synchronizes, and answers metadata over TLS on 8531 with a certificate that chains to the SBD root; WSUS Administrators holds only the named operators and Tier 0 task accounts; the server is in SBD Tier 0 Console Hosts and forwards its events; and the scope, the database decision, the written Ring 4 procedure, and its residual risk with the Tier 0 target are recorded.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep the installation and configuration output, the scope and database decisions, the certificate and binding details, the WSUS Administrators list, the group memberships, the written Ring 4 procedure, and the exception-record entry for the residual risk and its Tier 0 target.

lessons.title: Carry updates across the air gap

Each month a second WSUS server on the connected side synchronizes the recorded scope and downloads its files; its metadata export and content folder cross on approved media, hashed on both sides, and SBD-WSUS01 imports them — the two-server path Microsoft describes for air-gapped networks.

Package and files cross hashed, under custody.

It sits outside the boundary and never connects to the lab; its only output is media.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: After each month's synchronization, approve the updates you need on the export server so it downloads their files, and wait until nothing is still downloading — those approvals only switch the downloads on, and they stay outside. Then, as a local administrator on the export server, run wsusutil export for the metadata package and copy the WsusContent folder: the package carries the update metadata, and the files travel beside it (after the first crossing, only those added since the last one).

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Hash the package and every file into connected-side-hashes.csv, which travels with the media, and carry the set under the course 1.1 media procedure with its custody record, on the run that also carries SBD-REPO01's snapshot. Declining an update doesn't stop it from being exported, so the export server's scope is the real limit on what crosses.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: On SBD-WSUS01, hash the media's contents into lab-side-hashes.csv and compare the two lists before opening anything: one mismatch stops the import and becomes a finding. Copy the files into D:\WSUS\WsusContent first, then run wsusutil import locally as a local administrator — Microsoft warns never to import an export from a source you don't trust, and the custody record and matching hashes are how this network earns that trust. A large import can run for hours.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: Check the import log, confirm the month's updates now appear in the console, and file the crossing in C:\Evidence\patch-protect\transfer: dates, carrier, file count, the package hash, both hash lists and the import log. If WSUS later shows an approved update as still waiting for its files, wsusutil reset makes it re-check its content folder against the database.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
# Connected side, on the export server, once every needed file has downloaded
& "$env:ProgramFiles\Update Services\Tools\wsusutil.exe" export E:\2026-10\wsus-export.xml.gz E:\2026-10\export.log
robocopy D:\WSUS\WsusContent E:\2026-10\WsusContent /E   # the first crossing carries the whole folder
Get-ChildItem E:\2026-10 -Recurse -File | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 | Export-Csv E:\connected-side-hashes.csv -NoTypeInformation
# Inside, on SBD-WSUS01, with the media as E: (no output from Compare-Object means every hash matches)
$t = 'C:\Evidence\patch-protect\transfer\2026-10'; New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force $t | Out-Null
Get-ChildItem E:\2026-10 -Recurse -File | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 | Export-Csv "$t\lab-side-hashes.csv" -NoTypeInformation
Compare-Object (Import-Csv E:\connected-side-hashes.csv).Hash (Import-Csv "$t\lab-side-hashes.csv").Hash
robocopy E:\2026-10\WsusContent D:\WSUS\WsusContent /E
& "$env:ProgramFiles\Update Services\Tools\wsusutil.exe" import E:\2026-10\wsus-export.xml.gz "$t\import.log"
Copy-Item E:\connected-side-hashes.csv, E:\2026-10\export.log -Destination $t

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: The export server's scope matches lesson 2's record, every hash matches on both sides, the import log reports success, the month's updates appear on SBD-WSUS01, and the crossing record is complete.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep the export server's scope settings, both hash lists and their comparison, the custody record, the export and import logs, and the crossing record with the package hash and file count.

quizzes.question: Why must the export server synchronize exactly the recorded scope?
answers: Because everything it holds is exported, and that is what crosses the boundary
Because Microsoft Update charges by product
Because SBD-WSUS01 synchronizes from it over the network
quizzes.explanation: Declining an update doesn't stop it from being exported: the export server's database is the shipment. A tight scope there keeps every crossing small and reviewable.

quizzes.question: The lab-side hash of one file doesn't match the connected-side list. What happens?
answers: Import anyway — clients check signatures
Copy that one file again from the media and carry on
The import stops and the mismatch becomes a finding; the set is carried again

quizzes.question: What does the metadata package carry?

The update metadata — the files travel beside it as the WsusContent folder
The update files and every approval

lessons.title: Target the rings with computer groups and Group Policy
lessons.summary: Rings become mechanics: a computer group per ring on SBD-WSUS01, plus one for SBD-AUDIT01, client-side targeting so each computer files itself into its ring, and one Group Policy object per ring that names the server, the ring and its install behaviour. The domain controllers get a ring of their own: they download on their own but install only when Tier 0 starts it, and SBD-AUDIT01 waits for its audit custodian the same way.
objectives: Create the ring groups and switch WSUS to client-side targeting.
Build and link one Group Policy object per ring, with the pilot set by security filtering.
Set install behaviour and deadlines, and prove every computer reports to its ring.
recap: A group per ring, plus SBD-AUDIT01's own, and computers file themselves in by Group Policy.
Rings 1–3 install on schedule and by deadline; Ring 4 waits for Tier 0, and SBD-AUDIT01 for its custodian.
An empty Unassigned Computers list: every machine has a ring.
lessons.next: Lesson 5 runs the first monthly cycle through the rings and proves it.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Complete courses 1.1–1.6: the domain with its DNS and time design, the STIG baselines and hardening policies, the PKI, DHCP, the tiered administration seats, SBD-REPO01, the logging pipeline with SBD-AUDIT01, run by its audit custodian (course 1.4), and the fleet of SBD-PC01–SBD-PC50 with its three pilot machines.

Provision SBD-WSUS01 (10.0.20.30, VLAN 20) as a Windows Server virtual machine with a separate data volume (D: in this sample) sized for the update files.

Outside the boundary, have an approved connected system that can run a second WSUS server with access to Microsoft Update, and the course 1.1 removable-media procedure for carrying its output across.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: This course gives every Windows system one road for updates. SBD-WSUS01 never touches the internet: each month a WSUS server on the connected side synchronizes the same scope, and its metadata and update files cross on hashed media to be imported inside. Microsoft deprecated WSUS in September 2024 — it gets no new features — but it still ships in Windows Server and is supported for production use, with security and quality updates under the product lifecycle. Ring timings and dates are sample values for your patch owner to set. Linux packages already have their road, SBD-REPO01 (course 1.2); endpoint protection and credentialed scanning are coming soon, as courses 1.9 and 1.10, and nothing here depends on them.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: On SBD-WSUS01, create the four ring groups — Ring 1 - Pilot, Ring 2 - Workstations, Ring 3 - Member servers and Ring 4 - Tier 0 — and Ring 3 - Audit archive for SBD-AUDIT01 alone, and set the Computers option to Use Group Policy or registry settings on computers. The groups must exist first: a computer whose policy names a group WSUS doesn't have waits in Unassigned Computers until the group is created.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: From AdminJumpBox01, create one GPO per ring, and one for Ring 3 - Audit archive, around the same core: Specify intranet Microsoft update service location, with https://SBD-WSUS01.sbd.test:8531 for both detection and statistics; Enable client-side targeting, with the ring's group name; and Do not connect to any Windows Update Internet locations, so no system keeps trying the public service. Leave Allow signed updates from an intranet Microsoft update service location disabled, so only Microsoft-signed updates install.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Set each ring's install behaviour in Configure Automatic Updates: option 4, download and schedule the install, at a time that suits the ring's work for Rings 1 to 3, and option 7 — download, then notify to install and to restart, a Windows Server option — for Ring 4, so a domain controller installs only when a Tier 0 operator starts it; Ring 3 - Audit archive uses option 7 too, so SBD-AUDIT01 installs only when its audit custodian starts it in a custodian session from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01. Deadlines go on the approvals (two days for Ring 1 and five for Rings 2 and 3 in this sample): at a deadline the update installs whatever the client's own schedule says. Ring 4's approvals carry none, and neither do Ring 3 - Audit archive's.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Link the GPOs where the rings live: Ring 2 at the Workstations OU; Ring 3 at the Servers and Admin Workstations OUs and at Admin Servers, filtered to SBD-ADMIN-SRV01; Ring 3 - Audit archive at the Audit Servers OU; Ring 4 at the Domain Controllers and Tier 0 Servers OUs and at Admin Servers, filtered to AdminJumpBox01. Link Ring 1 above the ring GPO on the Workstations and Servers OUs (link order 1), security-filtered to a new SBD WSUS Pilot group holding SBD-PC01–SBD-PC03 and SBD-WSUS01, and restart those four so the membership reaches their Kerberos tickets.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: Prove the targeting on one member of each ring: run gpupdate, read the policy values, and start a detection with the Windows Update Agent's DetectNow call; then confirm on SBD-WSUS01 that each computer sits in its ring's group and that Unassigned Computers is empty. Check Ring 4 from AdminJumpBox01, and record every ring's member list against lesson 1's table.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
# On SBD-WSUS01: the four ring groups and client-side targeting
$wsus = Get-WsusServer
'Ring 1 - Pilot', 'Ring 2 - Workstations', 'Ring 3 - Member servers', 'Ring 3 - Audit archive', 'Ring 4 - Tier 0' | ForEach-Object { [void]$wsus.CreateComputerTargetGroup($_) }
$config = $wsus.GetConfiguration(); $config.TargetingMode = 'Client'; $config.Save()
# On AdminJumpBox01 (Tier 0): the links in order, and the pilot GPO's security filter
(Get-GPInheritance -Target 'OU=Workstations,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test').GpoLinks | Select-Object Order, DisplayName
Get-GPPermission -Name 'SBD WSUS Ring 1 - Pilot' -All | Select-Object @{ n = 'Trustee'; e = { $_.Trustee.Name } }, Permission
# On one member of each ring, after gpupdate /force: its server, its ring, and a detection now
Get-ItemProperty HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WindowsUpdate | Select-Object WUServer, TargetGroup, DoNotConnectToWindowsUpdateInternetLocations
(New-Object -ComObject Microsoft.Update.AutoUpdate).DetectNow()
# Back on SBD-WSUS01: each ring's members, and nobody unassigned
Get-WsusComputer -ComputerTargetGroups 'Ring 1 - Pilot' | Select-Object FullDomainName, LastSyncTime
Get-WsusComputer -ComputerTargetGroups 'Unassigned Computers'   # expected: no computers

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: The four ring groups and Ring 3 - Audit archive exist and WSUS uses client-side targeting; each ring's GPO is linked where its computers live, with the pilot filter and link order in place; one member of each ring shows SBD-WSUS01 and its ring in its policy values; every Windows computer sits in its ring's group; and Unassigned Computers is empty.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep the GPO reports with their links and security filtering, the pilot group's members, each ring's member list from SBD-WSUS01, the policy values from one member per ring, and the install-time and deadline table, with SBD-AUDIT01's custodian-started installs.

quizzes.question: A pilot PC receives both the Ring 1 and the Ring 2 GPO. Why does it still report to Ring 1?
answers: The Ring 1 link has the higher precedence on that OU (link order 1), so its target group wins the conflict
WSUS always picks the lowest ring number
A computer can receive only one GPO
quizzes.explanation: Both GPOs apply; where they set the same value, the link with the higher precedence wins. Security filtering keeps the Ring 1 GPO off every PC that isn't in the pilot group.

quizzes.question: Why do the domain controllers use option 7 instead of a scheduled install?
answers: Option 7 makes downloads faster
A Tier 0 operator decides when each controller installs and restarts, so they never go down together and each is checked before the next
Domain controllers can't run scheduled installs
quizzes.explanation: Downloads still happen on their own; only the install and the restart wait for a person — one controller at a time, with replication checked in between.

quizzes.question: A new server's policy names Ring 3, but the group was mistyped on SBD-WSUS01. Where does the server land?
answers: In Ring 4, as the safest ring
Nowhere — it stops checking for updates
In Unassigned Computers, until a group with that exact name exists
quizzes.explanation: Client-side targeting only files a computer into a group WSUS already has. An empty Unassigned Computers list is part of the proof.

I linked each ring’s GPO where its computers live and confirmed the pilot filter and link order with gpresult.
I read SBD-WSUS01 and the ring name in the policy values of one member of each ring, checking Ring 4 from AdminJumpBox01.

lessons.title: Run the first cycle and prove it
lessons.summary: The design meets a real month: approve the imported updates for the pilot, promote them ring by ring on the written soak times, and install the domain controllers by hand. Then prove the result with WSUS's own reports, spot checks on the systems themselves, and the first SCAP baseline of SBD-WSUS01.
objectives: Promote one monthly cycle through all four rings on the written timing.
Report compliance per ring and spot-check it on the systems themselves.
Baseline SBD-WSUS01 and hand the course's records to course 1.8.
recap: The month moves pilot → workstations → servers → Tier 0, on record.
Ring 4: approvals checked by name, controllers one at a time.
Reports, spot checks and a first baseline prove it.
lessons.next: That completes course 1.7. Course 1.8 builds SBD-MGMT01 and the living inventory, with this course's WSUS records among its sources.

Provision SBD-WSUS01 (10.0.20.30, VLAN 20) as a Windows Server virtual machine with a separate data volume (D: in this sample) sized for the update files.

Outside the boundary, have an approved connected system that can run a second WSUS server with access to Microsoft Update, and the course 1.1 removable-media procedure for carrying its output across.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: This course gives every Windows system one road for updates. SBD-WSUS01 never touches the internet: each month a WSUS server on the connected side synchronizes the same scope, and its metadata and update files cross on hashed media to be imported inside. Microsoft deprecated WSUS in September 2024 — it gets no new features — but it still ships in Windows Server and is supported for production use, with security and quality updates under the product lifecycle. Ring timings and dates are sample values for your patch owner to set. Linux packages already have their road, SBD-REPO01 (course 1.2); endpoint protection and credentialed scanning are coming soon, as courses 1.9 and 1.10, and nothing here depends on them.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Approve the month's updates for Ring 1 only, with its deadline, and watch the pilots install and report. Before anything moves, check that the pilot PCs still sign in and apply policy and that SBD-WSUS01 still serves its clients; then approve Ring 2 and Ring 3 on the written soak times — Ring 3 - Audit archive with Ring 3, without a deadline — recording for each promotion the numbers that justified it. SBD-AUDIT01's audit custodian then starts its install in a custodian session from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 and records it; ordinary Tier 1 operators don't install there.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: If an update fails or does harm, stop: leave it unapproved for the later rings and, where the update supports removal, approve it for removal in the rings that installed it. Windows client quality updates delivered through the Unified Update Platform can't be removed through WSUS, so the pilot is where they have to prove themselves.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Ring 4 is Tier 0 work from AdminJumpBox01. First read the approval history and confirm that every Ring 4 approval was made by a Tier 0 account — WSUS records who approved what, for which group. Then install on SBD-DC02, restart it, and check it with dcdiag and repadmin /replsummary before touching SBD-DC01; the two Tier 0 servers follow, and AdminJumpBox01 goes last.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Report compliance per ring with the UpdateServices cmdlets (the console's built-in reports need Microsoft's Report Viewer runtime, one more package to carry across): computers that still need or failed an approved update, and computers silent for a week. Spot-check one system per ring on the machine itself against WSUS's view of it. WSUS reports what clients tell it, so the spot checks are the independent view.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: Close the cycle once every ring has installed: Invoke-WsusServerCleanup declines superseded updates that nothing still needs and expired ones, and removes unneeded files and computers silent for 30 days. Then take SBD-WSUS01's first SCAP baseline with course 1.1's SCC and benchmark versions, run locally in a Tier 1 session from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, answer the IIS server and site STIG items for the WSUS web site in a STIG Viewer checklist (staged across the air gap as in part 4), and classify every open item as part 4 taught — update files on HTTP 8530 are a deviation candidate, justified by signed files whose hashes travel in TLS-protected metadata.

sections.heading: Step 6
sections.body: Hand off to course 1.8: the ring table, WSUS's computer list and this cycle's compliance report become inventory sources, the crossing calendar sets when its reconciliation runs, and SBD-MGMT01 joins Ring 3 simply by landing in the Servers OU. Collect the course's records into C:\Evidence\patch-protect on SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 and hash them into a manifest.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
# On SBD-WSUS01 (Tier 1): approve for the pilot; deadlines are set in the console's Approve Updates dialog
Get-WsusUpdate -Classification All -Approval Unapproved -Status FailedOrNeeded | Approve-WsusUpdate -Action Install -TargetGroupName 'Ring 1 - Pilot'
Get-WsusComputer -ComputerTargetGroups 'Ring 1 - Pilot' -ComputerUpdateStatus FailedOrNeeded   # expected: none once the ring is clean
Get-WsusComputer -ToLastReportedStatusTime (Get-Date).AddDays(-7)   # computers silent for a week
# On AdminJumpBox01 (Tier 0): who approved each Ring 4 update, then each controller in turn
$wsus = Get-WsusServer -Name SBD-WSUS01.sbd.test -PortNumber 8531 -UseSsl
$wsus.GetUpdateApprovals((New-Object Microsoft.UpdateServices.Administration.UpdateScope)) | Where-Object { $_.GetComputerTargetGroup().Name -eq 'Ring 4 - Tier 0' } | Select-Object CreationDate, AdministratorName, Action
dcdiag /s:SBD-DC02 /q; repadmin /replsummary   # after SBD-DC02 restarts, before SBD-DC01
# Spot check from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01: what a system itself says it installed
Invoke-Command SBD-DHCP01 { Get-HotFix | Sort-Object InstalledOn -Descending | Select-Object -First 3 HotFixID, InstalledOn }
# Back on SBD-WSUS01, once every ring has installed
Invoke-WsusServerCleanup -DeclineSupersededUpdates -DeclineExpiredUpdates -CleanupObsoleteUpdates -CleanupUnneededContentFiles -CleanupObsoleteComputers

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: Each ring installed the month's updates in the written order with its promotion recorded, SBD-AUDIT01's custodian installed its updates, every Ring 4 approval names a Tier 0 account, both controllers were healthy between installs, no computer is failing or silent without an explanation, the spot checks agree with WSUS, SBD-WSUS01 has its first baseline with every open item classified, and the course's records are hashed.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep the per-ring approval and install timeline with the custodian's install record for SBD-AUDIT01, the Ring 4 approval history and install record, the compliance and silent-computer reports, the spot checks, the cleanup output, the SCC results and STIG Viewer checklist with classified findings, the manifest, and the handoff note to course 1.8.

It continues — the install itself succeeded
Approve it for every ring to see whether the problem spreads

Complete courses 1.1–1.7: every system those courses built is running, course 1.6's fleet inventory is filed, and SBD-WSUS01 serves all four update rings.

Provision SBD-MGMT01 (10.0.70.10, VLAN 70) as a Windows Server virtual machine with a separate data volume (D: in this sample) for the record.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: Course 1.6 handed over a snapshot of the fleet; this course makes the whole network's component inventory a living record on SBD-MGMT01 — NIST SP 800-53 CM-8 in practice. The server keeps the record and reaches into nothing: the directory, the DHCP leases, the WSUS computer list, SBD-REPO01's records and the baseline sessions it is checked against arrive through the administrators' existing sessions. Column names and the monthly cadence are sample values; the system owner decides.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Draw the boundary as CM-8 asks: every component of this network, each counted once, and nothing from outside it. That is every server and controller (SBD-ROOTCA01 included, offline in the vault), the three administration seats, each of the 50 PCs, the core and the VLAN 80 access switch, and the seven hypervisor hosts (SBD-HV01–SBD-HV07) on which the System Hub places the virtual machines. The connected-side systems that fill the media stay out; the crossing records name them.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Choose the columns, one per attribute: name, type, role, operating system and version, domain membership, address and VLAN, OU, tier, location (host and rack), update source (a WSUS ring, an SBD-REPO01 snapshot, or by hand at a ceremony), latest baseline, the course that built it, an accountable owner by role (CM-8(4)), and status — planned, active or retired. Record the systems the design names but no course has built yet, SBD-EPO01, SBD-NESSUS01 and the four VLAN 40 servers, as planned, so a reconciliation never mistakes them for missing.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Name the records that can contradict it and what each one proves: the directory shows what joined the domain, the DHCP leases what is on VLAN 80 now, WSUS's computer list what reports for updates and in which ring, SBD-REPO01's catalog and access log which Linux servers take packages, and the baseline sessions which hosts have a measured state. Any disagreement is a finding, and lesson 5 makes the comparison a monthly check.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Place the keeper as the System Hub does: SBD-MGMT01, Windows Server at 10.0.70.10 on VLAN 70 beside SBD-REPO01, a Tier 1 member server administered only from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 (rule A02). The model leaves its listeners to define: define them as management only, and give it no collection path of its own — source data arrives through the administrators' existing sessions, so the server that holds the record can't reach, or be used to reach, anything else. Its domain rows (F01–F03, F06 in Ring 3, F09, F17 and F18) already list it.

# On SBD-ADMIN-SRV01: start the course record with the inventory's columns
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force C:\Evidence\management-server | Out-Null
'Name,Type,Role,OS,Domain,Address,VLAN,OU,Tier,Location,UpdateSource,Baseline,BuiltIn,Owner,Status' | Set-Content C:\Evidence\management-server\inventory-columns.csv
# SBD-MGMT01 isn't registered yet; its neighbour on VLAN 70 is
Resolve-DnsName SBD-MGMT01.sbd.test -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue   # expected: no answer
Resolve-DnsName SBD-REPO01.sbd.test | Select-Object Name, IPAddress   # 10.0.70.20

quizzes.question: Why record the hypervisor hosts when every server is a virtual machine?
answers: They are optional decoration
They run every virtual machine, so whatever controls them controls the servers — they belong inside the boundary
The core requires it
quizzes.explanation: An inventory that lists the guests but not their hosts misses the components with the most reach. System Hub gives every server's host and rack for that reason.

quizzes.question: SBD-EPO01 is designed but not built. How does the inventory show it?
answers: It leaves it out until it exists
It lists it as active so the record looks complete
As planned, so the record matches the design and a reconciliation doesn't flag it as missing
quizzes.explanation: Status carries the difference between designed and installed. When the system is built, its row turns active as part of that build.

quizzes.question: Why does SBD-MGMT01 get no collection path of its own?
answers: A server that can reach every source becomes a path to all of them; letting data arrive through existing administration sessions keeps it a keeper, not a hub
Collection paths are slower
Windows Server can't read other servers

lessons.title: Build and harden SBD-MGMT01
lessons.summary: Build the inventory's keeper as a small, quiet member server, joined into the Servers OU so the hardening, tier and update policies apply from its first boot. It answers only the Tier 1 seat, and the record sits on its own volume behind permissions that admit administrators alone.
objectives: Build SBD-MGMT01 in its place with the network's policies applied from first boot.
Limit its administration to SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 and prove the limit.
Prepare the record's folders, permissions and version history.
recap: In the Servers OU: hardened, tiered and patched from first boot.
Management from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 only — proven by a refused attempt.
A record folder for administrators alone, with history and hashes.
lessons.next: Lesson 3 fills it with the first complete inventory.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Complete courses 1.1–1.7: every system those courses built is running, course 1.6's fleet inventory is filed, and SBD-WSUS01 serves all four update rings.

Provision SBD-MGMT01 (10.0.70.10, VLAN 70) as a Windows Server virtual machine with a separate data volume (D: in this sample) for the record.

Keep the records earlier courses produced within reach: the service-path register, course 1.7's ring table and WSUS computer list, course 1.2's snapshot catalog, each course's baseline sessions, and the exception record.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: Course 1.6 handed over a snapshot of the fleet; this course makes the whole network's component inventory a living record on SBD-MGMT01 — NIST SP 800-53 CM-8 in practice. The server keeps the record and reaches into nothing: the directory, the DHCP leases, the WSUS computer list, SBD-REPO01's records and the baseline sessions it is checked against arrive through the administrators' existing sessions. Column names and the monthly cadence are sample values; the system owner decides.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Build SBD-MGMT01 as a Windows Server virtual machine — on SBD-HV07 beside SBD-REPO01, where the System Hub places it — with the hypervisor's time synchronization turned off, so the domain is its only clock, a separate data volume for the record (D: in this sample), the static address 10.0.70.10/24 with the core's VLAN 70 interface as gateway (10.0.70.1 in this sample), and both domain controllers for DNS. Join it straight into the Servers OU, so course 1.1's STIG policies, part 8's tier logon policies, course 1.3's event-forwarding GPO (linked to the Servers OU in course 1.3) and course 1.7's Ring 3 update policy apply from its first boot.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Check that it took its place: time from a domain controller, as course 1.1, part 3 set up, and an update policy that names SBD-WSUS01 and Ring 3, with SBD-WSUS01 listing it there. Add it to SBD Event Sources from AdminJumpBox01, widen the collector's WinRM scope to 10.0.70.10 (F17) from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, and restart it so its security events reach SBD-SYSLOG01.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Close it to everything but its administration: Windows Defender Firewall on in every profile, and the existing Remote Desktop and Windows Remote Management rules scoped to SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 (10.0.60.20), because allow rules add up and a new, narrower rule would not restrict the broad ones. Install no other role and no agent; course 1.1's Servers OU policy already denies Tier 0 accounts here.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Prepare the record on D:: an Inventory folder with inheritance removed and full control for SYSTEM and Administrators only — the volume's inherited defaults let ordinary users read and create files — holding current, history, sources and findings folders. Every published version is copied into history with its SHA-256 in a hash list, and every change gets a line in a change log: who, what, why, and the change record it answers.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: Prove the closure: a remote session from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 opens, the same attempt from SBD-ADMIN-PC01 fails at the core because rule A02 names only the Tier 1 seat, and the firewall's remote-address lists show only 10.0.60.20 for management.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
# In a session on SBD-MGMT01 from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01
([adsisearcher]"(&(objectCategory=computer)(name=$env:COMPUTERNAME))").FindOne().Path   # ...OU=Servers,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test
w32tm /query /source   # a domain controller, never the local clock
Get-ItemProperty HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WindowsUpdate | Select-Object WUServer, TargetGroup   # Ring 3 - Member servers
Get-NetFirewallRule -DisplayGroup 'Remote Desktop', 'Windows Remote Management' -Enabled True | Get-NetFirewallAddressFilter | Select-Object InstanceID, RemoteAddress   # 10.0.60.20 only
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force D:\Inventory | Out-Null
icacls D:\Inventory /inheritance:r /grant:r 'SYSTEM:(OI)(CI)F' 'Administrators:(OI)(CI)F'
'current', 'history', 'sources', 'findings' | ForEach-Object { New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force "D:\Inventory\$_" | Out-Null }
icacls D:\Inventory
# From SBD-ADMIN-PC01: the same management path must fail
Test-NetConnection SBD-MGMT01.sbd.test -Port 5985   # expected: TcpTestSucceeded False

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: SBD-MGMT01 sits in the Servers OU with the hypervisor's time synchronization off and time from a domain controller, reports to Ring 3 on SBD-WSUS01, forwards its security events, accepts management only from 10.0.60.20 and refuses SBD-ADMIN-PC01, runs no extra role or agent, and holds an Inventory folder that only SYSTEM and Administrators can open.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep the OU placement, the time source, the update policy values and WSUS listing, the firewall scope, the refused connection from SBD-ADMIN-PC01, and the Inventory folder's permissions.

quizzes.question: Why scope the existing Remote Desktop and remote management rules instead of adding a narrow new rule?
answers: New rules are slower
Allow rules add up: a narrow new rule leaves the broad existing one letting everyone in
Windows allows only one rule per port
quizzes.explanation: Windows Defender Firewall admits a connection if any enabled allow rule matches. Narrow the rules that exist, then prove it from a seat that must be refused.

quizzes.question: SBD-ADMIN-PC01 shares VLAN 60 with SBD-ADMIN-SRV01. Why is its attempt on SBD-MGMT01 refused?
answers: Rule A02 names only SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 as the source for member-server management, so the core denies the Tier 2 seat — and the host firewall would too
Virtual machines can't use the network
SBD-MGMT01 is offline
quizzes.explanation: Sharing a VLAN grants nothing. The register names the seat, the core enforces it between VLANs, and the host firewall enforces it again.

quizzes.question: Why remove inheritance on the Inventory folder?
answers: To make backups faster
Inheritance can't be used on data volumes
A new volume's inherited permissions let ordinary users read and create files; the record should open to administrators alone
quizzes.explanation: Defaults are someone else's decision. The record's permissions are part of its integrity, alongside its version history and hashes.

I scoped the Remote Desktop and remote management rules to 10.0.60.20 and saw SBD-ADMIN-PC01’s attempt refused.
I created D:\Inventory with inheritance removed, for SYSTEM and Administrators only, with current, history, sources and findings folders.

lessons.title: Build the living inventory
lessons.summary: Course 1.6's fleet inventory was a snapshot of fifty PCs; SBD-MGMT01 makes the whole network's inventory a living record. Every component gets its place, ring, update source, baseline and owner, kept current by the procedures that change it.
objectives: Load every component into the inventory from the records the path already keeps.
Define how the inventory stays current and who owns it.
Publish the first version with its hash.
recap: One record of everything, with place, ring, update source, baseline and owner.
Every change updates it; a monthly reconciliation keeps it honest.
Owned, versioned, and ready to join the Body of Evidence.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Start from the records the path already keeps rather than from memory: course 1.6's fleet inventory for the 50 PCs (names, image ancestry, certificate thumbprints, sample status), the service-path register and the System Hub for names, addresses and locations, course 1.7's ring table for the update rings, course 1.2's snapshot catalog for SBD-REPO01, and each course's baseline set for the latest baseline date.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Load the inventory with every component the boundary lists — the fleet, the servers (SBD-REPO01 included, with its current snapshot as its update source), the admin plane, the core, the access switch and the hypervisor hosts — each with every column filled: the CM-8 component inventory, in one place. Add the planned systems as planned.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Define currency: every build, move and retirement updates the inventory as part of its own procedure (CM-8(1)), so each later course's build lesson adds its rows, and a monthly reconciliation compares the inventory against the directory, the DHCP leases and the WSUS computer list — drift between them is a finding.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Name the owner — a role, with a named deputy — who approves each change, and publish the first version: copy it into history with its hash and log the change. Course 2.2 shows how a record like this one joins the Body of Evidence for the configuration-management controls.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
# In a session on SBD-MGMT01 from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, once the record is filled in
$inv = Import-Csv D:\Inventory\current\inventory.csv
$inv | Group-Object Status | Select-Object Name, Count
$inv | Group-Object Name | Where-Object Count -gt 1 | Select-Object Name   # expected: nothing counted twice
$inv | Where-Object { $_.Status -eq 'active' -and (-not $_.Owner -or -not $_.UpdateSource -or -not $_.Location) } | Select-Object Name   # expected: nothing
$stamp = Get-Date -Format yyyy-MM-dd
Copy-Item D:\Inventory\current\inventory.csv "D:\Inventory\history\inventory-$stamp.csv"
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 "D:\Inventory\history\inventory-$stamp.csv" | Export-Csv D:\Inventory\history\hashes.csv -Append -NoTypeInformation

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: The inventory lists every component in the boundary exactly once with every column filled, planned systems are marked planned, the update-on-change rule and the monthly reconciliation are written with an owner and deputy, and the first version is in history with its hash.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence

answers: Pretty formatting
Update-on-change plus a scheduled reconciliation against sources the record doesn't control — the directory and the leases
Monthly printing

answers: Normal churn to ignore
A reason to restart DHCP
A finding — either an undocumented system or a broken process, and both matter
quizzes.explanation: The reconciliation exists to surface exactly this. Unknown hardware on the network is the classic first question of any assessment.

Physical security
Awareness training

lessons.title: Feed it from what the network already knows
lessons.summary: The inventory says what should exist; the network's own records say what does. Export the directory's computer objects, the DHCP leases, the WSUS computer list, SBD-REPO01's records and the baseline sessions through the sessions administrators already use, and file them on SBD-MGMT01 with hashes, in one shape lesson 5 can compare.
objectives: Export each discovery source through an existing administration path.
Know what each source can and can't prove.
File the exports on SBD-MGMT01 with hashes, in one comparable shape.
recap: Five sources, gathered through paths administrators already use.
Each proves something narrow; together they test the record.
Same day, one name key, hashed and filed on SBD-MGMT01.
