sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Complete courses 1.1–1.7: every system those courses built is running, course 1.6's fleet inventory is filed, and SBD-WSUS01 serves all four update rings.

Provision SBD-MGMT01 (10.0.70.10, VLAN 70) as a Windows Server virtual machine with a separate data volume (D: in this sample) for the record.

Keep the records earlier courses produced within reach: the service-path register, course 1.7's ring table and WSUS computer list, course 1.2's snapshot catalog, each course's baseline sessions, and the exception record.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: Course 1.6 handed over a snapshot of the fleet; this course makes the whole network's component inventory a living record on SBD-MGMT01 — NIST SP 800-53 CM-8 in practice. The server keeps the record and reaches into nothing: the directory, the DHCP leases, the WSUS computer list, SBD-REPO01's records and the baseline sessions it is checked against arrive through the administrators' existing sessions. Column names and the monthly cadence are sample values; the system owner decides.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Read the directory over LDAP from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01: every computer object's name, operating system, distinguished name (which gives its OU) and lastLogonTimestamp. Use an LDAP search rather than the Active Directory module, whose Web Services port the controllers open only to AdminJumpBox01, and read lastLogonTimestamp as a sign of staleness, not of last use: it is updated only when the stored value is 9 to 14 days old.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Export the leases on SBD-DHCP01 in a session from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01: every lease in the VLAN 80 scope with its address, client ID (the MAC address), host name, state and expiry. A lease shows what is plugged in now, joined or not; course 1.1's DHCP audit log shows what came and went between exports.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Export SBD-WSUS01's computer list the same way: each computer's name, address, last contact, last status report and requested ring. WSUS's cleanup removes computers silent for 30 days (course 1.7), so a machine missing there has been quiet for a month or more.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Copy SBD-REPO01's records over SSH as course 1.2 does, and count its web server's access log by client address to see which Linux servers actually take packages. List the baseline sessions in the evidence folders you hold, by host and date; Tier 0 reports its hosts' dates through the change record, because its evidence stays on AdminJumpBox01.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: File the set: hash every export into a dated list, copy both into D:\Inventory\sources on SBD-MGMT01 through a remoting session, and reduce every name to one key — the short host name, so a lease's SBD-PC07.sbd.test and the directory's SBD-PC07 meet. Take all the sources on the same day; sources taken weeks apart disagree about machines that simply moved.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
# On SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 (Tier 1): one dated folder for this month's sources
$d = "C:\Evidence\management-server\sources\$(Get-Date -Format yyyy-MM-dd)"; New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force "$d\repo01" | Out-Null
$s = [adsisearcher]'(objectCategory=computer)'; $s.PageSize = 500
$s.FindAll() | ForEach-Object { $p = $_.Properties; [pscustomobject]@{ Name = "$($p.name)"; OS = "$($p.operatingsystem)"; DN = "$($p.distinguishedname)"; LastLogon = if ("$($p.lastlogontimestamp)") { [datetime]::FromFileTime([long]"$($p.lastlogontimestamp)") } } } | Export-Csv "$d\directory.csv" -NoTypeInformation
Invoke-Command SBD-DHCP01 { Get-DhcpServerv4Lease -ScopeId 10.0.80.0 -AllLeases | Select-Object IPAddress, ClientId, HostName, AddressState, LeaseExpiryTime } | Export-Csv "$d\dhcp-leases.csv" -NoTypeInformation
Invoke-Command SBD-WSUS01 { Get-WsusComputer -All | Select-Object FullDomainName, IPAddress, LastSyncTime, LastReportedStatusTime, RequestedTargetGroupName } | Export-Csv "$d\wsus-computers.csv" -NoTypeInformation
scp -r <your-account>@SBD-REPO01.sbd.test:/srv/repo-records/* "$d\repo01\"
# On SBD-REPO01: who fetched packages
sudo awk '{print $1}' /var/log/httpd/access_log | sort | uniq -c
# Back on SBD-ADMIN-SRV01: hash the set and file it on SBD-MGMT01
Get-ChildItem $d -Recurse -File | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 | Export-Csv "$d-hashes.csv" -NoTypeInformation
$m = New-PSSession SBD-MGMT01; Copy-Item $d, "$d-hashes.csv" -Destination D:\Inventory\sources\ -ToSession $m -Recurse

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: Course 1.6 handed over a snapshot of the fleet; this course makes the whole network's component inventory a living record on SBD-MGMT01 — NIST SP 800-53 CM-8 in practice. The server keeps the record and reaches into nothing: the directory, the DHCP leases, the WSUS computer list, SBD-REPO01's records and the baseline sessions it is checked against arrive through the administrators' existing sessions. Column names and the monthly cadence are sample values; the system owner decides.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: On SBD-MGMT01, compare the inventory's active rows with each source by the name key: the domain-joined rows against the directory, the VLAN 80 rows against the leases, and the Windows rows against WSUS's computer list and its rings. In a source but not the record is an unrecorded component; recorded but absent where it should appear is a gap; present in both with a different value — a ring, an OU, an address — is drift.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Prove the comparison works before trusting a clean result: run it against a test copy of the inventory with one PC's row removed — the PC must appear as found in the directory but not in the record — and against another copy with one ring changed, which the ring comparison must report. Test copies are never published.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Classify every real difference and close it: correct the record through the change log, bring the component under management or remove it, or record the explanation — a PC switched off for a week has no lease and isn't missing. An unrecorded device is reported to the system owner the day it is found (CM-8(3)), and drift that keeps coming from one procedure is fixed in that procedure.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Take SBD-MGMT01's first SCAP baseline with course 1.1's SCC and benchmark versions, run locally in a Tier 1 session from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, classify its open items as part 4 taught, and enter the date in its own inventory row.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: Hand off: publish the reconciled version with its hash, set the monthly reconciliation in the week after course 1.7's cycle closes so the WSUS list is fresh, and note what later courses add — course 1.11 turns the VLAN 40 servers' planned rows active as it builds them, and course 1.12 carries D:\Inventory into the recovery set.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
# On SBD-MGMT01 (session from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01): the newest sources against the active record
$src = (Get-ChildItem D:\Inventory\sources -Directory | Sort-Object Name | Select-Object -Last 1).FullName
$short = { $args[0] -replace '\..*$' }
$active = Import-Csv D:\Inventory\current\inventory.csv | Where-Object Status -eq 'active'
$directory = (Import-Csv "$src\directory.csv").Name
$leases = Import-Csv "$src\dhcp-leases.csv" | Where-Object HostName | ForEach-Object { & $short $_.HostName }
$rings = Import-Csv "$src\wsus-computers.csv" | ForEach-Object { '{0}|{1}' -f (& $short $_.FullDomainName), $_.RequestedTargetGroupName }
Compare-Object ($active | Where-Object Domain -eq 'sbd.test').Name $directory   # <= recorded only, => directory only
Compare-Object ($active | Where-Object VLAN -eq '80').Name $leases
Compare-Object ($active | Where-Object UpdateSource -like 'Ring*' | ForEach-Object { '{0}|{1}' -f $_.Name, $_.UpdateSource }) $rings
# Prove it: with SBD-PC07's row left out of a test copy, SBD-PC07 must show as directory only
Compare-Object ($active | Where-Object { $_.Domain -eq 'sbd.test' -and $_.Name -ne 'SBD-PC07' }).Name $directory

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: Every difference between the record and the sources is listed and classified, the deliberate tests were caught, unrecorded components were reported to the system owner, SBD-MGMT01 has its first baseline, and the reconciled version is published with its hash and the next reconciliation date.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep the comparison output, the classified findings with their resolutions, the tests that proved detection, the SCC results with classified findings, the reconciled version's hash, and the handoff note.

To make the report longer
Because the real record might be deleted

answers: Delete it from the directory and move on

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Complete courses 1.1–1.8: the domain with its DNS, time and hardened OUs, the part 6 PKI and its autoenrollment GPO, DHCP and the admin seats, SBD-REPO01 and its Linux client package, the logging pipeline with course 1.4's KDS root key, SBD-SPLUNK01 as the Linux server pattern, the fleet, the update rings, and the SBD-MGMT01 inventory.

Provision the VLAN 40 hosts as virtual machines on SBD-HV05: SBD-FS01 (10.0.40.10), SBD-SQL01 (10.0.40.20) and SBD-APPS01 (10.0.40.30) on Windows Server, and SBD-WEB01 (10.0.40.40) on the Red Hat Enterprise Linux–family release course 1.2 chose, with Apache, to be joined to sbd.test with SSSD as SBD-SPLUNK01 was in course 1.5.

Have the service-path register, the course 1.1 SBD Server Authentication template, course 1.2's client package and Linux assessment set, and part 4's SCC media within reach — every service here gets a documented path, a real certificate and a first baseline.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The users finally get what the network exists for: files, licensing, and an internal web application with its application tier and database. The model's rule governs the whole course — permit only documented business service paths — so every service arrives with its register rows, its service identity, and its certificate, and nothing reaches it any other way.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Write the service-path rows into the register, with the IDs the System Hub gives them and an owner each: the fleet to SBD-FS01 on SMB 445 (F05), to SBD-APPS01 on its licensing port, recorded per application (F12), and to SBD-WEB01 on HTTPS 443 (F13); SBD-WEB01 to SBD-APPS01 for the application API on HTTPS 443 (F21); and SBD-APPS01 — and only SBD-APPS01 — to SBD-SQL01 on TCP 1433 with TLS (F22). Add the explicit deny from SBD-WEB01 to SBD-SQL01 (F14): the web tier has no database dependency. All four servers share VLAN 40, so the router never sees their traffic to each other — each server's host firewall enforces those rows. Everything else toward VLAN 40 stays denied, including endpoint-to-SQL directly.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Add the rows every new server needs: administration from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 (A02), and for the three Windows servers the domain rows (F01–F03, F09), Ring 3 updates (F06), event forwarding (F17), certificate publication (F18) and enrollment to SBD-SUBCA01 on the row course 1.1, part 6 confirmed. SBD-WEB01's Linux rows already name it: packages from SBD-REPO01 only (F19, HTTP with GPG-signed packages, course 1.2), syslog over TLS to the collector, SBD-SYSLOG01 (F07, TCP 6514), and time from both domain controllers (F09) — the same paths SBD-SPLUNK01 has used since course 1.5.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Choose the service identities: group managed service accounts (gMSAs) for the SQL and application services, so passwords rotate themselves. They rely on the forest's one KDS root key, which course 1.4 created: confirm it with Get-KdsRootKey and never create another. Each account is created from AdminJumpBox01 once its host has joined, allowed to that one computer, as course 1.4 did (lesson 3). Note delegated managed service accounts, introduced in the newest Windows Server release, as the migration path for any legacy service account this lab later inherits.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Create the access groups under the course 1.1 Groups OU from AdminJumpBox01 — per-share and per-application role groups — because permissions will be granted to roles, never to named humans.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: Plan the server certificates: one SBD Server Authentication certificate (course 1.1, part 6) each for SQL01, APPS01 (for its application API), and WEB01, with the host's DNS name in the subject alternative name. Each host requests its own in its build lesson through the part 6 process, so the private key never leaves it — the template allows exportable keys only where course 1.12's recovery plan says so. Part 6's autoenrollment GPO, linked at the domain root, already reaches every new member, so no other enrollment policy is created.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
# From AdminJumpBox01 (Tier 0): the course 1.4 KDS root key, the existing gMSAs, and the role groups
Invoke-Command SBD-DC01 { Get-KdsRootKey | Select-Object KeyId, EffectiveTime }   # one key, from course 1.4
Get-ADServiceAccount -Filter * | Select-Object Name, Enabled   # course 1.4's three; this course's arrive with their hosts
Get-ADGroup -SearchBase 'OU=Groups,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test' -Filter * | Select-Object Name

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: The register carries every VLAN 40 service row with its ID and owner — the SQL path restricted to APPS01 alone (F22), the WEB01-to-SQL01 deny (F14), and WEB01's repository, syslog and time rows — the course 1.4 KDS root key is the forest's only one, the role groups exist, and each server certificate is planned for the host that will request it.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep the service-path rows, the identity and group design, the KDS root key check, and the certificate plan.

quizzes.question: Who may reach SQL01 on 1433?
answers: Any domain member
WEB01 and APPS01
Only APPS01 — the application tier is the database's whole audience
quizzes.explanation: Browsers talk to the web tier, the web tier calls the application API, and only the application tier queries the database. The register encodes that chain — including an explicit deny from WEB01 to SQL01 — and denies shortcuts around it.

quizzes.question: Why gMSAs instead of a user account named svc-sql?
answers: The directory manages and rotates the password itself — no human knows it, nothing expires unnoticed
gMSAs run queries faster
Password accounts cannot start services
quizzes.explanation: Service account passwords are a classic standing weakness. Managed accounts remove the password from human hands entirely.

quizzes.question: Why grant access to role groups rather than people?
answers: Groups are alphabetical
Access follows the job: membership changes are one record, and permissions never accumulate on individuals
Permissions cannot hold user names
quizzes.explanation: Role-based access is what makes 'who can touch this data' answerable from group membership instead of archaeology.

objectives: Build SBD-FS01 in its place and create the shares with role-group permissions and no individual grants.
Confirm the SMB signing and encryption posture end to end.
Verify access and denial per role from the fleet.
recap: Roles own the ACLs; humans own role memberships.

sections.body: The users finally get what the network exists for: files, licensing, and an internal web application with its application tier and database. The model's rule governs the whole course — permit only documented business service paths — so every service arrives with its register rows, its service identity, and its certificate, and nothing reaches it any other way.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Build SBD-FS01 as a Windows Server virtual machine at 10.0.40.10/24, with the core's VLAN 40 interface as gateway (10.0.40.1 in this sample), both domain controllers for DNS, a separate data volume for the shares, and the hypervisor's time synchronization turned off. Join it straight into the Servers OU, so course 1.1's STIG policies, part 8's tier policies, course 1.3's event-forwarding GPO and course 1.7's Ring 3 update policy apply from its first boot, and check that it takes its time from a domain controller. Lessons 3 and 4 build SBD-SQL01 and SBD-APPS01 the same way.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Create the planned shares, granting NTFS permissions to the lesson-1 role groups only — share permissions stay simple, the filesystem carries the detail, and no named human appears in an access control list (ACL).

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Enable access-based enumeration so users see only what their roles permit — the quiet UX of least privilege.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Confirm the SMB posture. The newest Windows client release (Pro, Enterprise, and Education) requires SMB signing for both inbound and outbound connections, but the newest Windows Server release requires it only for its own outbound connections — so require signing on SBD-FS01 as well (RequireSecuritySignature in its SMB server configuration), and opt the sensitive share into SMB encryption. Verify both on a live connection from a fleet machine rather than assuming the defaults.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: Test as members of two different roles from fleet machines: each sees and opens exactly its shares, and the other's are invisible and, opened by path, denied. Turn on Audit Detailed File Share (failure) for SBD-FS01 in a GPO security-filtered to it, recorded as a documented addition as course 1.4 did for SBD-AUDIT01, so each refusal is event 5145 in its Security log; lesson 5 sends that event to the collector.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
# In a Tier 1 session on SBD-FS01 from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01
([adsisearcher]"(&(objectCategory=computer)(name=$env:COMPUTERNAME))").FindOne().Path   # ...OU=Servers,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test
w32tm /query /source   # a domain controller, never the local clock
Get-SmbShare | Select-Object Name, Path, FolderEnumerationMode, EncryptData
Get-SmbServerConfiguration | Select-Object RequireSecuritySignature   # expected True
icacls D:\Shares\Projects | Select-String 'SBD'
auditpol /get /subcategory:"Detailed File Share"   # Failure
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=5145} -MaxEvents 5 | Select-Object TimeCreated, Message
# On the fleet machine, during the test session
Get-SmbConnection | Where-Object ServerName -like 'SBD-FS01*' | Select-Object ShareName, Dialect, Signed, Encrypted

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: SBD-FS01 sits in the Servers OU with time from a domain controller, shares grant to role groups only, FS01 requires signing, a live connection from the fleet shows Signed True — or, on the encrypted share, Encrypted True, where Signed reads False because encryption, which also protects integrity, takes the place of signing — and the two-role test proves both the access and the invisible-denied behavior, with each refusal recorded as event 5145.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep the OU placement and time source, the share and NTFS permission reports, FS01's signing setting and the live connection's signing/encryption output, and the two-role test record with its 5145 events.

Complete courses 1.1–1.8: the domain with its DNS, time and hardened OUs, the part 6 PKI and its autoenrollment GPO, DHCP and the admin seats, SBD-REPO01 and its Linux client package, the logging pipeline with course 1.4's KDS root key, SBD-SPLUNK01 as the Linux server pattern, the fleet, the update rings, and the SBD-MGMT01 inventory.

Have the service-path register, the course 1.1 SBD Server Authentication template, course 1.2's client package and Linux assessment set, and part 4's SCC media within reach — every service here gets a documented path, a real certificate and a first baseline.

sections.body: The users finally get what the network exists for: files, licensing, and an internal web application with its application tier and database. The model's rule governs the whole course — permit only documented business service paths — so every service arrives with its register rows, its service identity, and its certificate, and nothing reaches it any other way.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Build SBD-SQL01 (10.0.40.20) and the host of its one caller, SBD-APPS01 (10.0.40.30), as SBD-FS01 was built in lesson 2. Then, from AdminJumpBox01, create one gMSA per service, each allowed to one computer as course 1.4 did: SBD-SQL$ for SBD-SQL01$ and SBD-Apps$ for SBD-APPS01$ (sample names). Install the database engine with SBD\SBD-SQL$ as its service account and no password — the install itself demonstrates the managed account working where a password account used to live.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Add SBD-SQL01 to the SBD TLS Servers group, then on SBD-SQL01 request its SBD Server Authentication certificate through the course 1.1 process, with SBD-SQL01.sbd.test in the subject alternative name. Give the gMSA read on the certificate's private key — without it the service won't start with the certificate — select the certificate in SQL Server Configuration Manager, set Force Encryption to Yes, and restart the service; the chain validates against pki.sbd.test like every other certificate on this network.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Create the application databases with role-based database access for one login only, SBD\SBD-Apps$, the identity SBD-APPS01's services run as in lesson 4 — least privilege continues inside the engine, not just at its port. Record the databases and the logins they depend on: course 1.12 backs them up, so this course sets up no backup job.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Prove the audience: allow TCP 1433 in SBD-SQL01's host firewall from 10.0.40.30 alone (F22), and turn on its dropped-packet logging if it is off. A connection from APPS01 succeeds. The same attempt from SBD-FS01 is refused by SBD-SQL01's host firewall — the two share VLAN 40, so the router never sees it, which is exactly how SBD-WEB01 will be refused in lesson 4 — and one from a fleet machine dies at the router with a deny-log entry.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
# From AdminJumpBox01 (Tier 0): one gMSA per service, each allowed to one computer
New-ADServiceAccount SBD-SQL -DNSHostName SBD-SQL.sbd.test -PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword 'SBD-SQL01$'
New-ADServiceAccount SBD-Apps -DNSHostName SBD-Apps.sbd.test -PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword 'SBD-APPS01$'
# In a Tier 1 session on SBD-SQL01 from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01: identity, encryption, certificate, firewall scope
Get-CimInstance Win32_Service -Filter "Name='MSSQLSERVER'" | Select-Object Name, StartName, State   # StartName SBD\SBD-SQL$
Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Microsoft SQL Server\*\MSSQLServer\SuperSocketNetLib' | Select-Object ForceEncryption, Certificate   # 1 and the thumbprint
$cer = Get-ChildItem Cert:\LocalMachine\My | Where-Object Subject -like '*SBD-SQL01*' | Export-Certificate -FilePath "$env:TEMP\sql01.cer"
certutil -verify -urlfetch $cer.FullName   # chain and revocation from pki.sbd.test
Get-NetFirewallPortFilter | Where-Object LocalPort -eq 1433 | Get-NetFirewallRule | Where-Object { $_.Enabled -eq 'True' -and $_.Direction -eq 'Inbound' } | Get-NetFirewallAddressFilter | Select-Object RemoteAddress   # 10.0.40.30 only
# From SBD-APPS01: expected TcpTestSucceeded True. From SBD-FS01 and from a fleet machine: expected False.
Test-NetConnection SBD-SQL01.sbd.test -Port 1433

sections.heading: What success looks like

lessons.summary: The application server and the internal web server complete the dependency chain: fleet to web, web to application, application to database — each hop a register row, the web tier hardened against its Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) guidance, and HTTPS served from the lab's own trust.
objectives: Stand up SBD-APPS01's licensing service and application API on their registered paths.

sections.heading: Before you start

Complete courses 1.1–1.8: the domain with its DNS, time and hardened OUs, the part 6 PKI and its autoenrollment GPO, DHCP and the admin seats, SBD-REPO01 and its Linux client package, the logging pipeline with course 1.4's KDS root key, SBD-SPLUNK01 as the Linux server pattern, the fleet, the update rings, and the SBD-MGMT01 inventory.

Provision the VLAN 40 hosts as virtual machines on SBD-HV05: SBD-FS01 (10.0.40.10), SBD-SQL01 (10.0.40.20) and SBD-APPS01 (10.0.40.30) on Windows Server, and SBD-WEB01 (10.0.40.40) on the Red Hat Enterprise Linux–family release course 1.2 chose, with Apache, to be joined to sbd.test with SSSD as SBD-SPLUNK01 was in course 1.5.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The users finally get what the network exists for: files, licensing, and an internal web application with its application tier and database. The model's rule governs the whole course — permit only documented business service paths — so every service arrives with its register rows, its service identity, and its certificate, and nothing reaches it any other way.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: On SBD-APPS01, built in lesson 3, and added to the SBD TLS Servers group, request its SBD Server Authentication certificate through the course 1.1 process and run both of its services as SBD\SBD-Apps$, or record an exception where the product can't use a gMSA: the licensing service, verified from the fleet on its registered vendor port (F12), and the application API on HTTPS 443 (F21), with its host firewall admitting the API from SBD-WEB01 (10.0.40.40) alone. APPS01 is the network's one SQL consumer — and the template for any future service: identity, row, evidence.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Build SBD-WEB01 at 10.0.40.40/24 from hashed install media of the Red Hat Enterprise Linux–family release course 1.2 chose, with both domain controllers for DNS and the hypervisor's time synchronization turned off. Before anything else, install course 1.1's chrony file (both domain controllers, maxdistance 16) and confirm a controller is selected with a small, steady offset; then apply course 1.2's client package, checked against its hashes, so SBD-REPO01 is its only package source (F19), and update from the current snapshot. Place the part 6 root in its system trust store by hand (/etc/pki/ca-trust/source/anchors, then update-ca-trust), its SHA-256 checked against part 6's record, as course 1.2 did for SBD-REPO01.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Join sbd.test with realm join into the Servers OU, as SBD-SPLUNK01 was joined in course 1.5, permit sign-in only to SBD Tier 1 Admins with realm permit -g, and give that group sudo through a drop-in file. Make the host firewall the register's copy: HTTPS 443 from the fleet (F13) and SSH from 10.0.60.20 alone. Then send its syslog over TLS to SBD-SYSLOG01 (F07) as course 1.3 enrolled SBD-REPO01: rsyslog-gnutls from the snapshot, the collector's certificate name checked, and SBD-WEB01 added to the collector's TCP 6514 sender list.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Request SBD-WEB01's SBD Server Authentication certificate through the course 1.1 process, with the key and request made on the host with openssl and SBD-WEB01.sbd.test in both subject and subject alternative name, and the key readable by root alone. Serve the internal application over HTTPS with its chain, and harden Apache against the DISA Apache Server 2.4 UNIX STIGs that course 1.2 staged — the 2,048-bit key floor from part 6's templates applies here as everywhere. Export the hardened configuration and hash it as the change record (course 1.12 backs up SBD-APPS01's and SBD-WEB01's configuration and certificates); lesson 5 measures the host.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: Prove the chain from a fleet machine: the HTTPS page loads with a validating certificate, and its data travels fleet → WEB01 → APPS01 → SQL01, every hop a register row — on SBD-SQL01, sys.dm_exec_connections shows APPS01's session (10.0.40.30) with encrypt_option TRUE. Then prove the shortcuts stay shut: a direct attempt from SBD-WEB01 to SQL01 on 1433 is refused by SQL01's host firewall, and the fleet still cannot touch 1433 at all — three courses of design visible in one browser request.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
# On SBD-WEB01 (Tier 1 SSH session from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01): time, packages, domain, firewall, logging, web
chronyc sources -v; chronyc tracking   # ^* one controller, ^+ or ^- the other
dnf repolist --all   # expected: only the sbd-repo01 repositories enabled
realm list   # sbd.test, kerberos-member, permitted group SBD Tier 1 Admins
sudo firewall-cmd --get-active-zones
openssl s_client -connect SBD-SYSLOG01.sbd.test:6514 -verify_hostname SBD-SYSLOG01.sbd.test </dev/null 2>/dev/null | grep 'Verify return code'   # 0 (ok): the SBD root is trusted
logger -t sbd-web-proof 'SBD-WEB01 syslog over TLS test'
sudo apachectl -S   # one HTTPS site on 10.0.40.40:443
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://SBD-APPS01.sbd.test/   # use your application's health path
timeout 5 bash -c '</dev/tcp/SBD-SQL01.sbd.test/1433' && echo open || echo 'refused or timed out'   # expected: refused or timed out
# On SBD-ADMIN-SRV01: the issued certificate's chain and revocation
certutil -verify -urlfetch C:\Evidence\business-services\web01.cer
# From a fleet machine: the page answers, the database does not
Test-NetConnection SBD-WEB01.sbd.test -Port 443
Test-NetConnection SBD-SQL01.sbd.test -Port 1433   # expected: False
# On SBD-SQL01, in a query: APPS01's live session is encrypted
# SELECT client_net_address, encrypt_option, auth_scheme FROM sys.dm_exec_connections WHERE client_net_address = '10.0.40.30'

courses.subtitle: Backups with custody, one rehearsed restore & the closing record
courses.description: Close the Build path by proving the network can come back: every backup in the network defined and scheduled in one place — the directory, the CA under ceremony-grade custody, Group Policy, DHCP, the repository and analysis configuration, the VLAN 40 business services with their permissions, logins and certificates, the log archive, and the living records — in one hashed catalog, a timed restore rehearsal in isolation, and the recovery record that completes the Body of Evidence.

lessons.title: Decide what recovery must prove
lessons.summary: Recovery starts as a list of promises: which systems and records must be restorable, how old a restored copy may be, how long restoration may take, and the one schedule that says how each is backed up — written as commitments the rest of the course exists to keep.
objectives: Name the recovery set: what must come back, in what order.
Set the recovery point and time objectives per item.
Write the backup schedule: every backup in the network, defined in one place.
Decide where backups live and who can touch them.
recap: The recovery set is ordered by dependency, directory first, VLAN 40 included.
Point and time objectives exist to be measured, not admired.
One schedule defines every backup in the network.
Backups get a protected home plus one offline, custody-tracked copy.
lessons.next: Lesson 2 puts the Tier 0 rows of the schedule into effect.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Complete courses 1.1–1.11 (courses 1.9 and 1.10 are coming soon and aren't needed): the full network, the VLAN 40 business services, their records, the protected log archive, and the living inventory all exist.

Provision the backup storage this course schedules into: a protected backup volume (E: in this sample) on every Windows server in the recovery set — both domain controllers, SBD-SUBCA01, SBD-DHCP01, SBD-MGMT01, SBD-FS01, SBD-SQL01 and SBD-APPS01 — never one of the volumes being backed up and written only by the backup jobs, and a separate volume mounted at /srv/backup, readable by root alone, on SBD-REPO01, SBD-SPLUNK01 and SBD-WEB01. Earlier courses set up no backup jobs; this course defines and schedules every one. Also provide an offline backup cabinet with removable media and a custody register, and an isolated recovery network segment (or host) for the restore rehearsal.

Have the custody records handy: the sealed Directory Services Restore Mode (DSRM) passwords set in course 1.1, part 1 and the part 6 ceremony record for SBD-ROOTCA01's protected backup — recovery is where those promises come due.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The model's final chapter: a network that cannot come back was never really built. This course is the one place every backup in the network is defined and scheduled — the directory, both CAs, Group Policy, DHCP, the repository and analysis configuration, the VLAN 40 business services with their permissions, logins and certificates, the log record, and the living records — then proves one real restore in isolation and files the tested-recovery evidence the authorization path expects.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Write the recovery set in dependency order — the order the path built it: the directory on both controllers first, because everything trusts it; then the certificate authorities (SBD-SUBCA01's database and key, and SBD-ROOTCA01's course 1.1, part 6 ceremony backup); Group Policy; SBD-DHCP01 (part 7); the boundary's records (the service-path register and the core router's configuration); SBD-REPO01's snapshot catalog and snapshots (course 1.2); SBD-SPLUNK01's configuration (course 1.5); the log archive and its catalog on SBD-AUDIT01 (course 1.4); the inventory on SBD-MGMT01 (course 1.8); the VLAN 40 business services (course 1.11) — SBD-FS01's share data with its NTFS permissions, SBD-SQL01's databases and the logins they depend on, SBD-APPS01's and SBD-WEB01's configuration and certificates; and the exception record.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Set the two numbers per item: how much history may be lost (recovery point) and how long restoration may take (recovery time) — lab-honest values you will actually measure against in lesson 5, not aspirations. A directory backup older than the forest's tombstone lifetime (180 days by default) can't be restored at all, so the directory's recovery point stays well inside it.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Write the backup schedule, the one place every backup in this network is defined: for each item, what is captured, the tool, when it runs, where it lands, and who restores it. No earlier course scheduled a backup; the one build-time copy is SBD-ROOTCA01's, taken inside the course 1.1 ceremony, and the schedule accounts for it rather than repeating it. Lessons 2 and 3 put each row into effect.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Decide backup placement: each protected backup volume is written only by its backup jobs and readable by the recovery role, and custodians of the matching tier carry copies to the offline backup cabinet on media — the air-gapped network's version of an off-site copy. There is no backup server and no network path to the cabinet.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: Confirm the standing custody items: the DSRM passwords set in course 1.1, part 1 are sealed and findable, and SBD-ROOTCA01's protected backup from the part 6 ceremony is accounted for — recovery depends on secrets that must exist before the bad day.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
# On each Windows server in the recovery set: capture the current protection state before this course changes it.
wbadmin get versions
Get-Volume -DriveLetter E | Select-Object DriveLetter, FileSystemLabel, SizeRemaining   # the protected backup volume

sections.body:
Complete courses 1.1–1.11 (courses 1.9 and 1.10 are coming soon and aren't needed): the full network, the VLAN 40 business services, their records, the protected log archive, and the living inventory all exist.

Provision the backup storage this course schedules into: a protected backup volume (E: in this sample) on every Windows server in the recovery set — both domain controllers, SBD-SUBCA01, SBD-DHCP01, SBD-MGMT01, SBD-FS01, SBD-SQL01 and SBD-APPS01 — never one of the volumes being backed up and written only by the backup jobs, and a separate volume mounted at /srv/backup, readable by root alone, on SBD-REPO01, SBD-SPLUNK01 and SBD-WEB01. Earlier courses set up no backup jobs; this course defines and schedules every one. Also provide an offline backup cabinet with removable media and a custody register, and an isolated recovery network segment (or host) for the restore rehearsal.

Have the custody records handy: the sealed Directory Services Restore Mode (DSRM) passwords set in course 1.1, part 1 and the part 6 ceremony record for SBD-ROOTCA01's protected backup — recovery is where those promises come due.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The model's final chapter: a network that cannot come back was never really built. This course is the one place every backup in the network is defined and scheduled — the directory, both CAs, Group Policy, DHCP, the repository and analysis configuration, the VLAN 40 business services with their permissions, logins and certificates, the log record, and the living records — then proves one real restore in isolation and files the tested-recovery evidence the authorization path expects.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: In a Tier 0 session from AdminJumpBox01, schedule Windows Server Backup on SBD-DC01 and SBD-DC02, each to its own protected backup volume, with the system state and all critical volumes (wbadmin's -systemState and -allCritical): the system state is what a directory restore in DSRM needs, and the critical volumes let the same backup rebuild a controller whose hardware is gone. Two controllers, two independent backups — replication is availability and was never recovery, as course 1.1, part 1 put it.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: After the first run, verify each backup's completion, record its version identifier in the backup catalog (C:\Evidence\recovery on AdminJumpBox01), and hash the catalog — an unverified backup is a hope with a timestamp.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Back up the issuing CA. Schedule SBD-SUBCA01's own system state and critical-volume backup to its protected volume, so the server can be rebuilt; then take the CA's own backup — database and private key — with certutil to E:\Backups\CA, with its registry configuration exported beside it, on the cadence the schedule sets and after every CA key renewal. It prompts for the password that protects the key, so it is a Tier 0 task, never an unattended one. Never write it to C:\Evidence: the private key is a secret, and secrets never go into evidence. Record custody and put only the hashes in evidence; SBD-ROOTCA01's ceremony backup is verified against its record, never duplicated or brought onto the network.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Schedule the Group Policy backup: a daily task on SBD-DC01, running as SYSTEM from a script folder only Tier 0 administrators can write, that runs Backup-GPO -All into a dated folder on E:\Backups\GPO and exports every link beside it — a restored GPO brings back its settings and permissions, not its links. That covers the whole estate, course 1.1's SBD Certificate Autoenrollment and part 8's tier logon GPOs included; the GPO reports and link exports parts 5 and 6 filed stay as their change records.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: Enable the Active Directory Recycle Bin from the Tier 0 seat — a one-way, forest-level change run against the domain naming master (SBD-DC01) and recorded as the change it is — so a deleted user or OU comes back intact without touching system state. Objects deleted before it was enabled can come back only from a backup.

sections.heading: Step 6
sections.body: Write the restore decision tree: deleted object → Recycle Bin; corrupted DC on its own hardware → system state restore in DSRM (lesson 5's rehearsal); DC whose hardware is gone → full server (bare-metal) recovery from the critical-volumes backup; a damaged GPO → Restore-GPO from the dated set, then its links from the export; whole-forest loss → the Microsoft forest recovery guide, referenced and staged with the evidence rather than improvised on the day.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
# Tier 0 session from AdminJumpBox01: daily schedules on each controller and the issuing CA (E: is never a volume being backed up)
Invoke-Command SBD-DC01.sbd.test, SBD-DC02.sbd.test, SBD-SUBCA01.sbd.test { wbadmin enable backup -addtarget:E: -schedule:21:00 -systemState -allCritical -quiet }
Invoke-Command SBD-DC01.sbd.test, SBD-DC02.sbd.test { wbadmin get versions }   # after the first run
# On SBD-SUBCA01 (Tier 0 session): the CA's own backup, to its protected volume, never to the evidence folder
certutil -backup E:\Backups\CA   # prompts for the password that protects the exported key
reg export HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CertSvc\Configuration E:\Backups\CA\certsvc-config.reg
Get-ChildItem E:\Backups\CA -Recurse -File | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 | Export-Csv E:\Backups\ca-backup-hashes.csv -NoTypeInformation   # only this list goes to C:\Evidence\recovery
# On SBD-DC01: C:\Scripts\Backup-SbdGpo.ps1 (writable by Tier 0 administrators only) runs these lines, then the task runs it daily
#   $d = 'E:\Backups\GPO\{0:yyyy-MM-dd}' -f (Get-Date); New-Item -ItemType Directory $d -Force | Out-Null; Backup-GPO -All -Path $d
#   @('DC=sbd,DC=test') + (Get-ADOrganizationalUnit -Filter *).DistinguishedName | ForEach-Object { (Get-GPInheritance -Target $_).GpoLinks } | Select-Object Target, Order, DisplayName, Enabled, Enforced | Export-Csv "$d\gpo-links.csv" -NoTypeInformation
Register-ScheduledTask 'SBD GPO backup' -Action (New-ScheduledTaskAction -Execute powershell.exe -Argument '-NoProfile -File C:\Scripts\Backup-SbdGpo.ps1') -Trigger (New-ScheduledTaskTrigger -Daily -At 22:00) -User 'NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM' -RunLevel Highest
# Back on AdminJumpBox01: the Recycle Bin, then the catalog
Enable-ADOptionalFeature 'Recycle Bin Feature' -Scope ForestOrConfigurationSet -Target sbd.test -Server SBD-DC01.sbd.test
Get-ADOptionalFeature -Filter {Name -like 'Recycle Bin*'} | Select-Object Name, EnabledScopes
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 C:\Evidence\recovery\backup-catalog.txt

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The model's final chapter: a network that cannot come back was never really built. This course is the one place every backup in the network is defined and scheduled — the directory, both CAs, Group Policy, DHCP, the repository and analysis configuration, the VLAN 40 business services with their permissions, logins and certificates, the log record, and the living records — then proves one real restore in isolation and files the tested-recovery evidence the authorization path expects.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: In Tier 1 sessions from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, schedule SBD-DHCP01: a daily task, running as SYSTEM from a script folder only SBD Tier 1 Admins can write, takes Backup-DhcpServer into the default backup folder, copies it to a dated folder on E:\Backups\DHCP with an Export-DhcpServer of the configuration and leases, and hashes both. File course 1.1's restore note with it: after Restore-DhcpServer, set the DNS update credential again with Set-DhcpServerDnsCredential from the sealed record, because the backup doesn't carry it. On SBD-MGMT01, schedule Windows Server Backup of D:\Inventory (course 1.8) to its E:.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Schedule SBD-FS01: Windows Server Backup of D:\Shares to its E: every night. It keeps each file's NTFS permissions, and a file recovery restores them by default — never run it with -notRestoreAcl. Beside it, after every access change, save the readable record: icacls /save of the share tree's ACLs and an export of the share definitions (the LanmanServer Shares registry key, which also holds the share permissions), so permissions can be checked or reapplied without restoring data.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Schedule SBD-SQL01 inside the engine: a nightly SQL Server Agent job backs up each application database and the master, model and msdb system databases WITH CHECKSUM to E:\Backups\SQL, then checks each file with RESTORE VERIFYONLY. The engine writes the files as its gMSA, so grant SBD\SBD-SQL$ modify on that folder alone. master is where the logins live, msdb holds the Agent jobs, and the application databases' users map to the SBD\SBD-Apps$ login by its directory SID — so record the logins and each database's user mappings, and write the restore order: the instance and master (or the logins, recreated from the record) before the application databases. Use the simple recovery model unless your lesson 1 recovery point needs log backups, and a rebuilt SBD-SQL01 requests a new certificate through the course 1.1 process.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Schedule SBD-APPS01's Windows Server Backup with system state and critical volumes to its E:, so its services' configuration and its certificate, private key included, come back with the server — which is why the course 1.1 template never needs exportable keys. On SBD-WEB01, a root cron job in /etc/cron.d writes a dated tar archive of /etc/httpd, /etc/pki/tls (the certificate and its root-only key) and /etc/sssd, with SELinux contexts and ACLs, to /srv/backup with its SHA-256; SBD-REPO01 does the same for /srv/repo-records and the current snapshot each time it changes, so the previous one is already on media (course 1.2), and SBD-SPLUNK01 for /opt/splunk/etc (course 1.5 — the indexes are a working copy, and the record itself lives on SBD-AUDIT01). The WEB01 and Splunk archives hold keys, so they stay on protected media.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: Account for the log archive: SBD-AUDIT01's hashed archives in D:\LogArchive and their catalog (D:\LogArchive\Catalog\catalog.csv) are themselves the record, so their backup is the audit custodian's offline copy on the schedule's cadence (lesson 4), and no job runs on that server.

sections.heading: Step 6
sections.body: Export the boundary and living records into the set: the service-path register, the exception record (C:\Evidence\exception-record.csv), this course's own sheets, and a read-only export of the core router's configuration taken with the router's own export function from AdminJumpBox01 — this course reads the router's configuration and changes nothing on it. Record every first run's hashes in C:\Evidence\recovery on SBD-ADMIN-SRV01. A recovered network without its records would pass no assessment.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
# Tier 1 sessions from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01. On SBD-DHCP01, the task script (C:\Scripts, writable by SBD Tier 1 Admins only):
$b = 'E:\Backups\DHCP\{0:yyyy-MM-dd}' -f (Get-Date); New-Item -ItemType Directory $b -Force | Out-Null; $dir = Join-Path $env:windir 'System32\dhcp\backup'
Backup-DhcpServer -Path $dir; Copy-Item $dir (Join-Path $b 'database') -Recurse; Export-DhcpServer -File (Join-Path $b 'SBD-DHCP01.xml') -Leases
# On SBD-MGMT01, SBD-FS01 and SBD-APPS01: one daily schedule each, to the local E:
wbadmin enable backup -addtarget:E: -include:D:\Inventory -schedule:22:00 -quiet   # SBD-MGMT01
wbadmin enable backup -addtarget:E: -include:D:\Shares -schedule:22:00 -quiet   # SBD-FS01; then, after each access change:
icacls D:\Shares\* /save E:\Backups\FS01\shares-acl.txt /t /c; reg export HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer\Shares E:\Backups\FS01\shares.reg /y
wbadmin enable backup -addtarget:E: -schedule:22:30 -systemState -allCritical -quiet   # SBD-APPS01
# On SBD-SQL01: the engine's identity may write the backup folder; the Agent job's step runs this T-SQL for each database
icacls E:\Backups\SQL /grant 'SBD\SBD-SQL$:(OI)(CI)M'
#   BACKUP DATABASE [master] TO DISK = N'E:\Backups\SQL\master.bak' WITH CHECKSUM, INIT;   -- then model, msdb, each application database
#   RESTORE VERIFYONLY FROM DISK = N'E:\Backups\SQL\master.bak' WITH CHECKSUM;
sqlcmd -S SBD-SQL01.sbd.test -E -Q "SELECT name, type_desc, sid FROM sys.server_principals WHERE type IN ('U','G','S')"   # the login record
# On SBD-WEB01 (and the same pattern on SBD-REPO01 and SBD-SPLUNK01): the cron job's work, run once by hand
sudo tar --selinux --acls --xattrs -czf /srv/backup/web01-$(date +%F).tar.gz /etc/httpd /etc/pki/tls /etc/sssd
sudo sha256sum /srv/backup/web01-*.tar.gz

quizzes.question: SBD-SQL01's application database is backed up nightly, but master isn't. What breaks on a rebuilt instance?

quizzes.question: SBD-FS01's Projects folder is restored from Windows Server Backup. What happens to its permissions?

They have to be granted again by hand

answers: They are the largest files
A restored network without its records has lost its assessable story — the evidence must survive what it evidences

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Assign custodians by tier: a Tier 0 custodian handles the controllers' system state, the issuing CA's database and key backup, the Group Policy set, and the router configuration export; the audit custodian (SBD Audit Custodians, course 1.1, part 8) handles the log archive and its catalog from SBD-AUDIT01; a Tier 1 server custodian handles the member-server sets — SBD-DHCP01, SBD-REPO01, SBD-SPLUNK01, SBD-MGMT01, and the VLAN 40 servers SBD-FS01, SBD-SQL01, SBD-APPS01 and SBD-WEB01. No one carries a tier they do not hold.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: On the cadence the backup schedule sets, for each copy, write the media ID, hash the backup on its protected volume, copy it to encrypted removable media, and verify the hash on the media before it leaves the room. Keep Windows Server Backup's WindowsImageBackup folder layout on the media so wbadmin can read it there.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Carry the media to the offline backup cabinet and record the handoff in the custody register: who, what, when, the hashes, and the storage slot. This is the course 1.1 media procedure used for backups.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Pull one copy back as a test: find it from the register, verify its hash, and confirm it is readable. Lesson 5's rehearsal restores from a copy that has made this round trip.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
# On SBD-DC02 (Tier 0), with encrypted media MEDIA-0012 attached as F:: hash on the volume, copy, hash on the media
Get-ChildItem E:\WindowsImageBackup\SBD-DC02 -Recurse -File | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 | Export-Csv F:\MEDIA-0012-volume.csv -NoTypeInformation
Copy-Item E:\WindowsImageBackup -Destination F:\ -Recurse
Get-ChildItem F:\WindowsImageBackup\SBD-DC02 -Recurse -File | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 | Export-Csv F:\MEDIA-0012-media.csv -NoTypeInformation
Compare-Object (Import-Csv F:\MEDIA-0012-volume.csv).Hash (Import-Csv F:\MEDIA-0012-media.csv).Hash   # no output means the copy matches
wbadmin get versions -backupTarget:F: -machine:SBD-DC02   # the media is readable as a backup

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: Every item in the recovery set has an offline copy with matching hashes on the volume and the media, a custody entry with a named custodian of the right tier, and one copy has been retrieved and verified.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep the custodian assignments, the hash pairs (copied into C:\Evidence\recovery on the tier's seat), the custody register entries, and the retrieval test record.

quizzes.question: Who carries the domain controllers' system-state backup to the cabinet?
answers: Any server operator who is free
A Tier 0 custodian
The help desk
quizzes.explanation: A DC backup holds the directory's secrets. Whoever can handle it can rebuild or read the domain, so it stays with Tier 0.

quizzes.question: Why is there no network path to the offline backup cabinet?
answers: So ransomware or an intruder on the network cannot reach or encrypt the copies
Because backups are too large to send
Because NIST forbids network backups
quizzes.explanation: An offline copy survives an attack that takes the whole network. The custody record replaces the network path as the proof of what happened.

quizzes.question: The hash on the media does not match the hash on the volume. What do you do?
answers: Store it anyway and note it
Delete the original
Do not store it; recopy and investigate, because the copy is not trustworthy
quizzes.explanation: A mismatch means the copy is not the backup you verified. Storing it would put an untrusted copy where you will look on the worst day.

checklist: I assigned custodians by tier, so no one carries a backup from a tier they do not hold.
I recorded matching hashes on the volume and on the media for every copy, and logged each handoff in the custody register.
I retrieved one copy using only the register, verified its hash, and confirmed it is readable.

Hash, copy, and verify each backup on media
Record each handoff in the custody register
Retrieve and verify one copy as a test

lessons.title: Rehearse a real restore, in isolation
lessons.summary: One restore, actually performed: a domain controller's system state brought back on the isolated segment, timed against the objective, verified against the directory — plus the small restore everyone will someday need, from the Recycle Bin.
objectives: Restore a DC's system state in Directory Services Restore Mode on the isolated recovery segment.
Measure the restore against the time objective and verify directory health.
Perform and record an object-level Recycle Bin restore.
recap: One real restore, isolated, timed, verified, and torn down.
The measured number replaced the hoped-for one.
The everyday restore is proven alongside the dramatic one.
lessons.next: The final lesson files the recovery record and closes the Build path.

sections.body:

Earlier courses set up no backup jobs; this course defines and schedules every one. Also provide an offline backup cabinet with removable media and a custody register, and an isolated recovery network segment (or host) for the restore rehearsal.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The model's final chapter: a network that cannot come back was never really built. This course is the one place every backup in the network is defined and scheduled — the directory, both CAs, Group Policy, DHCP, the repository and analysis configuration, the VLAN 40 business services with their permissions, logins and certificates, the log record, and the living records — then proves one real restore in isolation and files the tested-recovery evidence the authorization path expects.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Stage the rehearsal: the isolated recovery segment has no path to the production VLANs — a restored controller believing it is authoritative must never meet the live directory; that isolation rule is written before the restore starts. Turn the hypervisor's time synchronization off on the rehearsal copy, as for every virtual machine in the path.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Restore SBD-DC02 from the offline copy retrieved in lesson 4, timing the work from decision to directory services running against the lesson 1 objective. A system state restore needs the same server instance, so use a copy of SBD-DC02's virtual machine attached only to the isolated segment, start it in DSRM (bcdedit /set safeboot dsrepair, restart, sign in with the DSRM password), and run wbadmin start systemstaterecovery with -authsysvol: the copy is the only controller in its isolated world, so its SYSVOL must be authoritative or SYSVOL and NETLOGON never come up. Restoring to different hardware needs a full server (bare-metal) recovery from the critical-volumes backup instead.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Remove the DSRM boot setting (bcdedit /deletevalue safeboot), restart normally, and verify the restored directory the course 1.1 way — services, the SYSVOL and NETLOGON shares, a directory query. Then check the clock: the copy comes back with the time it was saved with, and with no SBD-DC01 to follow nothing corrects it, so compare it with the reference and record the offset; a restored SBD-DC01 in production is checked against the reference before any member follows it (part 3). Record what the rehearsal taught — surprises, the measured time, decision-tree updates — then tear the rehearsal down completely.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Back in production, from AdminJumpBox01, run the everyday restore: delete a disposable test object, bring it back from the Recycle Bin with attributes intact, and file both rehearsals — the big one and the small one — as the tested-recovery evidence.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
# On the isolated copy of SBD-DC02: start in DSRM, then sign in with the DSRM password.
bcdedit /set safeboot dsrepair
shutdown /r /t 0
wbadmin get versions -backupTarget:F: -machine:SBD-DC02   # F: = the retrieved media
wbadmin start systemstaterecovery -version:<version-id> -backupTarget:F: -machine:SBD-DC02 -authsysvol
bcdedit /deletevalue safeboot   # then restart normally
# After the restart, on the restored copy
Get-Service NTDS, DNS, Netlogon, DFSR | Select-Object Name, Status
Get-SmbShare -Name SYSVOL, NETLOGON
Get-ADDomain -Server localhost | Select-Object DNSRoot, PDCEmulator
w32tm /query /status   # then compare Get-Date with the reference clock and record the offset
# Back in production, from AdminJumpBox01: the Recycle Bin rehearsal
Get-ADObject -Filter "Name -eq '<test object name>'" -IncludeDeletedObjects | Restore-ADObject

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: The isolated restore ran in DSRM and reached a healthy directory within (or honestly against) the time objective, its clock offset is recorded, the DSRM boot setting is removed, the teardown is confirmed, and the production object restore returned the test object intact.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep the timed rehearsal log with its verification output and clock reading, the lessons-learned and decision-tree updates, the teardown confirmation, and the object-restore record.

quizzes.question: Why must the rehearsal segment be isolated from production?
answers: To make the restore faster
A restored controller carries old directory state — meeting the live forest would inject the past into the present
Isolation is optional for labs
quizzes.explanation: The rehearsal's first rule protects production from the rehearsal. Old authoritative state on a live network is its own disaster.

quizzes.question: The restore took longer than the objective. What now?
answers: Hide the timing
Declare the objective met anyway
Record the honest number and either fix the process or revise the objective — both are legitimate; silence is not
quizzes.explanation: The rehearsal exists to replace belief with measurement. Either outcome — better process or truer objective — improves the real bad day.

quizzes.question: Why rehearse the Recycle Bin restore too?
answers: The most likely recovery event deserves the same tested-and-recorded treatment as the rare one
It is required before system state restores
Deleted objects expire daily
quizzes.explanation: Recovery evidence should match recovery reality: object-level loss is the common case, so its tool gets proven, not presumed.

quizzes.question: Your recovery host is new hardware. Which restore applies?
answers: A system state restore, exactly as on the original server
A full server (bare-metal) recovery from the critical-volumes backup — system state restores are for the same server instance
Copying NTDS.dit across by hand
quizzes.explanation: Microsoft's forest recovery guidance calls for a full server recovery when you restore to different hardware or a different operating system instance. A system state restore runs on the original instance, in DSRM.

checklist: I confirmed the recovery segment had no path to production before restoring the copy of SBD-DC02 in DSRM.
I timed the restore from decision to directory services running and recorded the honest number against the objective.
I removed the DSRM boot setting, verified the directory and recorded its clock offset, tore the rehearsal down, and restored a test object from the Recycle Bin.

Restore SBD-DC02’s system state in DSRM
Return to normal boot, verify, check the clock, tear down
Restore a test object from the Recycle Bin

lessons.title: File the recovery record and close the path
lessons.summary: The Build path ends the way it worked: owners, schedules, and evidence. The recovery record joins the living documents, the closing SCAP results snapshot the finished network, and the Body of Evidence is ready for the authorization courses to assemble.
objectives: Assemble the tested-recovery record with owners and review dates.
Take the closing SCAP snapshot across the finished network.
Hand the complete evidence set to the authorization path.
recap: Recovery has an owner, a date, and a measured track record.
The closing snapshot freezes the as-authorized picture.
The Body of Evidence exists — path 2 assembles, it doesn't excavate.
lessons.next: That completes the Build the Network path. Continue with course 2.1 to carry this network — and its evidence — through the Risk Management Framework to an authorization decision.

courses.title: RMF to ATO
courses.subtitle: Every RMF step: the lessons, the workspace and the templates
courses.description: Take the network the Build the Network courses (1.1–1.12) create, the system shown in the System Hub, through all seven steps of the Risk Management Framework (RMF) to an Authorization to Operate, following NIST SP 800-37 Revision 2 with the April 2016 Joint Special Access Program Implementation Guide (JSIG) mapped in. Each step pairs its lessons with the same task in the ATO Package Builder and its templates from the ATO Template Library: prepare and categorize the system, select and implement its controls, build the Body of Evidence, assess it and plan the fixes in a POA&M, assemble the package for a decision, and keep the authorization current.
