lessons.title: 01 · RMF roles, steps, and editions
lessons.summary: Explain who performs, assesses, and approves Risk Management Framework (RMF) work, and how NIST and the Joint Special Access Program Implementation Guide (JSIG) organize its steps and outputs.

sections.heading: Before the RMF steps
sections.body: NIST names roles by function (system owner, control assessor, common control provider, authorizing official); the JSIG uses SAP titles for the same work (ISO, SCA, CCP, AO) alongside the ISSM, ISSO, ISSE, and PSO. In both, only the AO accepts risk.

sections.heading: What this module produces
sections.body:
• A role map of who performs, assesses, and approves the work, in NIST and JSIG terms (the role assignments NIST covers in Task P-1)
• A record of the governing documents and editions: SP 800-37 Revision 2, the April 2016 JSIG or the successor your program directs, and the adopted SP 800-53 release
• The scope record, started with those roles and that governing direction

sections.heading: Where the JSIG and NIST differ
sections.body: The JSIG of 11 April 2016 follows SP 800-37 Revision 1’s six steps, starting at Categorize, with SP 800-53 Revision 4 and CNSSI 1253 (March 2014). Prepare is the NIST Revision 2 addition. DoDM 5205.07 refers to the JSIG or its successor.

sections.heading: Start with the mission, then ask about risk.
sections.body:
The Risk Management Framework (RMF) connects a system’s purpose to the safeguards, evidence, and decisions needed to operate it. Begin with what the organization needs the system to do. Then ask what could happen if its information is exposed, changed incorrectly, or unavailable.

Each step produces outputs the next one builds on, ending in an authorization package. An Authorization to Operate (ATO) is the authorizing official’s decision about the risk that remains; installing tools or finishing a checklist doesn’t make it.

sections.heading: Everyone contributes. The responsibilities differ.
sections.body:
NIST names roles by function: system owner, control assessor, common control provider, and authorizing official. The Joint Special Access Program (SAP) Implementation Guide (JSIG) uses SAP titles for that work: Information System Owner (ISO), Security Control Assessor (SCA), Common Control Provider (CCP), and Authorizing Official (AO).

An Information System Security Manager (ISSM) oversees the security program, an Information System Security Officer (ISSO) supports day-to-day implementation, and an Information System Security Engineer (ISSE) designs security in; SAP programs add a Program Security Officer (PSO). Local appointments set the exact split. Only the AO accepts risk.

sections.heading: Know which document, and which edition, you’re following.
sections.body:
NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-37 Revision 2 (December 2018) has seven steps: Prepare, Categorize, Select, Implement, Assess, Authorize, and Monitor. Each is a set of numbered tasks, such as P-11 for the authorization boundary, with expected outputs and responsible roles. SP 800-53 supplies the controls.

The JSIG of 11 April 2016 applies that foundation to SAP systems, with SP 800-53 Revision 4 and Committee on National Security Systems Instruction (CNSSI) 1253 of March 2014. It follows SP 800-37 Revision 1’s six steps, so it has no Prepare step; its tasks run from 1-1 to 6-7, and each step lists its outputs.

The public JSIG is this 2016 edition. Department of Defense Manual (DoDM) 5205.07 refers to the JSIG or its successor, so confirm what your program directs. This course follows the NIST steps, maps the JSIG tasks into each, and notes where the two differ.

sections.heading: From a claim to a decision
sections.body:
Claim: “Privileged account changes are logged and reviewed,” as the System Security Plan (SSP) states it for the practice system.

Evidence: The control owners supply the event-forwarding configuration, a sample account change from SBD-DC01, and the analyst’s review record in SBD-SPLUNK01.

Assessment: The assessor (SCA) tests the event and checks that the expected review happened.

Decision: The AO weighs the supported result and any remaining gap. Only the AO can accept the risk.

sections.heading: Build
sections.body: Start the scope record. Map who holds each role for the practice system (system owner or ISO, ISSM, ISSO, ISSE, SCA, CCP, AO, and a PSO if assigned) and mark who performs, assesses, and approves. Record the governing documents and editions, the adopted control release, and privacy responsibilities.

sections.heading: Prove
sections.body: Given a missing test result and an unresolved risk, identify who supplies the evidence, who assesses it, and who can accept the risk, in NIST and JSIG terms. Then explain why the 2016 JSIG has no Prepare step.

quizzes.question: Your program directs the public JSIG of 11 April 2016. Which statement fits it?
answers: It is built on SP 800-53 Revision 5 and begins with Prepare.
It replaces NIST, so SP 800-37 no longer applies.
It follows SP 800-37 Revision 1’s six steps, starting at Categorize, with SP 800-53 Revision 4 and CNSSI 1253.
quizzes.explanation: NIST is the foundation; the JSIG is SAP-specific direction for applying it. The 2016 edition predates the Revision 2 Prepare step and the Revision 5 controls, and your program may direct a successor.

lessons.title: 02 · Define and register the system
lessons.summary: Establish what is being authorized and why: the mission, stakeholders, assets, boundary, information and its life cycle, early risks, and requirements. Then register the system.

sections.heading: The RMF step · Prepare
sections.body: NIST gives the organization-level tasks (P-1 to P-7) to senior leaders and the risk executive function. At the system level, the mission or business owner and the system owner lead, the authorizing official determines the boundary (P-11), and the system owner registers the system (P-18). The 2016 JSIG has no Prepare step, so it assigns no roles here.

sections.heading: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2 tasks
sections.body:
P-1 · Risk management roles
P-2 · Risk management strategy
P-3 · Risk assessment—organization
P-4 · Organizationally-tailored baselines and Cybersecurity Framework Profiles (optional)
P-5 · Common control identification
P-6 · Impact-level prioritization (optional)
P-7 · Continuous monitoring strategy—organization
P-8 · Mission or business focus
P-9 · System stakeholders
P-10 · Asset identification
P-11 · Authorization boundary
P-12 · Information types
P-13 · Information life cycle
P-14 · Risk assessment—system
P-15 · Requirements definition
P-16 · Enterprise architecture
P-17 · Requirements allocation
P-18 · System registration

sections.heading: JSIG (11 April 2016) tasks
sections.body: The 2016 JSIG has no Prepare step.

sections.heading: What this module produces
sections.body:
• Mission and stakeholders, recorded in the scope record (P-8, P-9)
• An asset list and a documented authorization boundary, with dependencies and candidate common controls (P-10, P-11)
• Information types and their life cycle, including every boundary transfer (P-12, P-13)
• An early risk picture (P-14), carried into the draft Risk Assessment Report in module 04
• Requirements defined, placed in the architecture, and allocated to the system or its environment (P-15 to P-17)
• A registered system, recorded in the registration record (P-18)

sections.heading: Where the JSIG and NIST differ
sections.body: The 2016 JSIG has no Prepare step; it follows SP 800-37 Revision 1. It describes the system and its boundary (Task 1-2) and registers it (Task 1-3) in Categorize, and drafts its first Risk Assessment Report in Select. NIST does this work in Prepare (P-11, P-14, P-18).

sections.heading: Prepare starts above the system.
sections.body:
Prepare is the step NIST SP 800-37 Revision 2 added. Its organization-level tasks (P-1 to P-7) assign roles, set the risk strategy and tolerance, identify common controls systems can inherit, and set an organization-wide monitoring strategy. A system team works inside those decisions.

At the system level, start with the mission (P-8) and the stakeholders (P-9): what work the system supports, who depends on it, who owns its information, and what an interruption or misuse would affect.

sections.heading: Draw the boundary, then test the assumptions.
sections.body:
Identify the assets to protect (P-10), then the authorization boundary (P-11), which the authorizing official determines. It’s more than a subnet diagram: consider management interfaces, hosting, shared services, information flows, and dependencies.

List the information types the system processes, stores, and transmits (P-12), and follow each from creation to disposal (P-13). A component outside the boundary can still affect risk. Record the relationship and the responsible party; don’t use the boundary to make a hard dependency disappear.

sections.heading: Assess early, allocate the requirements, then register.
sections.body:
Assess system risk early (P-14): threats, weaknesses, and likely consequences, so the requirements can answer them. Then define the security and privacy requirements (P-15), place the system in the enterprise architecture (P-16), and allocate each requirement to the system or its environment (P-17).

Last, the system owner registers the system with the office the organization designates (P-18). The 2016 JSIG has no Prepare step, so it describes the system and its boundary and registers it in Categorize (Tasks 1-2, 1-3), and drafts its first Risk Assessment Report (RAR) in Select.

sections.heading: Resolve a boundary question
sections.body:
Question: Are the seven hypervisor hosts that run the enclave’s servers covered by this authorization?

Record: List SBD-HV01 to SBD-HV07, who administers them, and the systems each one runs, including the domain controllers and the issuing CA.

Resolve: They can control the domain controllers, so they are Tier 0 assets wherever the line falls. Propose inside or external with the reason, and route it to the authorizing official, who determines the boundary (P-11).

Prove: Keep the asset list, boundary diagram, scope record, and registration consistent with the decision.

sections.heading: Build
sections.body: Complete the scope record’s Prepare fields for the practice system: mission and stakeholders, assets and boundary, information types and life cycle, the early risk picture, and requirements and allocation. Check each information flow against the connection map in the System Hub, which shows every permitted, pending, and denied rule for a system. Then fill in the registration record.

sections.heading: Prove
sections.body: Explain whether a hypervisor host, the core switch’s management, a shared service, or an offline update transfer is inside the boundary, external, or inherited, with the supporting responsibility evidence. Say what changes in the registration if the boundary moves.

quizzes.question: Your program follows the 2016 JSIG, which has no Prepare step. Where does the boundary and registration work happen?
answers: In Categorize: describe the system and its boundary (Task 1-2), then register it (Task 1-3).
Nowhere. Without a Prepare step, the JSIG skips it.
In Monitor, once the system is operating.
quizzes.explanation: The JSIG follows SP 800-37 Revision 1, so work that NIST Revision 2 puts in Prepare (P-11, P-18) appears in the JSIG’s Categorize step.

lessons.title: 03 · Describe and categorize the system
lessons.summary: Describe the system, justify its confidentiality, integrity, and availability impacts in the draft System Security Plan (SSP), and route the categorization for approval. Treat privacy applicability as an explicit decision.

sections.heading: The RMF step · Categorize
sections.body: The system owner describes the system (C-1) and categorizes it with the information owner (C-2); the authorizing official or a designated representative approves the categorization (C-3). In the JSIG, the ISO categorizes with the ISSM/ISSO and ISSE (Task 1-1).

sections.heading: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2 tasks
sections.body:
C-1 · System description
C-2 · Security categorization
C-3 · Security categorization review and approval

sections.heading: JSIG (11 April 2016) tasks
sections.body:
1-1 · Categorize the system and document the results in the SSP
1-2 · Describe the system, including its boundary, and document it in the SSP
1-3 · Register the system with the appropriate SAP Service/Agency AO or designee

sections.heading: What this module produces
sections.body:
• A documented system description in the draft SSP (C-1; JSIG Task 1-2)
• Impact levels for each information type and security objective, with a written rationale (C-2)
• The system’s security categorization recorded in the draft SSP (C-2; JSIG Task 1-1)
• The categorization routed to the authorizing official or a designated representative for approval (C-3)
• The module 02 registration checked against the JSIG route (Task 1-3)

JSIG step outputs: Draft SSP; System registration

sections.heading: Where the JSIG and NIST differ
sections.body: NIST registers the system in Prepare (P-18) and describes it here (C-1). The JSIG describes the system and its boundary (Task 1-2) and registers it (Task 1-3) in this step.

sections.heading: Describe the system someone else will assess.
sections.body:
Categorize opens with a system description (C-1): what the system is for, what it contains, who uses it, what it connects to, and where its boundary lies, drawn from the Prepare records. The JSIG asks for the same in Task 1-2: describe the system, including its boundary, in the System Security Plan (SSP).

Write it so a reviewer who has never seen the system can follow it. Every later decision, from categorization to control selection, points back to this description.

sections.heading: Evaluate the consequences for each objective.
sections.body:
Confidentiality concerns inappropriate disclosure, integrity improper change, and availability reliable access when needed. For each information type, judge the impact of a loss on each objective, then set the system’s impact for each objective from those results (C-2), using the method that applies.

In the JSIG, the ISO categorizes the system with the ISSM or ISSO and the ISSE, and documents the results in the SSP (Task 1-1). Write a rationale someone else can review: the information, what’s affected, the consequence, and why each level fits. An isolated network alone doesn’t decide the result.

sections.heading: Apply the right authority, then get approval.
sections.body:
Federal systems categorize under Federal Information Processing Standard (FIPS) 199 with the information types in NIST SP 800-60; national security systems follow CNSSI 1253, and a SAP adds its program direction. Treat privacy applicability as an explicit decision.

NIST makes approval a task of its own (C-3): the authorizing official or a designated representative approves the categorization. In the JSIG, the categorization is documented in the draft SSP, and the whole plan is approved in Select (Task 2-4). This JSIG step also registers the system (Task 1-3), which NIST did in Prepare (P-18).

sections.heading: A new dependency reopens availability
sections.body:
Initial rationale: Engineering work can wait out a short outage of the internal web application, so the exercise input rates availability Low.

New information: A deadline-driven engineering process now depends on timely access to the application on SBD-WEB01 and its records in SBD-SQL01.

Review: Reevaluate the availability consequences for those information types under the applicable method (C-2).

Update: Record the new rationale in the draft SSP and the scope record’s categorization basis, route it for approval (C-3), and update the registration if the category changes.

sections.heading: Build
sections.body: Draft the SSP’s system description and security categorization from the scope record: information types, impact rationale, mission dependencies, privacy considerations, and approval routing. Justify the exercise planning input (Moderate confidentiality, Low integrity, Low availability); don’t copy it. Complete the scope record’s categorization basis and confirm the registration follows JSIG Task 1-3.

sections.heading: Prove
sections.body: Defend a changed availability impact after a new mission dependency, and explain why an air gap alone doesn’t establish a low impact level. Then say who approves the categorization in NIST terms and where the JSIG documents it.

quizzes.question: The system owner has categorized the system and wants to start selecting controls. What does NIST SP 800-37 Revision 2 call for first?
answers: Nothing more. The system owner’s categorization is final.
Review and approval of the categorization by the authorizing official or a designated representative (C-3).
A control assessment by the security control assessor.
quizzes.explanation: The system owner and information owner categorize (C-2); approval is a separate task (C-3). In the JSIG, the categorization is documented in the draft SSP (Task 1-1), and the plan is approved in Select (Task 2-4).

lessons.title: 04 · Select controls and plan monitoring
lessons.summary: Turn the approved categorization into a selected, tailored, and allocated control set, with a draft Risk Assessment Report and a continuous monitoring strategy, ready for plan review and approval.

sections.heading: The RMF step · Select
sections.body: The system owner and any common control provider select, tailor, and document the controls and the monitoring strategy (S-1, S-2, S-4, S-5); security architects and the system security officer allocate them (S-3); the authorizing official or a designee approves the plan (S-6). In the JSIG, the ISO does Tasks 2-1 to 2-3 with the ISSE and/or ISSM/ISSO; the AO, SCA, or AO designee approves (2-4).

sections.heading: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2 tasks
sections.body:
S-1 · Control selection
S-2 · Control tailoring
S-3 · Control allocation
S-4 · Documentation of planned control implementations
S-5 · Continuous monitoring strategy—system
S-6 · Plan review and approval

sections.heading: JSIG (11 April 2016) tasks
sections.body:
2-1 · Identify common controls and document them in a security plan
2-2 · Select the security controls for the information system and document the controls in the security plan
2-3 · Develop a strategy for continuous monitoring of security control effectiveness
2-4 · Review and approve the SSP

sections.heading: What this module produces
sections.body:
• Selected and tailored controls, with parameters and rationale, in the SCTM (S-1, S-2)
• Controls allocated to the system, its components, or a common control provider (S-3; JSIG Task 2-1)
• Planned implementations documented in the security plan and SCTM (S-4; JSIG Task 2-2)
• A draft Risk Assessment Report built from the early risk picture and the planned controls (JSIG Step 2 output)
• A system continuous monitoring strategy, including reporting and decommissioning (S-5; JSIG Task 2-3)
• The plan routed for review and approval (S-6; JSIG Task 2-4)

JSIG step outputs: Updated draft SSP/SCTM; Draft Risk Assessment Report (RAR); Documented Continuous Monitoring (ConMon) Plan/Strategy; Approved draft SSP/SCTM

sections.heading: Where the JSIG and NIST differ
sections.body: The JSIG produces a draft RAR in this step and updates it in Assess; NIST assesses system risk in Prepare (P-14) and analyzes and determines it in Authorize (R-2).

sections.heading: A catalog is not the same as a selected control set.
sections.body:
SP 800-53 is a catalog; a baseline is a starting set under a selection method, and overlays can change it. SP 800-53B holds the federal baselines; a national security system selects under CNSSI 1253 and its overlays, and a SAP adds the JSIG and approved program direction.

Select the controls (S-1), then tailor them (S-2): record why each is added, adjusted, or not applicable, resolve organization-defined parameters such as roles and frequencies, and note who approves. Difficulty alone doesn’t make a requirement not applicable.

sections.heading: Allocate the work before asking for evidence.
sections.body:
Allocate each control to the system, its components, or its environment (S-3), and name its owner: system-specific, common from a provider, or hybrid with shared responsibility. The JSIG begins Select here, with Task 2-1: identify the common controls and document them in a security plan.

Then document the planned implementations (S-4). The JSIG’s Task 2-2 selects the controls and documents them in the security plan. A Security Controls Traceability Matrix (SCTM) can record each control’s selection, parameters, allocation, and inheritance; its format follows local requirements.

sections.heading: Plan how you’ll know it still works, then get approval.
sections.body:
A system continuous monitoring strategy (S-5; JSIG Task 2-3) says which controls are monitored, how often, by whom, and what triggers action, within the organization’s strategy (P-7). The JSIG also drafts a Risk Assessment Report (RAR) here; NIST assessed system risk in Prepare (P-14).

Then the plan is reviewed and approved: by the authorizing official or a designated representative in NIST (S-6), or by the AO, SCA, or AO designee in the JSIG (Task 2-4). The JSIG calls the result the approved draft SSP/SCTM.

sections.heading: Credentialed scanning isn’t built yet
sections.body:
Proposal: “Mark RA-5 not applicable until a credentialed scanner exists.”

Question: Is the control inapplicable, or only hard to meet today? The network still runs software that needs vulnerability monitoring.

Decision: Keep RA-5 selected. Allocate what exists, SCAP Compliance Checker and Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG) results from the administration seats, and record credentialed scanning as a gap.

Record: The SCTM row shows the allocation and the gap, the draft RAR carries the risk, and the monitoring strategy reviews scan coverage.

sections.heading: Build
sections.body: Start the Security Controls Traceability Matrix (SCTM) with each selected control’s adopted revision, source, tailoring rationale, parameters, owner, and system-specific, common, or hybrid allocation. Draft the Risk Assessment Report (RAR) from the module 02 risk picture, write the continuous monitoring strategy, and route the plan for approval.

sections.heading: Prove
sections.body: Resolve a proposed not-applicable control and an inherited-control claim using evidence and the required approval path. Show which monitoring activity watches each draft RAR risk, and pin the control and assessment-procedure versions.

quizzes.question: A facility office says physical access to the server room is “covered.” What does the SCTM need before the plan goes for approval?
answers: Nothing more. Mark PE-3 inherited on the provider’s word.
Mark PE-3 not applicable, since the system team doesn’t run the building.
The provider, the parts it performs, its assessment information, and what the system team still does.
quizzes.explanation: An inherited or hybrid allocation needs an identified provider and applicable evidence. Record the split in the SCTM so the assessor knows what to ask of whom.

lessons.title: 05 · Implement and document the controls
lessons.summary: Implement the selected controls and record them as built in the System Security Plan (SSP) and Security Controls Traceability Matrix (SCTM), in statements an assessor can test.

sections.heading: The RMF step · Implement
sections.body: NIST gives I-1 and I-2 to the system owner and any common control provider, with engineers and security staff supporting. The Joint Special Access Program (SAP) Implementation Guide (JSIG) gives Tasks 3-1 and 3-2 to the Information System Owner (ISO), working with the Information System Security Engineer (ISSE).

sections.heading: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2 tasks
sections.body:
I-1 · Control implementation
I-2 · Update control implementation information

sections.heading: JSIG (11 April 2016) tasks
sections.body:
3-1 · Implement the security controls specified in the SSP
3-2 · Document the control implementation in the SCTM portion of the SSP

sections.heading: What this module produces
sections.body:
• The controls the Build the Network courses put in place, checked against the approved selection and parameter values (NIST I-1; JSIG 3-1)
• As-implemented SSP statements for each practice control: who, what, where, when, and which records (I-2)
• SCTM rows updated with implementation status and evidence references (JSIG 3-2, output “Updated SSP/SCTM”)
• Planned work and differences from the approved plan recorded, not presented as operating
• Supporting plans referenced by owner, version, and review status

JSIG step outputs: Updated SSP/SCTM

sections.heading: Where the JSIG and NIST differ
sections.body: The JSIG records the implementation in the SCTM portion of the SSP. NIST updates the security and privacy plans themselves, with as-implemented detail sufficient for an assessor to use.

sections.heading: Build what the approved plan describes.
sections.body:
Implement turns the approved plan into a working system. NIST Task I-1 implements the controls in the security and privacy plans; Task 3-1 of the Joint Special Access Program (SAP) Implementation Guide (JSIG) implements those specified in the System Security Plan (SSP).

The system owner is accountable, and engineers build to the approved selection, parameter values, and control revision. That revision matters: the public JSIG is the 11 April 2016 edition, built on SP 800-53 Revision 4 and CNSSI 1253, and a program may direct a successor or its own guidance.

sections.heading: Record the controls as they were built.
sections.body:
NIST Task I-2 updates the plans with the as-implemented state, in enough detail for an assessor to use. JSIG Task 3-2 records it in the Security Controls Traceability Matrix (SCTM) portion of the SSP. Both lead to the JSIG output “Updated SSP/SCTM.”

Write who performs each activity, what happens, where it applies, when it happens, and which records show it. “We comply with policy” leaves an assessor nothing to examine, interview, or test.

sections.heading: Keep planned work and supporting plans honest.
sections.body:
Describe what operates today, and mark planned work as planned. Where the build could not follow the plan, say so; the assessor will test each statement as written.

Configuration, access, incident response, contingency, and other supporting plans describe processes the SSP relies on. Reference each by owner, version, and review status instead of copying procedures that drift apart. A plan shows intent; records show the process happens.

sections.heading: Turn a vague statement into an as-implemented one
sections.body:
Before: “Audit records are reviewed according to policy.” It names no reviewer, sources, schedule, or record.

As built: Windows systems forward the selected events to SBD-SYSLOG01 by Windows Event Forwarding (F17), the Linux servers send syslog over TLS (F07), and the collector feeds SBD-SPLUNK01 (F10) and SBD-AUDIT01 (F11).

After: The assigned analyst reviews those events in SBD-SPLUNK01 on the approved schedule, records each exception and its follow-up, and keeps the review record.

Trace: Put the statement in the SSP and update the AU-6 row of the SCTM with its status and evidence identifiers, ready for the assessor.

sections.heading: Build
sections.body: Update the SSP that course 2.1 drafted with as-implemented statements for the practice controls (AU-2, AU-3, AU-6, AU-12): who performs each activity, what happens, where, when, and which records show it. Update the matching SCTM rows with implementation status and evidence references, and mark planned work as planned.

sections.heading: Prove
sections.body: Replace a vague “compliant with policy” statement with a specific as-implemented narrative. Reconcile it with the diagrams, inventory, and inheritance record, and show how you would record a difference between the build and the approved plan.

quizzes.question: The engineers built the log path differently from the approved plan. What does the Implement step call for?
answers: Leave the plan as approved and let the assessor find the difference.
Update the SSP and SCTM to the as-implemented state.
Change the system back, whatever the reason for the difference.
quizzes.explanation: NIST Task I-2 and JSIG Task 3-2 record the controls as actually implemented. The assessor tests that record, so it has to match the system.

lessons.title: 06 · Connect implementation to proof
lessons.summary: Collect technical and operational evidence of the as-built system, index it, and correct the SSP and SCTM wherever the evidence and the plan disagree.

sections.heading: The RMF step · Implement
sections.body: Engineers and administrators produce the records, and common control providers supply evidence for what the system inherits. The system owner (in the JSIG, the ISO with the ISSE) keeps the SSP and SCTM true to that evidence.

sections.heading: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2 tasks
sections.body:
I-1 · Control implementation
I-2 · Update control implementation information

sections.heading: JSIG (11 April 2016) tasks
sections.body:
3-1 · Implement the security controls specified in the SSP
3-2 · Document the control implementation in the SCTM portion of the SSP

sections.heading: What this module produces
sections.body:
• Configuration evidence with system, scope, version, and collection time: scan results, hardening checklists, exports (I-1)
• Operational records that show processes run, such as log reviews and a restore test
• A master evidence index giving each record an identifier, owner, date, scope, and version
• Coverage gaps and limitations recorded, including credentialed vulnerability scanning not yet available
• SSP and SCTM corrected to the as-built state (I-2; JSIG output “Updated SSP/SCTM”)

JSIG step outputs: Updated SSP/SCTM

sections.heading: Where the JSIG and NIST differ
sections.body: The JSIG calls the record an assessment rests on the Body of Evidence (BoE): the SSP, test plans, test procedures, test reports, and exceptions. NIST SP 800-37 treats the same material task by task: updated plans (I-2), assessment plans (A-2), assessment evidence (A-3), and assessment reports (A-4).

sections.heading: Capture the configuration and its context.
sections.body:
Evidence shows what Implement actually produced. A configuration export or Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG) checklist is useful when a reviewer can identify the system, setting, scope, version, and collection time. Keep the review record alongside it.

A passing automated check has a defined scope. Manual checks, applicability decisions, and technical limits still need attention.

sections.heading: Show that processes run, and how far the evidence reaches.
sections.body:
Logs, review records, tickets, access reviews, and restore tests support different claims. Connect each item to the question it can answer. Owning a security product does not show that a control is effective; its records might.

Check that every relevant system was included, the collection worked, and the data is current. Keep collection failures rather than silently excluding them, and say what an item cannot show: a backup job’s success message does not prove recovery.

sections.heading: Index the evidence, then let it correct the plan.
sections.body:
A master evidence index gives each record a stable identifier, title, scope, owner, collection date, version, and location, so nobody depends on a folder name or someone’s memory. One record can support several objectives, and one objective can need several records.

When the evidence shows the system differs from the SSP or SCTM, update them to the as-built state. That is still NIST Task I-2 and JSIG Task 3-2, and it means the assessor tests the real system.

sections.heading: A clean view with a coverage gap
sections.body:
Result: A Splunk search by host shows recent events from the domain controllers and member servers.

Inspection: The audit source inventory lists SBD-MGMT01, but none of its events reached SBD-SYSLOG01 in the collection period.

Conclusion: The evidence does not support complete source coverage, so the SSP’s AU-12 statement cannot claim it.

Follow-up: Record the gap in the evidence index and the SSP, and hand it to the assessor. Do not drop SBD-MGMT01 from the inventory to make the view look complete.

sections.heading: Build
sections.body: Collect configuration exports, reviewed STIG checklists, SCAP Compliance Checker results with their coverage, log review records, and the course 1.12 restore record, or equivalent supplied training records. Start the master evidence index, and correct the SSP and SCTM wherever the evidence shows the system differs from the plan.

sections.heading: Prove
sections.body: Explain what each item proves and leaves untested. Identify a scan that missed an in-scope host, an unreviewed alert, and a configuration screenshot that lacks system or time context. Record credentialed vulnerability scanning (RA-5) as a limitation: the practice network does not run it yet.

quizzes.question: A configuration scan reports no open findings, but one in-scope server is missing from its results. What does the scan support?
answers: A clean result for every in-scope server.
Nothing, so it should be deleted.
A clean result for the servers it covered; the missing server is a coverage gap to record and close.
quizzes.explanation: A result supports only the scope it covered. Keep it, record the gap, and collect the missing evidence before anyone relies on the result.

lessons.title: 07 · Prepare the assessment
lessons.summary: Select an independent assessor, hand over current evidence, and get a Security Assessment Plan approved before any testing starts.

sections.heading: The RMF step · Assess
sections.body: The Authorizing Official (AO) or a designated representative selects the assessor (A-1) and, in NIST, approves the plan the assessor develops (A-2). In the JSIG, the ISO develops the plan with the Information System Security Manager (ISSM), Information System Security Officer (ISSO), or ISSE, and the Security Control Assessor (SCA) reviews and approves it (4-1).

sections.heading: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2 tasks
sections.body:
A-1 · Assessor selection
A-2 · Assessment plan

sections.heading: JSIG (11 April 2016) tasks
sections.body: 4-1 · Develop, review, and approve a plan to assess the security controls

sections.heading: What this module produces
sections.body:
• An assessor or team selected by the AO or designated representative, with the independence required (NIST A-1)
• A record of the evidence handed over: SSP, SCTM, evidence index, and known exceptions, with versions
• A Security Assessment Plan with scope, objectives, methods, objects, procedures, sampling, schedule, and limits (A-2; JSIG 4-1)
• The plan’s review and approval, recorded before testing (JSIG output “Security Assessment Plan”)

JSIG step outputs: Security Assessment Plan

sections.heading: Where the JSIG and NIST differ
sections.body: Assessor selection is a separate task only in NIST (A-1). NIST has the assessor develop the plan for the AO’s approval; the JSIG has the ISO’s team develop it and the SCA approve it, and defines it as the SSP, the SCTM, and the Security Control Assessment Procedures.

sections.heading: Choose an assessor who can be trusted with the answer.
sections.body:
NIST Task A-1 opens Assess: the Authorizing Official (AO), or a designated representative, selects the assessor or team. In the JSIG, Step 4 starts with the plan, and the Security Control Assessor (SCA) is a defined role.

Choose for skill and independence. An impartial assessor does not assess their own work or advocate for the team that built it. The AO decides how much independence the system’s categorization and risk call for.

sections.heading: Hand over evidence the assessor can rely on.
sections.body:
The assessor starts from what Implement produced: the SSP, the SCTM, the evidence index, and the exceptions you already know about. Check that each record is current, and record the versions you hand over so the plan and results refer to the same material.

The JSIG describes this as the Body of Evidence (BoE): the SSP, test plans, test procedures, test reports, and exceptions. The system team supplies the plan and the exceptions; the assessment adds the rest.

sections.heading: Agree on the plan before anyone tests.
sections.body:
In NIST Task A-2, the assessor develops the plan from the implementation detail, and the AO or a designated representative approves it. In JSIG Task 4-1, the ISO develops it with the information system security manager, officer, or engineer, and the SCA reviews and approves it.

The JSIG’s Security Assessment Plan is made up of the SSP, the SCTM, and the Security Control Assessment Procedures. Either way, the plan states scope, objectives, methods, objects, coverage, responsibilities, schedule, and limits, with sampling decisions written down.

sections.heading: Plan the logging assessment
sections.body:
Assessor: The exercise AO’s designated representative selects a training assessor who did not build or operate the logging pipeline.

Evidence: The assessor receives the SSP and SCTM at their recorded versions, evidence index EI-001, and the known SBD-MGMT01 coverage gap.

Procedures: Examine the event configuration and source records, interview the analyst, test an approved account change on SBD-DC01, and replay the attack drill’s six attempts as negative tests.

Approval: Plan AP-001 is reviewed and approved before any testing: by the SCA in JSIG terms, or by the AO or a designated representative in NIST’s.

sections.heading: Build
sections.body: Record who selected the assessor and the independence they provide. List the evidence handed over, with versions and known exceptions. Draft a Security Assessment Plan for the practice logging objectives: scope, objectives, methods, objects, sampling rationale, the attack drill’s six attempts as negative tests, responsibilities, schedule, and limits. Record its review and approval.

sections.heading: Prove
sections.body: Check the handover before approval: find stale evidence, a missing record, and a mismatch between the SSP and an exported configuration, and record each gap’s effect on the plan. Explain why your assessor is independent enough for this system.

quizzes.question: The engineer who built the logging pipeline offers to assess it. What is the problem?
answers: An assessor should not assess their own work; the AO sets the independence required.
None, as long as the engineer follows the procedures.
Engineers cannot take part in an assessment at all.
quizzes.explanation: Independence keeps the result credible. The engineer still takes part, as someone the assessor interviews and observes.

lessons.title: 08 · Perform and report the assessment
lessons.summary: Assess the controls as planned, report supported findings in a Security Assessment Report (SAR), and remediate and reassess what can be fixed now.

sections.heading: The RMF step · Assess
sections.body: The control assessor performs the assessment and writes the report; in the JSIG that is the SCA or an AO designee, and the SCA submits the SAR with a recommended authorization decision. The system owner carries out initial remediation, and the assessor reassesses (A-5).

sections.heading: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2 tasks
sections.body:
A-3 · Control assessments
A-4 · Assessment reports
A-5 · Remediation actions

sections.heading: JSIG (11 April 2016) tasks
sections.body:
4-2 · Assess the security controls per the Security Assessment Plan
4-3 · Prepare the Security Assessment Report (SAR)
4-4 · Conduct initial remediation based on the SAR and reassess remediated controls

sections.heading: What this module produces
sections.body:
• Completed assessments with the observation and evidence for each objective (A-3; JSIG 4-2)
• A SAR with results, findings, limitations, and recommendations (A-4; JSIG output “SAR”)
• Initial remediation and reassessment, with original findings kept in the updated SAR (A-5; JSIG 4-4)
• The SSP updated where an implementation changed (A-5; JSIG output “Updated SSP”)
• The Risk Assessment Report (RAR) updated with the risk from confirmed weaknesses (JSIG output “Updated RAR”)

JSIG step outputs: SAR; Updated RAR; Updated SSP

sections.heading: Where the JSIG and NIST differ
sections.body: The JSIG updates the RAR here and has the SCA submit the SAR with a recommended authorization decision. NIST assesses system risk in Prepare (P-14) and analyzes and determines it in Authorize (R-2); its assessment report carries findings and recommendations for correcting deficiencies.

sections.heading: Run the approved procedures and record what you see.
sections.body:
NIST Task A-3 and JSIG Task 4-2 assess the controls the way the approved plan describes. Each assessment asks whether a control is implemented correctly, operating as intended, and producing the desired outcome.

Examine records and configurations, interview the people who run the process, and test behavior where the plan calls for it, including what should fail. Record the expected result, the observation, the evidence, and any limitation, using the adopted SP 800-53A procedures.

sections.heading: Report only what the evidence supports.
sections.body:
NIST Task A-4 and JSIG Task 4-3 produce the Security Assessment Report (SAR): what was assessed, the result for each objective, the findings and limitations, and recommendations for correcting deficiencies. An objective the evidence cannot support is “other than satisfied,” not a pass by default.

In the JSIG, the SCA submits the SAR with a recommended authorization decision. The recommendation informs the AO; it is not the decision.

sections.heading: Fix what you can, reassess it, and keep the record.
sections.body:
NIST Task A-5 and JSIG Task 4-4 cover initial remediation. Review each finding’s significance; the system owner corrects those that should be fixed now, and the assessor reassesses the changed controls. The SAR keeps the original finding beside the new result.

Then update what the results changed: the SSP for any implementation that moved and, in the JSIG, the Risk Assessment Report (RAR) drafted in Select. Whatever stays open goes to the Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M).

sections.heading: Assess the logging objectives
sections.body:
Test: Make an approved account change on SBD-DC01 and follow it through SBD-SYSLOG01 to SBD-SPLUNK01 and the analyst’s review. Replay the attack drill: all six attempts should be refused.

Observe: The event arrives and is reviewed (EV-003, EV-004), and every drill attempt is refused. SBD-MGMT01 has no verified events in the period, and one review exception has no recorded follow-up.

Report: SAR-001 records the results, FND-001 for SBD-MGMT01 coverage, and FND-002 for the missing follow-up, and cites the traffic matrix for the drill.

Remediate: The analyst records the follow-up, and the reassessment finds the AU-6 objective satisfied; FND-002 stays in the report as remediated. FND-001 needs a scheduled change, so it stays open for the POA&M.

sections.heading: Build
sections.body: Run the procedures in your approved plan and prepare a SAR excerpt. Include negative tests: run the six attempts in the System Hub attack drill, record each expected and observed result in the Operational verification column of the network traffic matrix, and cite the matrix in your SAR. Remediate one finding, reassess it, and update the SSP and the Risk Assessment Report (RAR) that course 2.1 drafted.

sections.heading: Prove
sections.body: Link each conclusion to its objective, evidence, observation, and limitation. Record unsupported objectives as other than satisfied rather than treating missing evidence as a pass, and show a remediated finding still in the report beside its reassessment.

quizzes.question: During the assessment, the team fixes a finding and the reassessment passes. What happens to the original finding in the SAR?
answers: It is deleted, since the control now works.
It stays, with the remediation and the reassessment result beside it.
It moves to the POA&M as an open item.
quizzes.explanation: Initial remediation (NIST A-5, JSIG 4-4) adds the reassessment to the report; it does not erase what the assessment found. Findings that remain open go to the POA&M.

lessons.title: 09 · Build the plan of action and milestones
lessons.summary: Turn the findings still open into a risk-ranked Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M) with accountable owners, resources, dated milestones, and closure criteria.

sections.heading: The RMF step · Assess
sections.body: NIST gives A-6 to the system owner and any common control provider. In the JSIG, the ISO initiates and updates the POA&M (5-1), and the AO uses it to monitor progress.

sections.heading: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2 tasks
sections.body: A-6 · Plan of action and milestones

sections.heading: JSIG (11 April 2016) tasks
sections.body: 5-1 · Initiate and update the POA&M from the SAR’s findings and recommendations

sections.heading: What this module produces
sections.body:
• A POA&M entry for each finding still open after initial remediation (A-6; JSIG output “POA&M”)
• Entries ranked by contextual risk, not technical severity alone
• An accountable owner, resources, milestones, and completion dates for each entry
• Closure criteria tied to reassessment, linked to the SAR finding and the RAR

JSIG step outputs: POA&M

sections.heading: Where the JSIG and NIST differ
sections.body: NIST prepares the POA&M at the end of Assess (A-6); the JSIG initiates it as the first task of Authorize (5-1). Both build it from the assessment report’s findings and recommendations.

sections.heading: Rank what is still open by risk.
sections.body:
Findings that survive initial remediation go into the Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M). NIST Task A-6 prepares it from the assessment report’s findings and recommendations; JSIG Task 5-1 initiates it the same way, as the first task of Authorize.

Rank the entries by risk in the system’s context: threat, exposure, mission consequence, existing safeguards, and remaining uncertainty. Technical severity informs the order, but it is not the complete risk determination.

sections.heading: Write an action someone can manage.
sections.body:
Each entry names the weakness, affected scope, accountable owner, planned actions, resources, milestones with completion dates, dependencies, and closure criteria. In the JSIG, the ISO keeps it updated with corrective actions, resources, milestone completion dates, and residual findings.

“Fix soon” is not a milestone. A useful milestone describes a verifiable action with a target date and a clearly accountable owner.

sections.heading: Track each entry to verified closure.
sections.body:
The AO reviews the POA&M and uses it to monitor progress. Close an entry only when a reassessment verifies the fix, and keep the original finding and dates when plans change.

A POA&M is a management record; it does not accept risk or grant permission to operate. Tracking a weakness and accepting its risk are different actions, and only the AO accepts risk.

sections.heading: Turn the open logging finding into a POA&M entry
sections.body:
Finding: FND-001: SBD-MGMT01 is not in verified audit collection. It remained open after initial remediation because the fix needs a scheduled change.

Risk: Privileged activity on a management server could go unreviewed. Weigh the local records that remain, then set the entry’s contextual risk and rank.

Milestones: Confirm the forwarding configuration, test a selected event end to end, and verify the analyst’s review covers SBD-MGMT01, each with an owner and a date.

Closure: Close PM-001 only after reassessment, then update the SSP, evidence index, RAR, and SAR. FND-002 was fixed during the assessment and needs no entry.

sections.heading: Build
sections.body: Rank the findings still open after initial remediation and write a POA&M entry for each: the weakness, affected assets and controls, owner, resources, milestones with target dates, status, and closure criteria tied to reassessment. Link each entry to its SAR finding and the RAR.

sections.heading: Prove
sections.body: Prioritize two findings with different exposure and mission impact, and defend the order. Explain why a finding fixed and reassessed during the assessment needs no entry, and why an open entry cannot close without a verified reassessment.

quizzes.question: Does adding a finding to the POA&M mean its risk has been accepted?
answers: Yes, automatically.
Only if the entry has a due date.
No. Only the AO accepts risk, as part of the authorization decision.
quizzes.explanation: The POA&M plans and tracks corrective action. Accepting the remaining risk is a separate decision that belongs to the AO.

lessons.title: 10 · Assemble the authorization package
lessons.summary: Assemble an authorization package whose plans, assessment results, and open risks agree, and submit it for the authorizing official’s decision.

sections.heading: The RMF step · Authorize
sections.body: The system owner (in the JSIG, the Information System Owner, ISO) assembles and submits the package; a common control provider does the same for the controls it provides. The Authorizing Official (AO) receives it and may direct additional evidence.

sections.heading: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2 tasks
sections.body: R-1 · Authorization package

sections.heading: JSIG (11 April 2016) tasks
sections.body: 5-2 · Assemble and submit the security authorization package to the AO

sections.heading: What this module produces
sections.body:
• An authorization package assembled and submitted to the AO (NIST R-1; JSIG output: Security Authorization Package)
• An executive summary of the system, the assessment results, and the remaining risk (NIST R-1)
• A versioned package manifest naming each component, its basis, owner, and review check
• A consistency review that reconciles scope, inventory, findings, and open actions across the SSP, SCTM, RAR, SAR, and POA&M

JSIG step outputs: Security Authorization Package

sections.heading: Where the JSIG and NIST differ
sections.body: The JSIG’s minimum package is the SSP (with the SCTM, continuous monitoring strategy, and RAR), the SAR, and the POA&M, plus any evidence the AO directs. NIST R-1 adds an executive summary and treats privacy plans and privacy assessment reports alongside the security ones.

sections.heading: Assemble what the decision needs.
sections.body:
In NIST SP 800-37 Revision 2, Task R-1, the system owner assembles the authorization package and submits it to the Authorizing Official (AO). It holds an executive summary, the security and privacy plans, the assessment reports, and the Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M).

The Joint Special Access Program (SAP) Implementation Guide (JSIG) applies that NIST foundation to SAP systems; its public edition, 11 April 2016, is built on SP 800-53 Revision 4. Its Task 5-2 sets a minimum: the System Security Plan (SSP), with its Security Controls Traceability Matrix (SCTM), continuous monitoring strategy, and Risk Assessment Report (RAR); the Security Assessment Report (SAR); and the POA&M. The AO can direct more.

sections.heading: Check that the documents agree.
sections.body:
Compare the boundary, inventory, selected controls, implementation statements, findings, and open actions across the SSP, SCTM, RAR, SAR, and POA&M. Resolve identifiers, status, dates, and scope that disagree.

Follow the risk as well: each significant SAR finding should reach the RAR, the POA&M or a proposed acceptance, and the executive summary. A package can be complete as a collection of files and still be unreliable.

sections.heading: Submit through the approved workflow.
sections.body:
Follow the authority’s system of record, required reviews, signatures, and submission steps. Whatever tool the authority uses, the records still need the same substance.

Submitting hands the package to the AO; it decides nothing. This course uses a generic record workflow, and no live government submission is part of the training.

sections.heading: A package consistency review
sections.body:
SSP: Describes 21 named systems, two of them planned and not yet built (SBD-NESSUS01, SBD-EPO01), and 50 Windows workstations.

SAR: Reports testing on the network for 18 named systems and the workstation sample.

Reconcile: Nothing claims the planned servers’ controls. SBD-ROOTCA01 is never on the network, so it is assessed during its key ceremonies: a stated limitation, not a missing test.

Record: Note each explanation in the manifest’s review checks and the executive summary before submitting.

sections.heading: Build
sections.body: Assemble the practice system’s package: an executive summary, the SSP with its SCTM, continuous monitoring strategy, and RAR, the SAR, the POA&M, and a privacy applicability record. List each in a versioned manifest with its basis (JSIG 5-2 or NIST R-1), owner, and review check.

sections.heading: Prove
sections.body: Reconcile control identifiers, asset counts, findings, dates, and status across the SSP, SCTM, RAR, SAR, and POA&M, and explain each difference you keep. Walk the package through a generic submission workflow using training data.

quizzes.question: Your authority follows the JSIG. What must the authorization package contain at a minimum?
answers: The executive summary only; the AO requests the rest.
The SSP and the latest scan report.
The SSP (with its SCTM, continuous monitoring strategy, and RAR), the SAR, and the POA&M, plus any evidence the AO directs.
quizzes.explanation: That is the JSIG Task 5-2 minimum. NIST Task R-1 adds an executive summary and puts privacy plans and assessment reports alongside the security ones.

lessons.title: 11 · Support the authorization decision
lessons.summary: Brief the risk the authorizing official must determine, propose a response to each significant risk, and record what an authorization decision contains.

sections.heading: The RMF step · Authorize
sections.body: The AO, helped by a designated representative for everything but the decision itself, determines the risk and chooses the response; making and signing the decision stays with the AO. The system owner (JSIG: ISO) and the Security Control Assessor (SCA) brief the risk and answer questions.

sections.heading: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2 tasks
sections.body:
R-2 · Risk analysis and determination
R-3 · Risk response
R-4 · Authorization decision
R-5 · Authorization reporting

sections.heading: JSIG (11 April 2016) tasks
sections.body:
5-3 · Determine the risk
5-4 · Determine whether the risk is acceptable (the authorization decision)

sections.heading: What this module produces
sections.body:
• A risk determination for operating the system, informed by the package and risk assessments (NIST R-2; JSIG 5-3)
• A response to each significant risk: mitigation tracked in the POA&M or set as conditions, acceptance, or avoidance (NIST R-3)
• An authorization decision document: ATO, IATT, or DATO, with terms and conditions and a duration (NIST R-4; JSIG 5-4)
• A report of the decision and any significant control deficiencies to the officials who oversee risk (NIST R-5)
• An executive risk summary and AO briefing that support the decision without making it

JSIG step outputs: Authorization decision document

sections.heading: Where the JSIG and NIST differ
sections.body: The JSIG’s decisions are ATO, IATT, and DATO; NIST names authorization to operate, authorization to use, common control authorization, or a denial. NIST also makes risk response (R-3) and authorization reporting (R-5) tasks of their own; the JSIG covers the AO’s work in Tasks 5-3 and 5-4.

sections.heading: Support the AO’s risk determination.
sections.body:
In NIST Task R-2, the AO analyzes the package and determines the risk of operating the system. In JSIG Task 5-3, risk assessments, formal or informal, inform the AO’s final determination.

Your briefing supports that analysis: the mission, the assessed posture, significant findings and their consequences, limitations, and the recommendation the Security Control Assessor (SCA) made with the SAR. A request for more evidence is part of the process, not a setback.

sections.heading: Choose a response for each significant risk.
sections.body:
In NIST Task R-3, the AO chooses a response to the risk determined. Planned mitigation is tracked in the POA&M, and conditions on operation go into the decision. Accepted deficiencies stay documented in the assessment report and are watched for change. Avoiding a risk can mean limiting the operation.

A POA&M entry tracks work; it doesn’t accept risk. JSIG Task 5-4 puts the explicit acceptance of risk with the AO, who decides whether the risk to organizational operations and assets, individuals, other organizations, or national security is acceptable.

sections.heading: Record the decision so people can act on it.
sections.body:
The authorization decision document records the decision, its terms and conditions, and its duration. JSIG decisions are an Authorization to Operate (ATO), an Interim Authorization to Test (IATT), for testing rather than operation, or a Denied Authorization to Operate (DATO). NIST Task R-4 names authorization to operate or to use, common control authorization, or a denial.

Duration is time-driven or ongoing, backed by robust continuous monitoring. Only the AO makes and signs the decision. NIST Task R-5 then reports it, with any significant control deficiencies, to the officials who oversee risk.

sections.heading: From an open finding to a decision record
sections.body:
Determine: FND-001: SBD-MGMT01 is missing from verified audit collection, so privileged activity there could go unseen in Splunk review.

Respond: Mitigate through PM-001, and propose an interim condition: the Information System Security Officer (ISSO) reviews SBD-MGMT01’s local Security log and records each review.

Decide: The reviewer, acting as AO, records an exercise decision: the type, terms and conditions tied to PM-001, and a duration.

Report: Monitoring reports PM-001’s milestones and the interim reviews. A course score is not an ATO.

sections.heading: Build
sections.body: Write the executive risk summary and a five-minute AO briefing for the practice system. Then complete a fictional decision record: the decision type, terms and conditions, duration, and what monitoring must report.

sections.heading: Prove
sections.body: Defend one unresolved finding and answer a request for more evidence. Propose a response (mitigate, accept, or avoid), and explain why the decision belongs to the AO and why a complete package or a passing score doesn’t produce an ATO.

quizzes.question: The AO will allow operation while an open finding is fixed. What must the decision document record?
answers: The decision, the terms and conditions tied to that finding, and the duration.
Only the POA&M due dates.
Nothing more: the open POA&M entry already accepts the risk.
quizzes.explanation: The decision document carries the decision, its terms and conditions, and its duration. A POA&M tracks corrective work; accepting the risk is the AO’s decision.

lessons.title: 12 · Monitor and maintain authorization
lessons.summary: Keep the authorization true as the system changes: analyze each change, assess and report as the strategy requires, support ongoing authorization, and plan disposal.

sections.heading: The RMF step · Monitor
sections.body: The system owner (JSIG: ISO), with the Information System Security Manager (ISSM) and the ISSO, analyzes changes, remediates, updates the package, reports status, and carries out disposal. The control assessor (JSIG: SCA) runs the ongoing assessments. The AO, or in the JSIG a designee, reviews the status and decides whether the risk is still acceptable.

sections.heading: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2 tasks
sections.body:
M-1 · System and environment changes
M-2 · Ongoing assessments
M-3 · Ongoing risk response
M-4 · Authorization package updates
M-5 · Security and privacy reporting
M-6 · Ongoing authorization
M-7 · System disposal

sections.heading: JSIG (11 April 2016) tasks
sections.body:
6-1 · Determine the security impact of proposed or actual changes
6-2 · Assess a selected subset of controls under the AO-approved monitoring strategy
6-3 · Conduct remediation actions from monitoring, risk assessment, and open POA&M items
6-4 · Update the SSP, SAR, and POA&M
6-5 · Report the security status
6-6 · Review the reported status: is the risk still acceptable?
6-7 · Implement a decommissioning strategy

sections.heading: What this module produces
sections.body:
• A security impact analysis for each proposed or actual change (NIST M-1; JSIG 6-1)
• Ongoing assessment results under the approved monitoring strategy (NIST M-2; JSIG 6-2)
• Remediation and an updated SSP, SAR, and POA&M that keep the original information (NIST M-3, M-4; JSIG 6-3, 6-4)
• Security status reports to the AO, event-driven, time-driven, or both (NIST M-5; JSIG 6-5)
• An ongoing authorization review, with the authorization updated as appropriate (NIST M-6; JSIG 6-6)
• A decommissioning strategy carried out when the system is retired (NIST M-7; JSIG 6-7)

JSIG step outputs: Periodic ConMon deliverables; Updated SSP, SAR, POA&M; Updated Security Authorization, as appropriate

sections.heading: Where the JSIG and NIST differ
sections.body: The steps match task for task. The JSIG is more specific: a security impact analysis that notifies the SCA, updates that keep the original information for oversight and audit, and a decommissioning strategy that includes a decommission letter. NIST reports security and privacy posture together.

sections.heading: Analyze a change before it changes the risk.
sections.body:
NIST Task M-1 watches the system and its environment for changes that affect its security and privacy posture. JSIG Task 6-1 makes that a security impact analysis (SIA): determine the impact of a proposed or actual change, notify the SCA, and revise the package as required.

A new component, information flow, dependency, control provider, or threat can undercut the assessment the decision relied on. The size of a technical change doesn’t tell you the size of its consequence.

sections.heading: Assess, respond, update, and report.
sections.body:
The continuous monitoring (ConMon) strategy the AO approved sets which controls are assessed, how often, and by whom; JSIG Task 6-2 assesses a selected subset (NIST M-2). Continuous doesn’t mean testing every control constantly.

Results feed remediation and risk response (M-3, 6-3) and updates to the SSP, SAR, and POA&M that keep the original information needed for oversight and audit (M-4, 6-4). The system owner reports status to the AO, event-driven, time-driven, or both (M-5, 6-5).

sections.heading: Keep the decision current until the system retires.
sections.body:
In NIST Task M-6 and JSIG Task 6-6, the AO (or, in the JSIG, a designee) reviews the reported status to decide whether the risk is still acceptable. If not, the AO decides what follows: new conditions, reassessment, or a new decision.

Disposal closes the loop (M-7, 6-7). The JSIG’s decommissioning strategy covers media sanitization, a records retention plan the AO approves, inventory updates, notifications, a review of inherited relationships, and a decommission letter.

sections.heading: A change goes through security impact analysis
sections.body:
Change: A second licensed application is proposed for SBD-APPS01, adding its vendor licensing port to rule F12 for the VLAN 80 workstations.

Impact: New software and a changed flow: configuration (CM-6, a SCAP Compliance Checker rescan), the vendor’s update path (SI-2), its events (AU-2, AU-12), and the course 1.12 recovery set (CP-9).

Decide: Notify the SCA, reassess before go-live, and give the SIA to the AO or designee, who decides whether it fits the current authorization.

Update: Update the inventory, SSP, SCTM, rule register, and evidence index, report the change in the next status report, and keep the prior versions.

sections.heading: Build
sections.body: Run one cycle of the continuous monitoring strategy course 2.1 drafted: the controls assessed, owners, evidence, reporting dates, and escalation triggers. Write a security impact analysis for one proposed change and a status report for the AO.

sections.heading: Prove
sections.body: Process a new licensed application on SBD-APPS01 (rule F12), a missed update in one of SBD-WSUS01’s rings, and a changed common control such as the server room’s badge access: what is reassessed, which records change, what the status report says, and when the AO is engaged. Then list the disposal steps if SBD-WEB01’s service were retired, including what depends on it.

quizzes.question: A proposed change adds a port to a documented information flow. What comes first?
answers: Make the change; the current authorization covers future services.
A security impact analysis: identify the affected controls and records, notify the SCA, and follow the required review.
Nothing until the next reauthorization.
quizzes.explanation: NIST Task M-1 and JSIG Task 6-1 evaluate a change against the assessed and authorized scope before it quietly changes the risk.
